Q1CUET 2026 · 24 May, Shift 1 · Q1NTA final key
Water movement from soil into plant roots and subsequently into upper portion of the plant is partly due to phenomenon of
  1. Edema
  2. Osmosis
  3. Reverse Osmosis
  4. Evaporation
Concept to recallOsmosis: solvent flows through a semipermeable membrane from the dilute side to the concentrated side.
  1. Root-cell sap holds sugars and salts, so it is more concentrated than soil water.
  2. Water therefore enters the root hairs through their membranes by osmosis and passes on up the plant.
  3. Edema is swelling of animal tissue; reverse osmosis needs an applied pressure; evaporation is loss from leaves.

Answer: option (2) — Osmosis

TrapTranspiration (evaporation) helps pull water up, but the entry from soil into roots is osmosis, as NCERT says.
Q2CUET 2026 · 24 May, Shift 1 · Q4NTA final key
Which of the following salts would have the same value of the van’t Hoff factor as that of Al(NO3)3 in aqueous solution? Assume complete dissociation of electrolytes.
(A) K2SO4 (B) KCl (C) Al2(SO4)3 (D) K3[Fe(CN)6]
  1. (A) and (B) only
  2. (B) and (C) only
  3. (D) only
  4. (C) and (D) only
Concept to recallFor complete dissociation, i = number of ions per formula unit; a complex ion counts as one ion.
  1. Al(NO3)3 → Al3+ + 3NO3−: i = 4.
  2. K2SO4: 3; KCl: 2; Al2(SO4)3: 5.
  3. K3[Fe(CN)6] → 3K+ + [Fe(CN)6]3−: 4. Only (D) matches.

Answer: option (3) — (D) only

Trap[Fe(CN)6]3− does not split into CN− ions; counting 10 ions is the slip.
Q3CUET 2026 · 24 May, Shift 1 · Q5NTA final key
Which of the following statements are true for the elevation of boiling point?
(A) The boiling point of a solution is always higher than the boiling point of the pure solvent in which the solution is prepared.
(B) The boiling point of a solution is always lower than the boiling point of the pure solvent in which the solution is prepared.
(C) The elevation of boiling point is directly proportional to the molal concentration of the solute in solution.
(D) Unit of Kb = K kg mol−1
  1. (A), (B) and (D) only
  2. (B), (C) and (D) only
  3. (A), (B), (C) and (D)
  4. (A), (C) and (D) only
Concept to recallΔTb = Kbm (non-volatile solute); Kb = ΔTb/m has unit K kg mol−1.
  1. A non-volatile solute lowers the vapour pressure, so the solution must be heated more to boil: (A) true, (B) false.
  2. ΔTb ∝ m: (C) true.
  3. Kb = K ÷ (mol kg−1) = K kg mol−1: (D) true.

Answer: option (4) — (A), (C) and (D) only

Q4CUET 2026 · 24 May, Shift 1 · Q6NTA final key
Match List-I with List-II
List-IList-II
(A) Osmotic pressure(I) Formation of bubbles of nitrogen in the blood
(B) Anoxia(II) Pressure applied on the solution side that just stops the flow of solvent
(C) Bends(III) Impermeable to impurities
(D) Cellulose acetate(IV) Low blood oxygen causes climbers to become weak
  1. (A)–(I), (B)–(II), (C)–(III), (D)–(IV)
  2. (A)–(II), (B)–(I), (C)–(IV), (D)–(III)
  3. (A)–(II), (B)–(IV), (C)–(I), (D)–(III)
  4. (A)–(III), (B)–(IV), (C)–(I), (D)–(II)
Concept to recallHenry’s law applications (NCERT): bends = N2 bubbles in blood on fast ascent of a diver; anoxia = low O2 at altitude. Reverse osmosis membranes (cellulose acetate) pass water, not impurities.
  1. Osmotic pressure is the excess pressure on the solution that just stops osmosis: (A)–(II).
  2. Anoxia: climbers at altitude get too little O2: (B)–(IV).
  3. Bends: dissolved N2 forms bubbles in blood: (C)–(I).
  4. Cellulose acetate membrane in RO is impermeable to impurities and ions: (D)–(III).

Answer: option (3) — (A)–(II), (B)–(IV), (C)–(I), (D)–(III)

Q5CUET 2026 · 24 May, Shift 1 · Q7NTA final key
Match List-I with List-II
Type of solutionExample
(A) Ideal solution(I) 95% by volume of ethanol
(B) Positive deviation from Raoult’s law(II) Bromoethane and chloroethane
(C) Negative deviation from Raoult’s law(III) Ethanol and acetone
(D) Azeotrope(IV) Phenol and aniline
  1. (A)–(II), (B)–(IV), (C)–(III), (D)–(I)
  2. (A)–(II), (B)–(III), (C)–(IV), (D)–(I)
  3. (A)–(I), (B)–(III), (C)–(II), (D)–(IV)
  4. (A)–(III), (B)–(IV), (C)–(I), (D)–(II)
Concept to recallIdeal: similar molecules (C2H5Br/C2H5Cl). Positive deviation: A–B weaker (ethanol + acetone breaks H-bonds). Negative: A–B stronger (phenol + aniline H-bond). 95% ethanol by volume is a minimum-boiling azeotrope.
  1. (A) bromoethane/chloroethane are alike: ideal → (II).
  2. (B) acetone breaks ethanol’s H-bonds → (III).
  3. (C) phenol–aniline O–H···N bonding → (IV).
  4. (D) 95% ethanol cannot be concentrated further by distillation → (I).

Answer: option (2) — (A)–(II), (B)–(III), (C)–(IV), (D)–(I)

Q6CUET 2026 · 6 June, Shift 1 · Q41NTA final key
Passage (summarised): Concept of solution (6 June 2026, Q41–45)

The concentration of a solution can be stated in several ways: molality, molarity, mole fraction, ppm, mass per cent and so on. Liquid–liquid solutions are ideal or non-ideal according to Raoult’s law. If the two components are A and B, the pure liquids have A–A and B–B attractions and the mixture also has A–B attractions; when the A–B forces are nearly equal to the A–A and B–B forces an ideal solution forms. Properties that depend only on the number of solute particles relative to the total number of particles, not on their nature, are colligative properties.

What would be the molality of 1.5 g of ethanoic acid (CH3COOH) in 75 g of benzene?
  1. 0.55 mol kg−1
  2. 0.33 mol kg−1
  3. 0.44 mol kg−1
  4. 0.22 mol kg−1
Concept to recallm = moles of solute / mass of solvent in kg.
  1. M(CH3COOH) = 60 g mol−1: n = 1.5/60 = 0.025 mol.
  2. m = 0.025/0.075 = 0.333 mol kg−1.

Answer: option (2) — 0.33 mol kg−1

Q7CUET 2026 · 6 June, Shift 1 · Q42NTA final key
Passage (summarised): Concept of solution (6 June 2026, Q41–45)

The concentration of a solution can be stated in several ways: molality, molarity, mole fraction, ppm, mass per cent and so on. Liquid–liquid solutions are ideal or non-ideal according to Raoult’s law. If the two components are A and B, the pure liquids have A–A and B–B attractions and the mixture also has A–B attractions; when the A–B forces are nearly equal to the A–A and B–B forces an ideal solution forms. Properties that depend only on the number of solute particles relative to the total number of particles, not on their nature, are colligative properties.

Which one of the following is not correct for an ideal solution?
  1. It must obey Raoult’s law.
  2. ΔmixH = 0
  3. ΔmixV = 0
  4. ΔmixH ≠ 0, and ΔmixV = 0
Concept to recallIdeal solution: obeys Raoult’s law at all compositions, ΔmixH = 0 and ΔmixV = 0.
  1. ΔmixH ≠ 0 contradicts ideality, so the last statement is not correct.

Answer: option (4) — ΔmixH ≠ 0, and ΔmixV = 0

Q8CUET 2026 · 6 June, Shift 1 · Q43NTA final key
Passage (summarised): Concept of solution (6 June 2026, Q41–45)

The concentration of a solution can be stated in several ways: molality, molarity, mole fraction, ppm, mass per cent and so on. Liquid–liquid solutions are ideal or non-ideal according to Raoult’s law. If the two components are A and B, the pure liquids have A–A and B–B attractions and the mixture also has A–B attractions; when the A–B forces are nearly equal to the A–A and B–B forces an ideal solution forms. Properties that depend only on the number of solute particles relative to the total number of particles, not on their nature, are colligative properties.

The vapour pressure of pure benzene at 25°C is 0.950 bar. When a 0.5 g non-volatile, non-electrolyte solute is added to 39.0 g of benzene (molar mass 78 g mol−1), then the vapour pressure of solution becomes 0.945 bar. What is the molar mass of the solute?
  1. 170 g mol−1
  2. 190 g mol−1
  3. 210 g mol−1
  4. 180 g mol−1
Concept to recallRelative lowering: (p° − p)/p° = x2 ≈ n2/n1 = (w2M1)/(M2w1) for a dilute solution.
  1. (0.950 − 0.945)/0.950 = 0.00526.
  2. n1 = 39/78 = 0.5 mol; so 0.00526 = (0.5/M2)/0.5 = 1/M2.
  3. M2 = 190 g mol−1 (the exact mole-fraction form gives 189).

Answer: option (2) — 190 g mol−1

Q9CUET 2026 · 6 June, Shift 1 · Q44NTA final key
Passage (summarised): Concept of solution (6 June 2026, Q41–45)

The concentration of a solution can be stated in several ways: molality, molarity, mole fraction, ppm, mass per cent and so on. Liquid–liquid solutions are ideal or non-ideal according to Raoult’s law. If the two components are A and B, the pure liquids have A–A and B–B attractions and the mixture also has A–B attractions; when the A–B forces are nearly equal to the A–A and B–B forces an ideal solution forms. Properties that depend only on the number of solute particles relative to the total number of particles, not on their nature, are colligative properties.

The solution of acetone in ethanol:
  1. shows positive deviation from Raoult’s law.
  2. shows negative deviation from Raoult’s law.
  3. obeys Raoult’s law.
  4. shows both negative and positive deviation from Raoult’s law.
Concept to recallPositive deviation when A–B attractions are weaker than A–A and B–B: vapour pressure higher than Raoult predicts.
  1. Acetone molecules get between ethanol molecules and break some of their hydrogen bonds.
  2. Weaker overall attraction: positive deviation.

Answer: option (1) — shows positive deviation from Raoult’s law.

Q10CUET 2026 · 6 June, Shift 1 · Q45NTA final key
Passage (summarised): Concept of solution (6 June 2026, Q41–45)

The concentration of a solution can be stated in several ways: molality, molarity, mole fraction, ppm, mass per cent and so on. Liquid–liquid solutions are ideal or non-ideal according to Raoult’s law. If the two components are A and B, the pure liquids have A–A and B–B attractions and the mixture also has A–B attractions; when the A–B forces are nearly equal to the A–A and B–B forces an ideal solution forms. Properties that depend only on the number of solute particles relative to the total number of particles, not on their nature, are colligative properties.

Which of the following concentration term is temperature dependent?
  1. Molality
  2. Mole fraction
  3. Molarity
  4. ppm
Concept to recallTerms built only on masses or moles (molality, mole fraction, mass %, ppm by mass) do not change with T; molarity uses volume, which expands with T.
  1. Molarity = mol per litre of solution; volume changes with temperature, so molarity does.

Answer: option (3) — Molarity

Q11CUET 2026 · 11 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q1 also 2026 29 May S1 Q7 (memory-based, collegedunia)key re-derived
When blood cells are placed in 1% (w/v) NaCl aqueous solution:
  1. Cell will burst
  2. Cell will shrink
  3. Cell will swell
  4. Cell remains as such
Concept to recall0.9% (w/v) NaCl is isotonic with blood. A more concentrated outside solution is hypertonic: water leaves the cell by osmosis (plasmolysis / crenation).
  1. 1% NaCl is more concentrated than 0.9% NaCl, so it is hypertonic to the cell.
  2. Solvent flows from lower to higher solute concentration: water moves out of the cell.
  3. The cell shrinks.

Answer: option (2) — Cell will shrink

TrapSwelling and bursting happen in a hypotonic solution (less than 0.9%), e.g. pure water.
Q12CUET 2026 · 11 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q6key re-derived
At the state of dynamic equilibrium, for solute + solvent ⇌ solution,
  1. Rate of dissolution = Rate of unsaturation.
  2. Rate of dissolution = Rate of crystallization
  3. Rate of dissolution = Rate of saturation
  4. Rate of crystallization = Rate of saturation.
Concept to recallA saturated solution is a dynamic equilibrium: solute dissolves and crystallises at equal rates.
  1. Forward process: dissolution. Reverse process: crystallisation.
  2. At equilibrium the two rates are equal, so the concentration stays constant.

Answer: option (2) — Rate of dissolution = Rate of crystallization

Trap“Saturation” is a state, not a process; it has no rate.
Q13CUET 2026 · 18 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q1key re-derived
The Henry’s law constant (KH) values for four gases W, X, Y, and Z in water at 298 K are 4.0 × 104, 2.5 × 10−2, 1.5 × 103, and 8.0 × 101 bar, respectively. What is the correct order of their solubility in water under the same partial pressure?
  1. W > Y > Z > X
  2. X > Z > Y > W
  3. X > Y > Z > W
  4. W > Z > Y > X
Concept to recallHenry’s law p = KH x: at a fixed partial pressure x = p/KH, so the larger KH, the less soluble the gas.
  1. Order of KH: X (0.025) < Z (80) < Y (1500) < W (40 000).
  2. Solubility runs the other way: X > Z > Y > W.

Answer: option (2) — X > Z > Y > W

TrapHigher KH means lower solubility; option (4) is the KH order itself.
Q14CUET 2026 · 18 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q3key re-derived
Why do aquatic species, such as fish, generally feel more comfortable in cold water than in warm water?
  1. The solubility of oxygen gas increases as the temperature of the water decreases.
  2. The solubility of oxygen gas decreases as the temperature of the water decreases.
  3. The Henry’s law constant (KH) for oxygen decreases as temperature increases.
  4. Warm water contains more dissolved toxic gases that harm aquatic metabolism.
Concept to recallDissolving a gas is exothermic, so gas solubility falls as temperature rises (KH rises with T).
  1. KH for O2 increases with temperature, so x(O2) = p/KH falls in warm water.
  2. Cold water holds more dissolved oxygen: (1).

Answer: option (1) — The solubility of oxygen gas increases as the temperature of the water decreases.

Trap(3) has the direction of KH reversed: KH increases with temperature.
Q15CUET 2026 · 18 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q6key re-derived
Ethylene glycol (ethane-1,2-diol) is widely added to car radiators as an antifreeze agent. How does its addition protect the engine in extreme climates?
  1. It raises the freezing point of water and lowers its boiling point.
  2. It lowers the freezing point of water and raises its boiling point.
  3. It lowers both the freezing point and the boiling point of water equally.
  4. It reacts chemically with the metal radiator walls to reduce thermal expansion.
Concept to recallA non-volatile solute lowers the vapour pressure: boiling point rises (ΔTb = Kbm) and freezing point falls (ΔTf = Kfm).
  1. Glycol is practically non-volatile and dissolves freely in water.
  2. Both colligative effects act together: freezing point down (winter), boiling point up (summer).

Answer: option (2) — It lowers the freezing point of water and raises its boiling point.

TrapA solute never raises the freezing point.
Q16CUET 2026 · 22 May, Shift 2 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q1key re-derived
Which of the following liquid mixtures forms an ideal solution that strictly obeys Raoult’s Law across the entire concentration range at a constant temperature?
  1. Ethanol + Acetone
  2. Chloroform + Acetone
  3. n-Hexane + n-Heptane
  4. Water + Nitric acid
Concept to recallIdeal solution: A–B interactions equal to A–A and B–B, so ΔHmix = 0 and ΔVmix = 0 (e.g. n-hexane/n-heptane, benzene/toluene).
  1. Ethanol + acetone: positive deviation (H-bonds broken).
  2. Chloroform + acetone and water + HNO3: negative deviation (new H-bonds).
  3. Hexane + heptane: near-identical non-polar molecules: ideal.

Answer: option (3) — n-Hexane + n-Heptane

TrapChloroform–acetone is the textbook negative deviation.
Q17CUET 2026 · 26 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q1worked here
Given below are two statements :
Given: Molar masses of C, H, O, Cl are 12, 1, 16 and 35.5 g mol−1 respectively.
Statement I: In 30% (w/w) solution of methanol in CCl4 (at T K), the mole fraction of CCl4 is equal to 0.33.
Statement II: Mixture of methanol and CCl4 shows positive deviation from Raoult’s law.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the option given below :
  1. Both Statement I and Statement II are true
  2. Both Statement I and Statement II are false
  3. Statement I is true but Statement II is false
  4. Statement I is false but Statement II is true
Concept to recallxB = nB/(nA + nB). Mixing an H-bonded liquid with a non-polar one breaks H-bonds: positive deviation.
  1. 100 g solution: 30 g CH3OH (30/32 = 0.9375 mol) + 70 g CCl4 (70/154 = 0.4545 mol).
  2. x(CCl4) = 0.4545/1.392 = 0.327 ≈ 0.33: Statement I is true.
  3. Methanol–CCl4 interactions are weaker than methanol’s own H-bonds: positive deviation. Statement II is true.

Answer: option (1) — Both Statement I and Statement II are true

Trap0.33 is the mole fraction of CCl4, not of methanol (0.67).
NoteThe site prints option (4) as its key, but its own working gets x(CCl4) = 0.326 ≈ 0.33 and calls Statement I true. Our derivation agrees with that working: both statements are true.
Q18CUET 2026 · 29 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q8key re-derived
Which of the following solutions is isotonic with human blood?
  1. 0.1% NaCl solution
  2. 0.5% NaCl solution
  3. 0.9% NaCl solution
  4. 2% NaCl solution
Concept to recallNormal saline, 0.9% (m/V) NaCl, has the same osmotic pressure as blood plasma.
  1. Isotonic: equal osmotic pressure, no net flow of water.
  2. NCERT: 0.9% NaCl is isotonic with blood (lower is hypotonic, higher hypertonic).

Answer: option (3) — 0.9% NaCl solution

Trap2% NaCl would shrink red cells; 0.1% would burst them.
Q19CUET 2025 · 13 May, Shift 1 · Q1NTA final key
The value of van’t Hoff factor, i, for CH3COOH solution in water will be
  1. Between 1 and 2
  2. Less than 1
  3. 2
  4. 1
Concept to recalli = (particles actually present)/(formula units dissolved). Full dissociation into n ions gives i = n; partial dissociation gives 1 < i < n; association gives i < 1.
  1. In water acetic acid is a weak acid: CH3COOH ⇌ CH3COO− + H+, only slightly ionised.
  2. With degree of dissociation α, i = 1 + α (n = 2), and 0 < α < 1.
  3. So 1 < i < 2.

Answer: option (1) — Between 1 and 2

Trap“Less than 1” is the value in benzene, where acetic acid dimerises through hydrogen bonds. Read the solvent.
Q20CUET 2025 · 13 May, Shift 1 · Q2NTA final key
The following solutions were prepared by dissolving 1 g of solute in 1 L of the solution. Arrange the following solutions in decreasing order of their molarity
  1. (A) Glucose (molar mass = 180 g mol−1)
  2. (B) NaOH (molar mass = 40 g mol−1)
  3. (C) NaCl (molar mass = 58.5 g mol−1)
  4. (D) KCl (molar mass = 74.5 g mol−1)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (A), (D), (C), (B)
  2. (A), (B), (D), (C)
  3. (B), (C), (D), (A)
  4. (D), (C), (A), (B)
Concept to recallMolarity = (mass/M)/V. At equal mass in equal volume, molarity ∝ 1/(molar mass).
  1. Same 1 g in the same 1 L, so the smallest molar mass gives the most moles.
  2. Molar masses: NaOH 40 < NaCl 58.5 < KCl 74.5 < glucose 180.
  3. Decreasing molarity: NaOH > NaCl > KCl > glucose, i.e. (B), (C), (D), (A).

Answer: option (3) — (B), (C), (D), (A)

TrapOption (1) is the increasing order; molarity runs opposite to molar mass.
Q21CUET 2025 · 13 May, Shift 1 · Q3NTA final key
Match List-I with List-II
List-I (Solutions)List-II (Explanation)
(A) Saturated solution(I) Solution having two components.
(B) Isotonic solutions(II) A solution whose osmotic pressure is more than that of another.
(C) Binary solution(III) A solution which contains the maximum amount of solute that can be dissolved in a given amount of solvent at a given temperature.
(D) Hypertonic solution(IV) The solutions having same osmotic pressure at a given temperature.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (A) – (I), (B) – (II), (C) – (III), (D) – (IV)
  2. (A) – (I), (B) – (III), (C) – (II), (D) – (IV)
  3. (A) – (I), (B) – (II), (C) – (IV), (D) – (III)
  4. (A) – (III), (B) – (IV), (C) – (I), (D) – (II)
Concept to recallSaturated: no more solute dissolves at that T. Isotonic: equal π. Hypertonic: higher π than the other solution. Binary: two components.
  1. Saturated → maximum solute at that temperature (III).
  2. Isotonic → same osmotic pressure (IV).
  3. Binary → two components (I).
  4. Hypertonic → osmotic pressure more than the other (II).

Answer: option (4) — (A) – (III), (B) – (IV), (C) – (I), (D) – (II)

Q22CUET 2025 · 13 May, Shift 1 · Q4NTA final key
Give the reason for low concentration of oxygen in the blood and tissues of people living at high altitude
  1. Both low temperature and high atmospheric pressure
  2. low temperature
  3. Low atmospheric pressure
  4. High atmospheric pressure
Concept to recallHenry’s law: p = KH x. The solubility of a gas is proportional to its partial pressure above the liquid.
  1. At high altitude the atmospheric pressure, and with it the partial pressure of O2, is low.
  2. By Henry’s law less O2 dissolves in blood: the condition called anoxia.

Answer: option (3) — Low atmospheric pressure

TrapLow temperature would increase gas solubility, so it cannot explain a shortage.
Q23CUET 2025 · 13 May, Shift 1 · Q5NTA final key
Calculate the molality of KI if the density of 20% (mass/mass) aqueous solution of KI is 1.202 g mL−1.
(Molar mass of KI is 166 g mol−1)
  1. 1.5 mol kg−1
  2. 1.2 mol kg−1
  3. 15 mol kg−1
  4. 0.12 mol kg−1
Concept to recallMolality m = moles of solute / kg of solvent. A mass-% figure gives it directly; density is needed only for molarity.
  1. Take 100 g of solution: 20 g KI and 80 g = 0.080 kg water.
  2. Moles of KI = 20/166 = 0.1205 mol.
  3. m = 0.1205/0.080 = 1.51 ≈ 1.5 mol kg−1.

Answer: option (1) — 1.5 mol kg−1

TrapThe density (1.202 g mL−1) is a distractor here; it is needed for molarity (1.45 M).
Q24CUET 2025 · 21 May, Shift 2 · Q1 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here
What is the mass percentage of NaCl in the solution if 1.75g of NaCl is dissolved in 5.85g of water.
  1. 23.02
  2. 29.9
  3. 23.98
  4. 25.00
Concept to recallMass % = mass of solute / mass of solution × 100.
  1. Mass of solution = 1.75 + 5.85 = 7.60 g.
  2. Mass % = 1.75/7.60 × 100 = 23.03 ≈ 23.02.

Answer: option (1) — 23.02

Trap29.9 divides by the mass of water (1.75/5.85) instead of the solution.
Q25CUET 2025 · 21 May, Shift 2 · Q20 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here
Which of the following statements are correct?
  1. (A) A solution which obeys Raoult’s law strictly is called an ideal solution.
  2. (B) A solution which shows deviations from Raoult’s law is called a real solution.
  3. (C) If Tb is the boiling point of the solvent and T is the boiling point of the solution, then the difference in boiling points (ΔTb = Tb − T) is called elevation of boiling point.
  4. (D) The elevation of boiling point is related to the lowering of vapor pressure.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (A), (B) and (D) only
  2. (A), (B) and (C) only
  3. (A), (B), (C) and (D)
  4. (B), (C) and (D) only
Concept to recallΔTb = Tb − Tb0 (solution minus pure solvent) = Kb m; it arises because the solute lowers the vapour pressure.
  1. (A) is the definition of an ideal solution; (B) non-ideal solutions are the real ones: true.
  2. (C) puts the subtraction the wrong way round: the solution boils higher, so ΔTb = T − Tb, not Tb − T (which would be negative).
  3. (D) is true: lower vapour pressure means a higher temperature is needed to reach 1 atm.

Answer: option (1) — (A), (B) and (D) only

Q26CUET 2025 · 21 May, Shift 2 · Q32 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here
Which of the following is not true with reference to evaporation of liquid?
  1. The liquids having low inter-molecular forces evaporate faster.
  2. The higher the temperature, the higher is the rate of evaporation.
  3. Larger the surface area, larger is the rate of evaporation.
  4. The evaporation rate follows the order of Water > Alcohol > Ether.
Concept to recallVolatility rises as intermolecular attraction falls: ether (no H-bonding) > alcohol > water (extensive H-bonding).
  1. Statements 1–3 are the standard factors.
  2. Water evaporates slowest, ether fastest: the order in 4 is reversed, so 4 is not true.

Answer: option (4) — The evaporation rate follows the order of Water > Alcohol > Ether.

NoteNot in the CUET 2026 syllabus. Evaporation is Class XI (states of matter); filed here with vapour pressure.

Q28CUET 2025 · 21 May, Shift 2 · Q37 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here
Colligative properties are applicable to:
  1. dilute solution
  2. solid solutions
  3. concentrated solutions
  4. only aqueous solution
Concept to recallColligative relations (Δp/p0 = x2, ΔT = Km, π = CRT) assume dilute, ideal behaviour.
  1. The formulae are derived for dilute solutions, where the solution is nearly ideal.
  2. They are not restricted to water as solvent.

Answer: option (1) — dilute solution

Q29CUET 2025 · 23 May, Shift 2 · Q13 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here
Which of the following statements, with reference to a solution, are correct?
  1. (A) The osmotic pressure of the solution is proportional to the molarity of the solute.
  2. (B) The elevation of the boiling point (ΔTb) is directly proportional to the molal concentration of the solute in a solution.
  3. (C) The unit of Kb is K kg−1 mol−1.
  4. (D) ΔTb = Tb0 − Tb.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (A), (B) and (C) only
  2. (A) and (B) only
  3. (C) and (D) only
  4. (B), (C) and (D) only
Concept to recallπ = CRT (C = molarity); ΔTb = Kb m (molality); Kb in K kg mol−1; ΔTb = Tb − Tb0.
  1. (A) and (B) are the two laws as stated: true.
  2. (C) is wrong: Kb = ΔTb/m has units K/(mol kg−1) = K kg mol−1.
  3. (D) is reversed: the solution boils higher, so ΔTb = Tb − Tb0.

Answer: option (2) — (A) and (B) only

TrapThe kg goes in the numerator: molality is mol kg−1, and Kb divides by it.

The relative lowering of vapor pressure is equal to the
  1. mole fraction of solute
  2. boiling point of solvent
  3. mole fraction of solvent
  4. Vapor pressure of solute
Concept to recallRaoult’s law for a non-volatile solute: (p10 − p1)/p10 = x2.
  1. The relative lowering equals the mole fraction of the solute, x2.

Q31CUET 2025 · 23 May, Shift 2 · Q31 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here
If the solubility of the given gases in water decreases in the order of formaldehyde, methane, vinyl chloride, argon.
Match List-I with List-II.
List-I (Gas)List-II
(A) Formaldehyde(I) 40.3
(B) Vinyl Chloride(II) 0.413
(C) Argon(III) 1.83 × 10−5
(D) Methane(IV) 0.611
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (A) – (I), (B) – (II), (C) – (III), (D) – (IV)
  2. (A) – (I), (B) – (III), (C) – (II), (D) – (IV)
  3. (A) – (I), (B) – (II), (C) – (IV), (D) – (III)
  4. (A) – (III), (B) – (IV), (C) – (I), (D) – (II)
Concept to recallList-II are Henry’s constants KH (kbar, NCERT Table 1.2). p = KH x: the larger KH, the lower the solubility.
  1. Most soluble, formaldehyde, has the smallest KH: 1.83 × 10−5 (III).
  2. Least soluble, argon, has the largest: 40.3 (I).

Q33CUET 2025 · 23 May, Shift 2 · Q39 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here
50 g of ethylene glycol (C2H6O2) is mixed with 900 g of water. The freezing point of the solution will be (Kf of water = 1.86 K kg mol−1)
  1. 271.49 K
  2. 270.15 K
  3. 269.52 K
  4. 273.15 K
Concept to recallΔTf = Kf m; Tf = 273.15 K − ΔTf.

  2. Normality of gas in solution
  3. Volume of gas in solution
  4. Molality of gas in solution
Concept to recallHenry’s law: p = KH x, where x is the mole fraction of the gas in the solution.
  1. The NCERT statement of the law uses mole fraction: p = KHx.

Answer: option (1) — Mole fraction of gas in solution

Q35CUET 2025 · 24 May, Shift 2 · Q31 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here
Which of the following does not come under the category of colligative properties?
  1. Relative lowering of vapor pressure
  2. Osmotic pressure of solution
  3. Depression in Freezing point of the solvent
  4. Depression in Freezing point of the solute
Concept to recallThe four colligative properties depend only on the number of solute particles: relative lowering of vapour pressure, elevation of boiling point, depression of freezing point of the solvent, osmotic pressure.
  1. It is the solvent whose freezing point falls; a “depression in freezing point of the solute” is not a colligative property.

Answer: option (4) — Depression in Freezing point of the solute

Q36CUET 2025 · 24 May, Shift 2 · Q38 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here
The osmotic pressure of a solution at 0°C is 2 atm. What will be its osmotic pressure at 819 K ?
  1. 6 atm
  2. 2 atm
  3. 4 atm
  4. 3 atm
Concept to recallπ = CRT: at fixed concentration π ∝ T (kelvin).
  1. 0°C = 273 K; 819 K = 3 × 273 K.
  2. π = 2 × 3 = 6 atm.

Answer: option (1) — 6 atm

TrapForgetting to convert 0°C to 273 K makes the ratio meaningless.
Q37CUET 2025 · 24 May, Shift 2 · Q7 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here
Solubility of a gas in a liquid:
  1. Decreases with rise in temperature
  2. Increases with rise in temperature
  3. Does not depend on temperature
  4. First decreases and then increases with rise in the temperature
Concept to recallDissolution of a gas is exothermic (gas → dissolved, like condensation), so by Le Chatelier a rise in temperature lowers the solubility; KH rises with temperature.
  1. Gas + liquid ⇌ solution, ΔH < 0.
  2. Heating shifts the equilibrium back: less gas dissolves.
  3. Hence aquatic life is more comfortable in cold water.

Answer: option (1) — Decreases with rise in temperature

TrapSolubility of most solids rises with temperature; gases behave the other way.

Q39CUET 2025 · 26 May, Shift 2 · Q19 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here
Vapour pressures of chloroform (CHCl3) and dichloromethane (CH2Cl2) at 298 K are 200 mmHg and 415 mmHg, respectively. Calculate the vapor pressure of the solution prepared by mixing 0.2 mol of CHCl3 and 0.5 mol of CH2Cl2 at 298 K
  1. 360.5 mmHg
  2. 353.57 mmHg
  3. 878.57 mmHg
  4. 307.5 mmHg
Concept to recallRaoult’s law for two volatile liquids: p = x1p1° + x2p2°.

Q40CUET 2025 · 26 May, Shift 2 · Q25 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here
The reverse osmosis occurs when
  1. Pressure on solution side is larger than osmotic pressure
  2. Pressure on solution side is smaller than osmotic pressure
  3. Pressure on solution side is equal to osmotic pressure
  4. Pressure on solution side is equal to atmospheric pressure
Concept to recallApplying a pressure larger than the osmotic pressure on the solution side drives solvent out of the solution through the semipermeable membrane: reverse osmosis (desalination).
  1. Equal pressure stops osmosis; a larger pressure reverses it.

Answer: option (1) — Pressure on solution side is larger than osmotic pressure

Q42CUET 2025 · 26 May, Shift 2 · Q36 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here

  1. 0.083 mm Hg

Q46CUET 2025 · 27 May, Shift 2 · Q21 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here
A solution containing 10 g/dm3 of urea (NH2CONH2) is isotonic with a 10% solution of a non-volatile solute. The molecular mass of the solute is:
  1. 300 g mol−1
  2. 600 g mol−1
  3. 150 g mol−1
  4. 100 g mol−1
Concept to recallIsotonic solutions have equal osmotic pressure, so equal molar concentration (non-electrolytes): w1/M1V = w2/M2V.
  1. Urea: 10 g L−1 / 60 = 1/6 mol L−1.
  2. 10% (w/v) solution: 10 g per 100 mL = 100 g L−1.
  3. 100/M = 1/6 → M = 600 g mol−1.

Answer: option (2) — 600 g mol−1

TrapEquating 10 g/L with 10 g/100 mL directly gives 60; the units differ by 10.
NoteOption numbers run into the values in the re-typeset (“1.300”, “2.600” ...); read as 300, 600, 150, 100 g mol−1. “10\%” is a LaTeX slip for 10%.
Q47CUET 2025 · 27 May, Shift 2 · Q27 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here
The vapour pressure of pure water at 25°C is 23.75 mmHg. The vapour pressure of the solution obtained by dissolving 34.2 g of sucrose (C12H22O11) in 100 g of water will be:
  1. 23.33 mmHg
  2. 24.00 mmHg
  3. 22.50 mmHg
  4. 23.75 mmHg
Concept to recallRaoult: p = xsolventp° (non-volatile solute).
  1. n(sucrose) = 34.2/342 = 0.1 mol; n(water) = 100/18 = 5.556 mol.
  2. x(water) = 5.556/5.656 = 0.9823.
  3. p = 0.9823 × 23.75 = 23.33 mmHg.

Answer: option (1) — 23.33 mmHg

Q48CUET 2025 · 27 May, Shift 2 · Q40 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here
The degree of dissociation (α) of a weak electrolyte AxBy is related to the van’t Hoff factor (i) by the expression:
  1. α = (i − 1)(x + y − 1)
  2. α = (i − 1)(x + y + 1)
  3. α = (x + y − 1)(i − 1)
  4. α = (x + y + 1)(i − 1)
Concept to recallAxBy → xA + yB: n = x + y ions; i = 1 − α + nα = 1 + (n − 1)α.
  1. i = 1 + (x + y − 1)α.
  2. α = (i − 1)/(x + y − 1).

Answer: option (1) — α = (i − 1)(x + y − 1)

Q49CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Sets A–D · Set A Q2NTA final key
Arrange the following in decreasing order of number of molecules contained in:
  1. (A) 16 g of O2
  2. (B) 16 g of CO2
  3. (C) 16 g of CO
  4. (D) 16 g of H2
Choose the correct order from the options given below:
  1. (A), (B), (C), (D)
  2. (D), (C), (A), (B)
  3. (B), (A), (D), (C)
  4. (C), (B), (D), (A)
Concept to recallNumber of molecules = (mass/M) × NA: for equal masses, the smaller the molar mass, the more molecules.
  1. M: H2 2 < CO 28 < O2 32 < CO2 44.
  2. Molecules decrease: H2 > CO > O2 > CO2 = D, C, A, B.

Answer: option (2) — (D), (C), (A), (B)

Q50CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Sets A–D · Set A Q3NTA final key
A molecule X associates in a given solvent as per the following equation:
X ⇌ (X)n
For a given concentration of X, the van’t Hoff factor was found to be 0.80 and the fraction of associated molecules was 0.3. The correct value of ‘n’ is:
  1. 2
  2. 3
  3. 1
  4. 5
Concept to recallAssociation nX ⇌ Xn with degree α: particles = 1 − α + α/n, so i = 1 − α(1 − 1/n).
  1. 0.80 = 1 − 0.3(1 − 1/n) ⇒ 1 − 1/n = 0.2/0.3 = 2/3.
  2. 1/n = 1/3 ⇒ n = 3.

Answer: option (2) — 3

Q51CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Sets A–D · Set A Q42NTA final key
Camphor in nitrogen gas is a type of solution
  1. Gas – Gas
  2. Solid – Gas
  3. Liquid – Gas
  4. Solid – Liquid
Concept to recallTypes of solution are named by the solute’s state and the solvent’s state. NCERT: camphor in nitrogen gas is a solid (solute) in gas (solvent).
  1. Camphor is a solid; nitrogen is the gaseous solvent: solid in gas.

Answer: option (2) — Solid – Gas

Q52CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Sets A–D · Set A Q44NTA final key
Consider the following statements regarding osmotic pressure:
  1. (A) Molar mass of a protein can be determined using osmotic pressure method.
  2. (B) The osmotic pressure is proportional to the molarity.
  3. (C) Reverse osmosis occurs when a pressure larger than osmotic pressure is applied to the concentrated solution side.
  4. (D) Edema occurs due to retention of water in tissue cells as a result of osmosis.
Choose the correct statements with reference to osmotic pressure:
  1. (A), (B) and (D) only
  2. (A), (B) and (C) only
  3. (A), (B), (C) and (D)
  4. (B), (C) and (D) only
Concept to recallπ = CRT (∝ molarity); measurable at room temperature and large even for dilute solutions, so it suits macromolecules; pressure above π on the solution side drives reverse osmosis; water retention by osmosis causes edema (NCERT).
  1. All four statements are NCERT facts.

Answer: option (3) — (A), (B), (C) and (D)

Q53CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Sets A–D · Set A Q45NTA final key
Vapour pressures of pure liquids ‘A’ and ‘D’ at 50°C are 500 mm Hg and 800 mm Hg respectively. The binary solution of ‘A’ and ‘D’ boils at 50°C and 700 mm Hg pressure. The mole percentage of ‘D’ in the solution is:
  1. 33.33 mole percent
  2. 66.67 mole percent
  3. 25.75 mole percent
  4. 75.25 mole percent
Concept to recallA liquid boils when its total vapour pressure equals the external pressure; Raoult: p = p°AxA + p°DxD.
  1. 700 = 500(1 − xD) + 800xD = 500 + 300xD.
  2. xD = 200/300 = 0.6667 ⇒ 66.67 mole percent.

Answer: option (2) — 66.67 mole percent

Q54CUET 2024 · 29 May (pen & paper, 306 E New) · Book A · Q22NTA final key
Arrange the following in increasing order of their osmotic pressure generation at 298 K :

  2. (B) If a cell containing 0.25 moles of solute dissolved in 1 L of water is immersed in pure water.
  3. (C) If a cell containing 0.1 moles of solute dissolved in 0.01 L of water is immersed in pure water.
  4. (D) If a cell containing 0.2 moles of solute dissolved in 0.05 L of water is immersed in pure water.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

  2. (D) < (A) < (B) < (C)
  3. (B) < (A) < (D) < (C)
  4. (C) < (A) < (B) < (D)
Concept to recallπ = CRT: at fixed T the osmotic pressure is proportional to the concentration n/V.
  1. C: (A) 0.5/1 = 0.5 M; (B) 0.25/1 = 0.25 M; (C) 0.1/0.01 = 10 M; (D) 0.2/0.05 = 4 M.
  2. Increasing: (B) 0.25 < (A) 0.5 < (D) 4 < (C) 10.

Answer: option (3) — (B) < (A) < (D) < (C)

Q55CUET 2024 · 29 May (pen & paper, 306 E New) · Book A · Q32NTA final key
Which of the following gases at 298 K and 1 atm pressure is having maximum solubility in water ?

  3. Methane, KH = 0.41
  4. CO2, KH = 1.6

Q56CUET 2024 · 29 May (pen & paper, 306 E New) · Book A · Q33NTA final key

Carbon disulphide319.4
  1. Chloroform
  2. Diethyl Ether
  3. Benzene
  4. Carbon disulphide

Q57CUET 2024 · 29 May (pen & paper, 306 E New) · Book A · Q45NTA final key

  2. Gas constant

Q58CUET 2024 · 19 Jul (re-test, CBT) · Q4NTA final key
Which of the following is an example of solid solution ?

  2. Oxygen gas in water
  3. Ethanol in water

Concept to recallThe type of solution is named by the solvent (the state of the solution): solid solutions are gas-in-solid (H2 in Pd), liquid-in-solid (Hg in Na amalgam), solid-in-solid (alloys).
  1. Camphor in N2: gaseous solution. O2 in water, ethanol in water: liquid solutions.
  2. Sodium amalgam (Hg in Na): liquid-in-solid, a solid solution.

Answer: option (4) — Amalgam of mercury with sodium

Q59CUET 2024 · 19 Jul (re-test, CBT) · Q6NTA final key

Q60CUET 2024 · 19 Jul (re-test, CBT) · Q7NTA final key
What kind of problem arises when bubbles of nitrogen gas dissolves in blood ?

  2. Red fever
  3. Sleeping sickness
  4. Bends
Concept to recallUnder high pressure (deep diving) more N2 dissolves in blood (Henry’s law); on fast ascent it forms bubbles that block capillaries: the bends.

Q61CUET 2024 · 19 Jul (re-test, CBT) · Q8NTA final key
A perfectly ideal solution is rare but some solution behave nearly ideal. Which of the following does not fall in this category ?
  1. n-hexane and n-heptane
  2. Ethanol and acetone
  3. Benzene and toluene
  4. Bromoethane and chloroethane
Concept to recallNearly ideal: components with similar A–A, B–B and A–B interactions. Ethanol + acetone breaks ethanol’s H-bonds: positive deviation.
  1. Hexane/heptane, benzene/toluene, bromoethane/chloroethane: similar molecules, nearly ideal.
  2. Ethanol + acetone shows positive deviation from Raoult’s law.

Answer: option (2) — Ethanol and acetone

Q62CUET 2023 · 21 May, Shift 3 · Q1 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
The solubility of a gas in a liquid
  1. Decreases with increase of pressure
  2. Decreases with increase of both temperature and pressure
  3. Increases with increase of both pressure and temperature
  4. Increases with decrease of temperature
Concept to recallHenry’s law: p = KHx — solubility rises with pressure. Dissolving a gas is exothermic, so solubility falls as temperature rises.
  1. Pressure up ⇒ solubility up (Henry’s law), so options (1) and (2) are wrong.
  2. Temperature up ⇒ solubility down (KH rises with T), so (3) is wrong.
  3. Hence solubility increases as temperature decreases.

Answer: option (4) — Increases with decrease of temperature

TrapOption (3) gets pressure right but temperature backwards.
Q63CUET 2023 · 21 May, Shift 3 · Q11 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
Identify the solution which is nearly ideal in behaviour
  1. Ethanol and Acetone
  2. Phenol and Aniline
  3. Bromoethane and Chloroethane
  4. Chloroform and Acetone
Concept to recallIdeal solutions form when A–B interactions equal A–A and B–B: chemically similar, non-polar or similarly polar pairs.
  1. Bromoethane and chloroethane are near-identical in structure and polarity ⇒ nearly ideal.
  2. Ethanol + acetone: H-bonds broken ⇒ positive deviation. Phenol + aniline, chloroform + acetone: new H-bonds ⇒ negative deviation.

Answer: option (3) — Bromoethane and Chloroethane

Q64CUET 2023 · 21 May, Shift 3 · Q23 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
At what temperature a solution containing 5.60 g of glucose per 1000 g of water would boil at 1.013 bar? (Kb for water is 0.52 K kg mol−1)
  1. 203.321 K
  2. 273.15 K
  3. 303.202 K
  4. 373.166 K
Concept to recallΔTb = Kbm; water boils at 373.15 K at 1.013 bar.
  1. m = (5.60/180)/1 kg = 0.0311 mol kg−1.
  2. ΔTb = 0.52 × 0.0311 = 0.016 K.
  3. Tb = 373.15 + 0.016 = 373.166 K.

Answer: option (4) — 373.166 K

Q65CUET 2023 · 22 May, Shift 3 · Q22NTA final key
The vapour pressure curve of the mixture of ethanol and acetone is higher than its constituents because :
  1. Weaking of interactions between molecules takes place
  2. Strengthening of interactions between molecules takes place
  3. New hydrogen bonds are formed
  4. Molecules are not able to escape from the solution
Concept to recallPositive deviation from Raoult’s law: A–B attractions weaker than A–A/B–B; ΔmixH > 0, molecules escape more easily.
  1. Acetone gets between ethanol molecules and breaks some of their hydrogen bonds.
  2. Weaker net attractions ⇒ higher escaping tendency ⇒ vapour pressure above the ideal line.

Answer: option (1) — Weaking of interactions between molecules takes place

Q66CUET 2023 · 22 May, Shift 3 · Q23NTA final key
Which of the following is not an expression of Dalton’s law of partial pressures ?
  1. P = P1 + P2
  2. P = P1° x1
  3. P = P1° + (P2° − P1°)x2
  4. P1 = P − P2
Concept to recallDalton: Ptotal = p1 + p2; combined with Raoult (pi = pi°xi) it gives P = p1° + (p2° − p1°)x2.
  1. (1) and (4) are Dalton’s law; (3) is Dalton + Raoult for a binary solution.
  2. (2) equates the total pressure to one component’s partial pressure (Raoult’s law for p1), so it is not an expression of Dalton’s law.

Answer: option (2) — P = P1° x1

  3. N2 is less soluble at the higher temperature, so 89 belongs to 303 K.

Q68CUET 2023 · 23 May, Shift 3 · Q16NTA final key
The osmotic pressure of a solution prepared by dissolving 50 mg of H2SO4 in 2 liters of water at 25°C will be
  1. 5.2700 atm
  2. 0.0187 atm
  3. 187.3 atm
  4. 0.527 atm

  2. π = 3 × 2.55 × 10−4 × 0.0821 × 298 = 0.0187 atm.

Q69CUET 2023 · 23 May, Shift 3 · Q25NTA final key
For the equimolal solutions, increasing order of osmotic pressure is

(B) 1 m BaCl2
(C) 1 m KCl
(D) 1 m glucose
(E) 1 m H3PO4
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. A < D < C < B < E
  2. E < B < C < D < A
  3. A < B < C < D < E
  4. E < C < B < D < A
Concept to recallπ = i C R T: at equal concentration, compare van’t Hoff factors.
  1. i: C6H5COOH ½ (dimer), glucose 1, KCl 2, BaCl2 3, H3PO4 4.
  2. A < D < C < B < E.

Answer: option (1) — A < D < C < B < E

Q73CUET 2023 · 25 May, Shift 3 · Q36 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived

Q74CUET 2023 · 26 May, Shift 3 (Oswaal typed copy) · Q20key re-derived
When 1.5 g of a non-volatile solute is dissolved in 30 g of a solvent, the boiling point of the solvent is raised by 2 K. Calculate the molar mass of the solute, given that Kb for the solvent is 1.85 K kg mol−1.

Q78CUET 2023 · 31 May, Shift 2 · Q46NTA final key
Passage: Osmotic pressure measurements are less accurate and difficult to carry out, so the method is not used for ordinary molecular weights, but it is used for polymers, proteins and starch. Knowing the osmotic pressure of a solution, the molecular weight of the solute can be calculated using the van’t Hoff equation.

  1. 8.622 atm
  2. 7.398 atm
  3. 2.79 atm
  4. 4.43 atm
Concept to recallπ = iCRT (R = 0.0821 L atm K−1 mol−1).
  1. C = 20/58.5 = 0.342 M; T = 308 K.
  2. Without dissociation: π = 0.342 × 0.0821 × 308 = 8.6 atm → option (1).
  3. With full dissociation (i = 2) it would be 17.3 atm, which is not offered.

Q79CUET 2023 · 31 May, Shift 2 · Q47NTA final key
Passage: Osmotic pressure measurements are less accurate and difficult to carry out, so the method is not used for ordinary molecular weights, but it is used for polymers, proteins and starch. Knowing the osmotic pressure of a solution, the molecular weight of the solute can be calculated using the van’t Hoff equation.
When osmotic pressure and temperature for two solutions are same, equal volumes of solutions would contain same number of:
  1. Moles of solute
  2. Moles of solvent
  3. Moles of solution
  4. Molecules of solutions
Concept to recallπ = (n/V)RT: equal π and T ⇒ equal n/V of solute (isotonic).
  1. Equal volumes therefore hold equal moles of solute particles.

Answer: option (1) — Moles of solute

Q80CUET 2023 · 31 May, Shift 2 · Q48NTA final key
Passage: Osmotic pressure measurements are less accurate and difficult to carry out, so the method is not used for ordinary molecular weights, but it is used for polymers, proteins and starch. Knowing the osmotic pressure of a solution, the molecular weight of the solute can be calculated using the van’t Hoff equation.
A solution which shows deviations from Roult’s law is called :
  1. Ideal solution
  2. Real solution
  3. Saturated solution
  4. Uniform solution
Concept to recallSolutions obeying Raoult’s law at all compositions are ideal; those that deviate are non-ideal (real).
  1. Deviation from Raoult’s law ⇒ non-ideal (real) solution.

Answer: option (2) — Real solution

Q81CUET 2023 · 31 May, Shift 2 · Q49NTA final key
Passage: Osmotic pressure measurements are less accurate and difficult to carry out, so the method is not used for ordinary molecular weights, but it is used for polymers, proteins and starch. Knowing the osmotic pressure of a solution, the molecular weight of the solute can be calculated using the van’t Hoff equation.
Determine the molarity of a solution containing 4 g of NaOH in 1L solution
  1. 4 M

  3. 0.1 M
  4. 0.4 M

  1. 4/40 = 0.1 mol in 1 L ⇒ 0.1 M.

Answer: option (3) — 0.1 M

Q82CUET 2023 · 31 May, Shift 2 · Q50NTA final key
Passage: Osmotic pressure measurements are less accurate and difficult to carry out, so the method is not used for ordinary molecular weights, but it is used for polymers, proteins and starch. Knowing the osmotic pressure of a solution, the molecular weight of the solute can be calculated using the van’t Hoff equation.
In a nearly saturated solution, which of the following statements are correct?
  1. A. If dissolution process is endothermic, solubility increases with increase in temperature.
  2. B. If dissolution process is endothermic, solubility decreases with increase in temperature.
  3. C. If dissolution process is exothermic, solubility decreases with increase in temperature.
  4. D. If dissolution process is exothermic, solubility increases with increase in temperature.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. B and D only
  2. A and C only
  3. A and D only
  4. B and C only
Concept to recallLe Chatelier for a near-saturated solution: heating favours the endothermic direction.
  1. Endothermic dissolution ⇒ solubility rises with T (A); exothermic ⇒ falls (C).

Answer: option (2) — A and C only

Q83CUET 2023 · 5 June, Shift 1 · Q10 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
We have four aqueous solutions labelled as:
(A) 0.1 M NaCl
(B) 0.01 M NaCl

Choose the correct increasing order of van’t Hoff factor from the options given below:
  1. iC < iA < iB < iD
  2. iD < iC < iB < iA
  3. iD < iA = iB < iC
  4. iC < iA = iB < iD
Concept to recallFor complete dissociation i = number of ions per formula unit; it does not depend on concentration (ideal case).
  1. Sucrose 1; NaCl 2 (both solutions); BaCl2 3.
  2. iD < iA = iB < iC.

Answer: option (3) — iD < iA = iB < iC

Q84CUET 2023 · 5 June, Shift 1 · Q14 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
The volume of mixing (ΔV) is not zero for which of the following solutions?
  1. Chloroethane and Bromoethane
  2. Benzene and Toluene
  3. Ethanol and Acetone
  4. n-Hexane and n-Heptane
Concept to recallIdeal solutions: ΔmixH = 0 and ΔmixV = 0. Non-ideal ones have ΔV ≠ 0.
  1. (1), (2), (4) are near-ideal pairs.
  2. Ethanol + acetone: H-bonds in ethanol are broken ⇒ positive deviation, ΔV > 0.

Answer: option (3) — Ethanol and Acetone

Q85CUET 2023 · 5 June, Shift 1 · Q21 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
0.01 molal aqueous solutions of strong electrolytes NaCl, KCl, MgSO4 and K2SO4 are prepared. Which of the following statements is correct regarding their osmotic pressure? (Assume complete dissociation of solute particles)
  1. All of them exhibit equal osmotic pressure
  2. Osmotic pressure of all of them are different
  3. MgSO4 has highest osmotic pressure
  4. K2SO4 has highest osmotic pressure
Concept to recallπ = iCRT: equal concentrations, so π follows i.
  1. i: NaCl 2, KCl 2, MgSO4 2, K2SO4 3.
  2. K2SO4 has the highest π.

Answer: option (4) — K2SO4 has highest osmotic pressure

Q86CUET 2023 · 07 Jun, Shift 3 · Prepp reconstruction · Q14key re-derived
The vapour pressure of pure Benzene is 0.900 bar. If a nonvolatile electrolytic solid is added, vapour pressure of the solution becomes 0.200 bar. If numbers of moles of solute is 1 and solvent is 2 respectively in solution, what is the value of van’t Hoff factor (i)?
  1. 2.33
  2. 0.56
  3. 1.56
  4. 2.00
Concept to recallNCERT’s van’t Hoff form of Raoult’s law: (p° − p)/p° = i·n2/n1.
  1. (p° − p)/p° = (0.900 − 0.200)/0.900 = 0.778.
  2. n2/n1 = 1/2.
  3. i = 0.778 × 2 = 1.56.

Answer: option (3) — 1.56

TrapUsing x2 = 1/3 instead of n2/n1 gives 2.33. That is no more exact: with ions the true solute mole fraction is in2/(n1 + in2), which would give 7. The question is set on NCERT’s formula.
NoteThe data are not self-consistent, so the three textbook routes give three answers: NCERT’s modified equation (p° − p)/p° = i·n2/n1 gives 1.56; i·x2 with x2 = 1/3 gives 2.33; treating the i·n2 particles exactly, i·1/(2 + i) = 0.778, gives i = 7 (not offered). The question hands over n2 and n1 separately, which is exactly NCERT’s form, so 1.56 is the intended answer; Prepp’s unofficial key also prints (3).
Q87CUET 2023 · 07 Jun, Shift 3 · Prepp reconstruction · Q28key re-derived
Which of the following is an example of minimum boiling azeotrope?
  1. Phenol and aniline
  2. Chloroform and acetone
  3. Nitric acid and water
  4. Ethanol and acetone
Concept to recallPositive deviation from Raoult’s law (weaker A–B attraction) → minimum-boiling azeotrope; negative deviation → maximum-boiling.
  1. Phenol–aniline, chloroform–acetone, HNO3–water: negative deviation (H-bonding) → maximum boiling.
  2. Ethanol–acetone: positive deviation → minimum-boiling azeotrope.

Answer: option (4) — Ethanol and acetone

Q88CUET 2023 · 07 Jun, Shift 3 · Prepp reconstruction · Q32key re-derived
Which of the following is the correct formula of a colligative property?

  2. ΔTb = (Kb × 1000 × w2)/(M1 × w1)
  3. ΔTf = (Kf × 1000 × w2)/(M2 × w1)
  4. π = ΔTfRT
Concept to recallSubscript 1 = solvent, 2 = solute. RLVP = x2; ΔT = K·1000w2/(M2w1); π = CRT.
  1. (1) should be x2; (2) should have M2 (solute) in the denominator; (4) should be CRT.
  2. (3) is the correct freezing-point expression.

Answer: option (3) — ΔTf = (Kf × 1000 × w2)/(M2 × w1)

Q89CUET 2023 · 08 Jun, Shift 3 · Prepp reconstruction · Q2key re-derived
Which solutions will have the highest boiling point?
  1. 1 M BaCl2 solution
  2. 1 M NaCl solution
  3. 1 M C6H12O6 solution
  4. 1 M (NH2)2CO solution
Concept to recallΔTb = i Kbm: at equal concentration, the most particles give the highest boiling point.
  1. i: BaCl2 3, NaCl 2, glucose 1, urea 1.
  2. BaCl2 gives the largest ΔTb.

Answer: option (1) — 1 M BaCl2 solution

Q90CUET 2023 · 08 Jun, Shift 3 · Prepp reconstruction · Q21key re-derived
Experimentally determined molar mass is always lower than the true value in case of:
  1. Strong electrolytes
  2. Weak electrolytes
  3. Non-electrolytes
  4. Dimers
Concept to recallDissociation increases the number of particles (i > 1), so the colligative property is larger and the calculated molar mass smaller.
  1. Strong electrolytes dissociate (almost) completely: i > 1 every time, so the observed molar mass is always low.
  2. Dimers (association) give a higher value; non-electrolytes give the true one.

Answer: option (1) — Strong electrolytes

Q91CUET 2023 · 08 Jun, Shift 3 · Prepp reconstruction · Q28key re-derived
An aqueous solution of urea has a freezing point of −0.52 °C. Predict the osmotic pressure of the solution at 37 °C [Kf = 1.86, assuming that the molar concentration and molality are numerically equal]

  2. 7.1 atm
  3. 11 atm
  4. 8.5 atm
Concept to recallΔTf = Kfm; π = CRT with C ≈ m for a dilute aqueous solution.
  1. m = 0.52/1.86 = 0.280 mol kg−1 ≈ 0.280 mol L−1.

Answer: option (2) — 7.1 atm

Q92CUET 2023 · 08 Jun, Shift 3 · Prepp reconstruction · Q7key re-derived
Which of the following colligative property is associated with concentration in terms of molarity?

  2. Depression in freezing point

Answer: option (3) — Osmotic pressure

Q93CUET 2023 · 10 Jun, Shift 1 · Prepp reconstruction · Q10worked here
The vapour pressure of chloroform (CHCl3) and dichloromethane (CH2Cl2) at 298 K are 400 mm Hg and 615 mm Hg, respectively. What is the mole fraction of CHCl3 in vapour phase in solution prepared by mixing 30 g of CHCl3 and 45 g of CH2Cl2?
  1. 0.76
  2. 0.23
  3. 0.82
  4. 0.18
Concept to recallRaoult: pi = xip°i; Dalton: yi = pi/ptotal.
  1. n(CHCl3) = 30/119.5 = 0.251; n(CH2Cl2) = 45/85 = 0.529; x(CHCl3) = 0.251/0.780 = 0.322.
  2. p(CHCl3) = 0.322 × 400 = 128.7 mm; p(CH2Cl2) = 0.678 × 615 = 417.0 mm; total 545.7 mm.
  3. y(CHCl3) = 128.7/545.7 = 0.236 ≈ 0.23.

Answer: option (2) — 0.23

Q94CUET 2023 · 10 Jun, Shift 1 · Prepp reconstruction · Q12key re-derived

Q96CUET 2023 · 11 Jun, Shift 3 · Q29 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
The desalination of sea water plant stops working due to which of the following reasons?
  1. The pressure applied on the saline water was less than osmotic pressure.
  2. The pressure applied on the saline water was greater than osmotic pressure.
  3. The osmotic pressure application has no significance.
  4. Salinity of water decreased and osmotic pressure was more than pressure applied.
Concept to recallReverse osmosis: pure water is pushed out of sea water only if the applied pressure exceeds its osmotic pressure.
  1. If applied pressure < osmotic pressure, solvent flows the normal way (into the sea water), so no fresh water is produced.
  2. Option (4) is self-contradictory: lower salinity lowers the osmotic pressure.

Answer: option (1) — The pressure applied on the saline water was less than osmotic pressure.

Q97CUET 2023 · 11 Jun, Shift 3 · Q6 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived

Concept to recallFor a strong electrolyte, i = number of ions per formula unit.
  1. K4[Fe(CN)6] → 4K+ + [Fe(CN)6]4−: i = 5.
  2. AlCl3, AlF3: 4 ions; Al2(SO4)3 → 2Al3+ + 3SO42−: 5 ions.

Q98CUET 2023 · 13 Jun, Shift 3 · Q16 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
Vapour pressure of an aqueous solution of non-volatile solute which boils at 101.56 °C at 25 °C will be (V.P. of pure water at 25 °C is 200 mmHg and Kb for water is 0.52 K kg mol−1)
  1. 198.98 mmHg
  2. 189.8 mmHg
  3. 179.6 mmHg
  4. 184.7 mmHg

  1. m = 1.56/0.52 = 3 mol per kg of water; 1 kg water = 55.5 mol.

  3. p = 200 × 0.9487 ≈ 189.8 mmHg.

Q99CUET 2023 · 13 Jun, Shift 3 · Q20 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
Identify the correct relation between the molar mass of solute and ebullioscopic constant. (w1 = mass of solvent, w2 = mass of solute, both in g)

Q100CUET 2023 · 15 Jun, Shift 1 · Q20 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived

Q101CUET 2023 · 15 Jun, Shift 1 · Q21 · Prepp reconstructionworked here
Decreasing order of freezing point of 0.1 M aqueous solution of the following will be:

  2. Highest freezing point = smallest i: urea > HCl > K2SO4 > AlCl3 > K4[Fe(CN)6], i.e. C > E > B > D > A.

Q102CUET 2023 · 15 Jun, Shift 1 · Q22 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived

Q103CUET 2023 · 20 Jun, Shift 3 · Q3NTA final key

  2. Molarity (M)
  3. Molality (m)
  4. Strength (S)

  1. % (w/v), molarity and strength (g L−1) all use the solution’s volume, which expands with temperature.
  2. Molality uses only masses, so it is temperature-independent → most reliable.

Answer: option (3) — Molality (m)

Q104CUET 2023 · 20 Jun, Shift 3 · Q4NTA final key
Match List I with List II
LIST ILIST II
A. K2SO4(aq) with 60 % dissociationI. i = 3.7
B. K3[Fe(CN)6](aq) with 90% dissociationII. i = 1.8
C. AlCl3 (aq) with 80% dissociationIII. i = 2.2
D. K2HgI4 (aq) with 40% dissociationIV. i = 3.4

  2. A-I, B-III, C-IV, D-II
  3. A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV 
  4. A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II

Q105CUET 2023 · 20 Jun, Shift 3 · Q5NTA final key

Q106CUET 2023 · 22 Jun, Shift 2 · Q28NTA final key
Which of the following is not correct?

Q108CUET 2023 · 22 Jun, Shift 2 · Q38NTA final key
