Q110CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q41NTA final key
Passage (23 Jun 2023, Q41–45): colligative properties

Properties that depend on the number of solute particles, irrespective of their nature, relative to the total number of particles in the solution are called colligative properties: relative lowering of vapour pressure of the solvent, depression of freezing point, elevation of boiling point and osmotic pressure. All of them help in calculating the observed molar mass of the solute; osmotic pressure is considered best for determining the molecular mass.

The binary liquid mixtures which show negative deviation from Raoult’s law are:
  1. (A) n-hexane and n-heptane
  2. (B) phenol and acetone
  3. (C) Ethanol and acetone
  4. (D) Chloroform and acetone
  5. (E) Benzene and toluene
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (A) and (B) only
  2. (C) and (E) only
  3. (B) and (D) only
  4. (A) and (E) only
Concept to recallNegative deviation: A–B attractions stronger than A–A and B–B (often a new H-bond), so vapour pressure is lower than Raoult predicts; ΔmixH < 0.
  1. Hexane–heptane, benzene–toluene: nearly ideal.
  2. Ethanol–acetone: acetone breaks ethanol’s H-bonds → positive deviation.
  3. Phenol–acetone (phenol OH ··· O=C) and chloroform–acetone (Cl3C–H ··· O=C) form new H-bonds → negative deviation.
  4. Answer: (B) and (D).

Answer: option (3) — (B) and (D) only

NoteThe paper prints “n-heptone” for n-heptane.
Q111CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q42NTA final key
Passage (23 Jun 2023, Q41–45): colligative properties

Properties that depend on the number of solute particles, irrespective of their nature, relative to the total number of particles in the solution are called colligative properties: relative lowering of vapour pressure of the solvent, depression of freezing point, elevation of boiling point and osmotic pressure. All of them help in calculating the observed molar mass of the solute; osmotic pressure is considered best for determining the molecular mass.

A solution of 12.5 g of an unknown solute in 170 g water gave a boiling point elevation of 0.63 K. Kb for water is 0.53 K kg mol−1. The molar mass of the solute is:
  1. 61.85 g mol−1
  2. 87.3 g/mol
  3. 13.9 g mol−1
  4. 56.7 g mol−1
Concept to recallΔTb = Kb m ⇒ M = Kb × wB × 1000ΔTb × wA
  1. M = (0.53 × 12.5 × 1000)/(0.63 × 170).
  2. = 6625/107.1 = 61.9 g mol−1.

Answer: option (1) — 61.85 g mol−1

TrapForgetting the 1000 (g → kg) gives 0.062.
Q112CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q43NTA final key
Passage (23 Jun 2023, Q41–45): colligative properties

Properties that depend on the number of solute particles, irrespective of their nature, relative to the total number of particles in the solution are called colligative properties: relative lowering of vapour pressure of the solvent, depression of freezing point, elevation of boiling point and osmotic pressure. All of them help in calculating the observed molar mass of the solute; osmotic pressure is considered best for determining the molecular mass.

Which solution has the highest boiling point?
  1. 0.1 m glucose
  2. 0.5 m glucose
  3. 1 m glucose
  4. 2 m glucose
Concept to recallΔTb = i Kb m; glucose is a non-electrolyte (i = 1).
  1. Same solute, i = 1 for all; ΔTb ∝ m.
  2. Largest molality, 2 m, has the largest elevation and so the highest boiling point.

Answer: option (4) — 2 m glucose

Q113CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q44NTA final key
Passage (23 Jun 2023, Q41–45): colligative properties

Properties that depend on the number of solute particles, irrespective of their nature, relative to the total number of particles in the solution are called colligative properties: relative lowering of vapour pressure of the solvent, depression of freezing point, elevation of boiling point and osmotic pressure. All of them help in calculating the observed molar mass of the solute; osmotic pressure is considered best for determining the molecular mass.

Based on solute solvent interactions, arrange the following in order of increasing solubility in n-octane.
  1. (A) Cycloheptane
  2. (B) NaCl
  3. (C) CH3OH
  4. (D) CH3CN
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (D) < (C) < (B) < (A)
  2. (B) < (C) < (D) < (A)
  3. (A) < (D) < (C) < (B)
  4. (B) < (A) < (D) < (C)
Concept to recallLike dissolves like: n-octane is non-polar, so solubility rises as the solute becomes less polar.
  1. NaCl (ionic) is practically insoluble.
  2. CH3OH is polar and strongly H-bonded to itself; CH3CN is polar but cannot H-bond with itself, so it is slightly more soluble.
  3. Cycloheptane is non-polar → most soluble.
  4. B < C < D < A.

Answer: option (2) — (B) < (C) < (D) < (A)

Q114CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q45NTA final key
Passage (23 Jun 2023, Q41–45): colligative properties

Properties that depend on the number of solute particles, irrespective of their nature, relative to the total number of particles in the solution are called colligative properties: relative lowering of vapour pressure of the solvent, depression of freezing point, elevation of boiling point and osmotic pressure. All of them help in calculating the observed molar mass of the solute; osmotic pressure is considered best for determining the molecular mass.

A 1 litre solution of glucose containing 36 g of it has an osmotic pressure of 4.98 bar at 300 K. At the same temperature, the osmotic pressure of the solution is 1.52 bar. The concentration of the solution at 1.52 bar is:
  1. 0.0610 mol−1
  2. 10.9 mol−1
  3. 1.6 mol−1
  4. 0.00610 mol−1
Concept to recallπ = CRT ⇒ at fixed T, π ∝ C: C2 = C1 π2/π1.
  1. C1 = 36/180 = 0.20 mol L−1.
  2. C2 = 0.20 × 1.52/4.98 = 0.0610 mol L−1.

Answer: option (1) — 0.0610 mol−1

NoteThe options print the unit as “mol−1”; it should be mol L−1.
Q115CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q10NTA final key
When air was passed through glass bulb containing 16 g of an organic compound in 100 g of water and then through glass bulb containing only water at the same temperature and then finally through anhydrous CCl4 glass tube, the loss in mass of glass bulb containing water was 0.052 g and the gain in mass of CCl4 tube was 1.86 g. Calculate the molecular mass of the organic substance.
  1. 100 g
  2. 10 g
  3. 200 g
  4. 50 g
Concept to recallOstwald–Walker method: loss from the solution bulbs ∝ p, loss from the water bulb ∝ (p° − p), total vapour absorbed ∝ p°. So (p° − p)/p° = (loss of water bulb)/(total gain) = xB.
  1. Relative lowering = 0.052/1.86 = 0.02796 = xB.
  2. nwater = 100/18 = 5.556 mol; xB = nB/(nB + 5.556).
  3. nB = 0.02796 × 5.556/(1 − 0.02796) = 0.160 mol.
  4. M = 16/0.160 = 100 g mol−1 (the dilute approximation nB/nA gives 103, still nearest 100).

Answer: option (1) — 100 g

NoteThe Ostwald–Walker dynamic method is not in NCERT; the arithmetic is Raoult’s relative lowering of vapour pressure, which is.
Q116CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q3NTA final key
The partial pressure of the gas in vapour phase (P) is proportional to the mole fraction of the gas (x) in the solution. It is expressed as P = KHx. KH stands for:
  1. Arrhenius constant
  2. Gas constant
  3. Cryoscopic constant
  4. Henry’s law constant
Concept to recallHenry’s law: p = KH x; KH depends on the gas and on temperature; the larger KH, the lower the solubility.
  1. P = KHx is Henry’s law, and KH is Henry’s law constant.

Answer: option (4) — Henry’s law constant

Q117CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q4NTA final key
2 g of benzoic acid (C6H5COOH) dissolved in 25 g of benzene lowers its freezing point by 1.62 K. Molal depression constant is 4.9 K kg/mol. The value of ‘i’ when benzoic acid dimerises would be:
  1. 0.753
  2. 0.617
  3. 0.504
  4. 0.405
Concept to recalli = Mnormal/Mobserved; Mobs = Kf wB × 1000/(ΔTf wA).
  1. Mobs = 4.9 × 2 × 1000/(1.62 × 25) = 9800/40.5 = 242 g mol−1.
  2. Mnormal(C6H5COOH) = 122 g mol−1.
  3. i = 122/242 = 0.504 (about 99% of the acid is dimerised).

Answer: option (3) — 0.504

TrapInverting the ratio gives 1.98, the “degree of association” reading, not i.
Q118CUET 2022 · 10 Aug, Shift 1 (SET 06) · Q3NTA final key
Consider the 1M aqueous solution of the following compounds and arrange them in the increasing order of elevation in the boiling points.
(A) C6H12O6
(B) NaCl
(C) MgCl2
(D) AlCl3
(E) Al2(SO4)3
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. B < C < D < E < A
  2. A < E < D < C < B
  3. A < B < C < D < E
  4. E < D < C < B < A
Concept to recallΔTb = i Kb m: at equal molality the order follows the van’t Hoff factor i.
  1. i (complete dissociation): glucose 1, NaCl 2, MgCl2 3, AlCl3 4, Al2(SO4)3 5 (2Al3+ + 3SO42−).
  2. Increasing ΔTb: A < B < C < D < E.

Answer: option (3) — A < B < C < D < E

TrapOption (4) is the same order reversed (decreasing).
Q119CUET 2022 · 10 Aug, Shift 1 (SET 06) · Q4NTA final key
Calculate the molarity of a solution containing 5g of NaOH in 450 mL solution
  1. 0·278 × 10−3 M
  2. 0·278 M
  3. 2·78 × 10−3 M
  4. 2·78 M
Concept to recallM = moles of solute / volume of solution in litres.
  1. n(NaOH) = 5/40 = 0.125 mol.
  2. V = 450 mL = 0.450 L.
  3. M = 0.125/0.450 = 0.278 M.

Answer: option (2) — 0·278 M

TrapForgetting to convert mL to L gives the 10−3 options.

Electrochemistry122 questions

Q120CUET 2026 · 24 May, Shift 1 · Q41NTA final key
Passage (summarised): Electrochemical cells (24 May 2026, Q41–45)

Galvanic cells are built on the pattern of the Daniell cell from two half-cells, each a metal electrode in an electrolyte, joined externally by a wire through a voltmeter and internally by a salt bridge. For the cell Ni(s)|Ni2+(aq)||Ag+(aq)|Ag the cell reaction is Ni(s) + 2Ag+(aq) → Ni2+(aq) + 2Ag(s). The Nernst equation relates the emf of the cell to the standard emf and the concentrations of the oxidised and reduced species.

The Nernst equation for the given reaction Ni(s) + 2Ag+(aq) → Ni2+(aq) + 2Ag(s) is
  1. Ecell = E°cell − RT2F ln [Ni2+][Ag+]2
  2. Ecell = E°cell − RT2F ln [Ni2+][Ag+]
  3. Ecell = E°cell − RTF ln [Ni2+][Ag+]
  4. Ecell = E°cell + RTF ln [Ni2+][Ag+]
Concept to recallEcell = E°cell − (RT/nF) ln Q, with Q = [products]/[reactants] raised to their coefficients (solids omitted).
  1. n = 2 electrons transferred.
  2. Q = [Ni2+]/[Ag+]2 (coefficient 2 on Ag+).
  3. Ecell = E°cell − (RT/2F) ln([Ni2+]/[Ag+]2).

Answer: option (1) — Ecell = E°cell − RT2F ln [Ni2+][Ag+]2

TrapForgetting to square [Ag+] gives the second option.
Q121CUET 2026 · 24 May, Shift 1 · Q42NTA final key
Passage (summarised): Electrochemical cells (24 May 2026, Q41–45)

Galvanic cells are built on the pattern of the Daniell cell from two half-cells, each a metal electrode in an electrolyte, joined externally by a wire through a voltmeter and internally by a salt bridge. For the cell Ni(s)|Ni2+(aq)||Ag+(aq)|Ag the cell reaction is Ni(s) + 2Ag+(aq) → Ni2+(aq) + 2Ag(s). The Nernst equation relates the emf of the cell to the standard emf and the concentrations of the oxidised and reduced species.

The standard electrode potential for the cell Ni(s) + 2Ag+(aq) → Ni2+(aq) + 2Ag(s) is 0.80 V. The standard Gibbs energy for the reaction is:
  1. −154.379 kJ mol−1
  2. 154.379 kJ mol−1
  3. 212.2 kJ mol−1
  4. −212.2 kJ mol−1
Concept to recallΔrG° = −nFE°cell; negative for a spontaneous cell reaction.
  1. n = 2, E° = 0.80 V.
  2. ΔG° = −2 × 96487 × 0.80 = −154379 J mol−1 = −154.379 kJ mol−1 (with F = 96500 it is −154.4 kJ mol−1).

Answer: option (1) — −154.379 kJ mol−1

TrapDropping the minus sign gives the positive value; using n = 1 is not offered but is the other slip.
Q122CUET 2026 · 24 May, Shift 1 · Q43NTA final key
Passage (summarised): Electrochemical cells (24 May 2026, Q41–45)

Galvanic cells are built on the pattern of the Daniell cell from two half-cells, each a metal electrode in an electrolyte, joined externally by a wire through a voltmeter and internally by a salt bridge. For the cell Ni(s)|Ni2+(aq)||Ag+(aq)|Ag the cell reaction is Ni(s) + 2Ag+(aq) → Ni2+(aq) + 2Ag(s). The Nernst equation relates the emf of the cell to the standard emf and the concentrations of the oxidised and reduced species.

The relationship between the equilibrium constant of the reaction and the standard electrode potential of the cell in which that reaction takes place is given by
  1. E°cell = RT2.303 × nF log Kc
  2. E°cell = 2.303RTnF log Kc
  3. E°cell = 2.303RTnF ln Kc
  4. E°cell = 2.303RT ln Kc
Concept to recallAt equilibrium Ecell = 0 and Q = Kc, so E°cell = (RT/nF) ln Kc = (2.303RT/nF) log Kc.
  1. Put Ecell = 0 in the Nernst equation: E° = (RT/nF) ln Kc.
  2. Convert ln to log by the factor 2.303: E° = (2.303RT/nF) log Kc.

Answer: option (2) — E°cell = 2.303RTnF log Kc

Trap2.303 goes with log, never with ln.
Q123CUET 2026 · 24 May, Shift 1 · Q44NTA final key
Passage (summarised): Electrochemical cells (24 May 2026, Q41–45)

Galvanic cells are built on the pattern of the Daniell cell from two half-cells, each a metal electrode in an electrolyte, joined externally by a wire through a voltmeter and internally by a salt bridge. For the cell Ni(s)|Ni2+(aq)||Ag+(aq)|Ag the cell reaction is Ni(s) + 2Ag+(aq) → Ni2+(aq) + 2Ag(s). The Nernst equation relates the emf of the cell to the standard emf and the concentrations of the oxidised and reduced species.

In the given cell, Ni(s) + 2Ag+(aq) → Ni2+(aq) + 2Ag(s), which of the given species is the reducing agent?
  1. Ni2+(aq)
  2. Ni(s)
  3. Ag+(aq)
  4. Ag(s)
Concept to recallThe reducing agent is the species oxidised (it gives electrons).
  1. Ni(0) → Ni(+2): Ni is oxidised, so Ni(s) is the reducing agent.
  2. Ag+ is reduced: the oxidising agent.

Answer: option (2) — Ni(s)

Q124CUET 2026 · 24 May, Shift 1 · Q45NTA final key
Passage (summarised): Electrochemical cells (24 May 2026, Q41–45)

Galvanic cells are built on the pattern of the Daniell cell from two half-cells, each a metal electrode in an electrolyte, joined externally by a wire through a voltmeter and internally by a salt bridge. For the cell Ni(s)|Ni2+(aq)||Ag+(aq)|Ag the cell reaction is Ni(s) + 2Ag+(aq) → Ni2+(aq) + 2Ag(s). The Nernst equation relates the emf of the cell to the standard emf and the concentrations of the oxidised and reduced species.

Which of the following is the anodic half cell reaction? (Ni(s) + 2Ag+(aq) → Ni2+(aq) + 2Ag(s))
  1. Ni(s) → Ni2+(aq) + 2e−
  2. Ni2+(aq) + 2e− → Ni(s)
  3. Ag+(aq) + e− → Ag(s)
  4. Ag(s) → Ag+(aq) + e−
Concept to recallOxidation occurs at the anode (left electrode in the cell notation).
  1. Ni is the left electrode and is oxidised: Ni(s) → Ni2+(aq) + 2e−.
  2. Ag+ + e− → Ag is the cathode reaction.

Answer: option (1) — Ni(s) → Ni2+(aq) + 2e−

Q125CUET 2026 · 6 June, Shift 1 · Q14NTA final key
Match List-I with List-II
QuantityUnits
(A) Conductivity(I) ohm
(B) Molar Conductivity(II) S
(C) Resistance(III) S cm−1
(D) Conductance(IV) S cm2 mol−1
  1. (A)–(IV), (B)–(III), (C)–(I), (D)–(II)
  2. (A)–(III), (B)–(IV), (C)–(I), (D)–(II)
  3. (A)–(III), (B)–(IV), (C)–(II), (D)–(I)
  4. (A)–(IV), (B)–(III), (C)–(II), (D)–(I)
Concept to recallR in Ω; G = 1/R in S; κ = G(l/A) in S cm−1; Λm = κ/c in S cm2 mol−1.
  1. (A) κ: S cm−1 (III). (B) Λm: S cm2 mol−1 (IV).
  2. (C) R: ohm (I). (D) G: siemens (II).

Answer: option (2) — (A)–(III), (B)–(IV), (C)–(I), (D)–(II)

Q126CUET 2026 · 6 June, Shift 1 · Q23NTA final key
Standard electrode potentials (Mn+/M) of four metals A, B, C and D are given below:
(A) −1.2 V (B) +0.5 V (C) +1.2 V (D) −3.0 V
The correct increasing order for the reducing power of these metals will be:
  1. (D), (A), (C), (B).
  2. (D), (A), (B), (C).
  3. (C), (B), (A), (D).
  4. (B), (C), (A), (D).
Concept to recallThe more negative the reduction potential, the more readily the metal is oxidised: the stronger the reducing agent.
  1. Reducing power rises as E° falls: C (+1.2) < B (+0.5) < A (−1.2) < D (−3.0).

Answer: option (3) — (C), (B), (A), (D).

Q127CUET 2026 · 6 June, Shift 1 · Q32NTA final key
Which of the following statements are incorrect for thermodynamic properties?
(A) Both Ecell and ΔrG of reaction are extensive properties.
(B) Both Ecell and ΔrG of reaction are intensive properties.
(C) Ecell is an intensive property while ΔrG of reaction is an extensive property.
(D) Ecell is an extensive property while ΔrG of reaction is an intensive property.
  1. (A), (B) and (D) only
  2. (A), (B) and (C) only
  3. (B), (C) and (D) only
  4. (A), (C) and (D) only
Concept to recallΔrG = −nFEcell: Ecell does not depend on how much reacts (intensive); ΔrG scales with n (extensive).
  1. Only (C) is right.
  2. So the incorrect statements are (A), (B) and (D).

Answer: option (1) — (A), (B) and (D) only

Q128CUET 2026 · 6 June, Shift 1 · Q36NTA final key
The standard Gibbs energy for the reaction is −212.27 kJ mol−1.
Zn(s) + Cu2+(aq) → Zn2+(aq) + Cu(s)
The standard electrode potential for the Daniell cell is:
  1. 1.1 V
  2. 2.2 V
  3. 0.002 V
  4. 0.001 V
Concept to recallΔrG° = −nFE°cell.
  1. n = 2.
  2. E° = 212270/(2 × 96500) = 1.10 V.

Answer: option (1) — 1.1 V

TrapDropping n = 2 gives 2.2 V; leaving ΔG in kJ gives 0.001 V.
Q129CUET 2026 · 6 June, Shift 1 · Q6NTA final key
Limiting molar conductivities for some ions in water at 298 K (λ° / S cm2 mol−1) are: H+ 349.6, Na+ 50.1, Ca2+ 119.0, Mg2+ 106.0, Cl− 76.3, SO42− 160.
Choose the correct decreasing order of Λ°m for NaCl, HCl, CaCl2 and MgSO4.
  1. HCl, CaCl2, MgSO4, NaCl
  2. HCl, CaCl2, NaCl, MgSO4
  3. NaCl, CaCl2, MgSO4, HCl
  4. NaCl, HCl, CaCl2, MgSO4
Concept to recallKohlrausch: Λ°m = ν+λ°+ + ν−λ°− (count every ion in the formula).
  1. HCl = 349.6 + 76.3 = 425.9; CaCl2 = 119.0 + 2(76.3) = 271.6.
  2. MgSO4 = 106.0 + 160 = 266.0; NaCl = 50.1 + 76.3 = 126.4.
  3. Decreasing: HCl > CaCl2 > MgSO4 > NaCl.

Answer: option (1) — HCl, CaCl2, MgSO4, NaCl

TrapForgetting the factor 2 for Cl− in CaCl2 (195.3) puts it below MgSO4.
Q130CUET 2026 · 11 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q2key re-derived
A solution of copper sulphate cannot be stored in a zinc vessel because
  1. Copper is more reactive than zinc
  2. Reduction potential of copper is less than zinc
  3. Oxidation potential of copper is higher than zinc
  4. Reduction potential of copper is higher than zinc
Concept to recallA metal with a lower (more negative) E°red displaces the ions of a metal with a higher one.
  1. E°(Cu2+/Cu) = +0.34 V; E°(Zn2+/Zn) = −0.76 V.
  2. Cu2+ is reduced more readily, so Zn + Cu2+ → Zn2+ + Cu is spontaneous (E°cell = 1.10 V) and the vessel would be eaten away.

Answer: option (4) — Reduction potential of copper is higher than zinc

TrapOptions (2) and (3) say the same wrong thing in two ways: copper has the higher reduction potential and the lower oxidation potential.
Q131CUET 2026 · 11 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q8key re-derived
For the given Nernst equation Ecell = E°cell − (RT/nF) ln ([Mg2+]/[Ag+]), which of the following representation is correct?
  1. Ag+|Ag||Mg2+|Mg
  2. Mg2+|Mg||Ag|Ag+
  3. Mg|Mg2+||Ag+|Ag
  4. Mg|Mg2+||Ag|Ag+
Concept to recallQ = [products]/[reactants]; the cell is written anode | anode ion || cathode ion | cathode.
  1. Mg2+ sits in the numerator: it is formed, so Mg is oxidised (anode).
  2. Ag+ sits in the denominator: it is consumed, so Ag+ is reduced (cathode).
  3. Cell: Mg | Mg2+ || Ag+ | Ag (reaction Mg + 2Ag+ → Mg2+ + 2Ag).

Answer: option (3) — Mg|Mg2+||Ag+|Ag

TrapOn the cathode side the ion is written before the metal: Ag+ | Ag, not Ag | Ag+.
NoteStrictly Q = [Mg2+]/[Ag+]2 for n = 2; the recalled equation drops the square, which does not change which electrode is which.
Q132CUET 2026 · 11 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q9 also 2026 18 May S2 Q2 (memory-based, collegedunia)key re-derived
The oxidation potentials of A and B are +2.37 V and +1.66 V respectively. In chemical reactions
  1. A will be replaced by B
  2. A will replace B
  3. A will not replace B
  4. A and B will not replace each other
Concept to recallHigher oxidation potential = stronger reducing agent = more reactive; it displaces the less reactive one from its salt solution.
  1. E°ox(A) = 2.37 V > E°ox(B) = 1.66 V (these are Mg and Al).
  2. A loses electrons more readily, so A + Bn+ → Am+ + B is spontaneous: A replaces B.

Answer: option (2) — A will replace B

TrapThese are oxidation potentials: here the larger value means the more reactive metal.
Q133CUET 2026 · 12 May, Shift 2 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q4key re-derived
Which of the following is a strong electrolyte?
  1. Glucose solution
  2. Urea solution
  3. Acetic acid
  4. Sodium chloride solution
Concept to recallStrong electrolytes (salts, strong acids and bases) are almost completely ionised in water; weak ones (CH3COOH) only partly; glucose and urea are non-electrolytes.
  1. Glucose and urea do not ionise.
  2. Acetic acid ionises only slightly (weak).
  3. NaCl is fully ionised: strong electrolyte.

Answer: option (4) — Sodium chloride solution

TrapAcetic acid conducts, but weakly: it is a weak electrolyte.
Q134CUET 2026 · 15 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q1key re-derived
The molar conductivity of 0.5 mol/dm3 solution of AgNO3 with electrolytic conductivity of 5.76 × 10−3 S cm−1 at 298 K is:
  1. 0.086 S cm2/mol
  2. 28.8 S cm2/mol
  3. 2.88 S cm2/mol
  4. 11.52 S cm2/mol
Concept to recallΛm (S cm2 mol−1) = κ (S cm−1) × 1000 / M (mol L−1).
  1. Λm = 5.76 × 10−3 × 1000 / 0.5
  2. = 5.76 / 0.5 = 11.52 S cm2 mol−1.

Answer: option (4) — 11.52 S cm2/mol

TrapForgetting the factor 1000 (L → cm3) gives 0.0115.
Q135CUET 2026 · 19 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q3key re-derived
What is the cell potential (Ecell) for a concentration cell consisting of two hydrogen electrodes at 298 K, where the anode compartment is at pH = 3 and the cathode compartment is at pH = 1 under standard pressure conditions?
  1. 0.0591 V
  2. 0.1182 V
  3. −0.1182 V
  4. 0.0000 V
Concept to recallConcentration cell: E° = 0, E = (0.0591/n) log([ion]cathode/[ion]anode).
  1. [H+] cathode = 10−1 M, anode = 10−3 M; n = 1.
  2. E = 0.0591 log(10−1/10−3) = 0.0591 × 2 = 0.1182 V.

Answer: option (2) — 0.1182 V

TrapSwapping the two concentrations gives the negative value of (3).
Q136CUET 2026 · 19 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q4key re-derived
Which of the following expressions correctly relates the limiting molar conductivity (Λ°m) of aluminum sulfate, Al2(SO4)3, to its individual ionic components according to Kohlrausch’s Law?
  1. Λ°m = λ°(Al3+) + λ°(SO42−)
  2. Λ°m = 2λ°(Al3+) + 3λ°(SO42−)
  3. Λ°m = 3λ°(Al3+) + 2λ°(SO42−)
  4. Λ°m = ½λ°(Al3+) + ⅓λ°(SO42−)
Concept to recallKohlrausch: Λ°m(AxBy) = xλ°+ + yλ°−, with x, y the numbers of ions per formula unit.
  1. Al2(SO4)3 → 2Al3+ + 3SO42−.
  2. So Λ°m = 2λ°(Al3+) + 3λ°(SO42−).

Answer: option (2) — Λ°m = 2λ°(Al3+) + 3λ°(SO42−)

Trap(3) uses the charges instead of the subscripts.
Q137CUET 2026 · 22 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q10key re-derived
During an electrochemistry lab session, a student uses the Nernst Equation to calculate the cell potential (Ecell) of a galvanic system at a non-standard temperature. Which parameter option accurately defines the scaling behavior of the cell potential relative to changes in the reaction quotient (Q)?
  1. As the concentration of product ions increases relative to reactant ions (increasing Q), the value of Ecell decreases.
  2. The value of Ecell increases linearly with an increase in the value of Q.
  3. The value of Ecell remains completely independent of any concentration shifts in Q.
  4. An increase in Q causes an exponential jump in the net electrical voltage produced.
Concept to recallNernst: E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q. E falls (logarithmically) as Q rises.
  1. The ln Q term has a minus sign, so a larger Q lowers E.
  2. The dependence is logarithmic, neither linear nor exponential.

Answer: option (1) — As the concentration of product ions increases relative to reactant ions (increasing Q), the value of Ecell decreases.

TrapProducts up means the reaction is nearer equilibrium, so less driving force.
Q138CUET 2026 · 22 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q7key re-derived
What is the correct official unit measurement scale used to represent Molar Conductivity (Λm) profiles within electrolytic systems?
  1. S cm−2 mol−1
  2. S−1 cm2 mol
  3. Ω cm2 mol−1
  4. S cm2 mol−1
Concept to recallΛm = κ/C: (S cm−1)/(mol cm−3) = S cm2 mol−1.
  1. S cm−1 ÷ mol cm−3 = S cm2 mol−1 (= Ω−1 cm2 mol−1).

Answer: option (4) — S cm2 mol−1

TrapΩ cm2 mol−1 has the ohm upside down.
Q139CUET 2026 · 22 May, Shift 2 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q6key re-derived
When an aqueous solution of an electrolyte is progressively diluted by adding more solvent water, how do its Specific Conductivity (κ) and Molar Conductivity (Λm) respond?
  1. Both Specific Conductivity (κ) and Molar Conductivity (Λm) increase uniformly.
  2. Both Specific Conductivity (κ) and Molar Conductivity (Λm) decrease uniformly.
  3. Specific Conductivity (κ) increases, while Molar Conductivity (Λm) decreases.
  4. Specific Conductivity (κ) decreases, while Molar Conductivity (Λm) increases.
Concept to recallκ = conductance of 1 cm3: fewer ions per cm3 on dilution. Λm = conductance of all the ions from 1 mol: more ions free to move on dilution.
  1. Dilution lowers the number of ions per unit volume: κ falls.
  2. The volume holding one mole grows faster than κ falls (and ionisation/mobility increase): Λm rises.

Answer: option (4) — Specific Conductivity (κ) decreases, while Molar Conductivity (Λm) increases.

TrapThe two move in opposite directions; that is the whole point of this question.
Q140CUET 2026 · 30 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q3key re-derived
The molar conductivities at infinite dilution of HCl, CH3COONa and CH3COOH are 426.0, 91.0 and 390.5 Ω−1 cm2 mol−1, respectively. If the molar conductivity of 0.01 M acetic acid solution is 15.62 Ω−1 cm2 mol−1, the value of Ka is:
  1. 1.8 × 10−5
  2. 1.8 × 10−4
  3. 1.8 × 10−3
  4. 1.8 × 10−6
Concept to recallα = Λm/Λ°m; Ka = Cα2/(1 − α).
  1. Λ°m(CH3COOH) = 390.5 (given directly).
  2. α = 15.62/390.5 = 0.040.
  3. Ka = 0.01 × 0.0402/0.96 = 1.7 × 10−5 ≈ 1.8 × 10−5.

Answer: option (1) — 1.8 × 10−5

TrapUsing Cα2 without dividing by C, or α = 0.4, lands on the wrong power of ten.
NoteThe recalled data give 1.7 × 10−5; the options differ by powers of ten, so (1) is clearly the one intended. (The HCl and CH3COONa values are not needed once Λ°(CH3COOH) is given; in the original question the third value was probably NaCl, 126.5, which gives the same 390.5.)
Q141CUET 2026 · 30 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q4 also 2026 31 May S2 Q4 (memory-based, collegedunia) (as “the cell potential is closest to”, [Zn2+] = 0.10 M, [Cu2+] = 10−3 M, same answer)worked here
For the electrochemical cell Zn | Zn2+(10−2 M) || Cu2+(10−4 M) | Cu at 298 K, E°cell = 1.10 V. The minimum external potential required to just stop the spontaneous cell reaction is closest to:
  1. 0.98 V
  2. 1.04 V
  3. 1.16 V
  4. 1.22 V
Concept to recallTo stop the cell you must oppose its actual emf: E = E° − (0.0591/n) log([Zn2+]/[Cu2+]).
  1. Q = 10−2/10−4 = 102; n = 2.
  2. E = 1.10 − (0.0591/2)(2) = 1.10 − 0.059 = 1.04 V.
  3. An external potential just above 1.04 V stops the reaction.

Answer: option (2) — 1.04 V

TrapProduct ion (Zn2+) in excess lowers the emf below 1.10 V, not above.
NoteThe site prints (3) 1.16 V, but its own working substitutes Q = 102 into the Nernst equation, which gives 1.04 V. 1.16 V would need the log term added instead of subtracted.

  3. 0.50
  4. 0.60

Q143CUET 2025 · 13 May, Shift 1 · Q10NTA final key
A galvanic cell behaves as electrolytic cell when ?
  1. Ecell = Eext
  2. Ecell = 0
  3. Eext > Ecell
  4. Ecell > Eext
Concept to recallAn opposing external potential: Eext < Ecell, current flows from the cell; Eext = Ecell, no current; Eext > Ecell, the reaction runs backwards (electrolysis).
  1. Apply an external potential opposing the Daniell cell (1.1 V).
  2. When Eext exceeds Ecell, electrons are pushed the other way: Zn deposits and Cu dissolves.
  3. The cell now consumes electrical energy: it behaves as an electrolytic cell.

Answer: option (3) — Eext > Ecell

TrapEext = Ecell is the balance point: no current flows at all.

Q153CUET 2025 · 23 May, Shift 2 · Q46 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here
Passage (summarised): electrochemistry

Electrochemistry covers two kinds of process. In galvanic cells such as the Daniell cell the energy of a spontaneous redox reaction is turned into electricity; the Nernst equation relates the cell potential to the standard potential and the concentrations of the species involved. In electrolytic cells electrical energy drives a non-spontaneous reaction. The conductance of an electrolytic solution depends on many factors, including the nature of the electrolyte and the dimensions of the cell.

The conductivity of ionic electrolytic solutions does not depend on:
  1. Concentration of electrolyte.
  2. Viscosity of solvent.
  3. Solvation of ion.
  4. Pressure.
Concept to recallNCERT: conductivity of electrolytic solutions depends on the nature and concentration of the electrolyte, the size and solvation of the ions, the nature and viscosity of the solvent, and temperature.
  1. Concentration, solvent viscosity and ion solvation are all on the NCERT list.
  2. Pressure is not (solutions are nearly incompressible).

Answer: option (4) — Pressure.

  4. (D) Type of electrolyte.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (A), (B) and (D) only
  2. (A), (B) and (C) only
  3. (A), (B), (C) and (D)
  4. (B), (C) and (D) only
Concept to recallNCERT: “The value of the constant A for a given solvent and temperature depends on the type of electrolyte i.e., the charges on the cation and anion produced on the dissociation of the electrolyte.”
  1. Solvent and temperature fix A for a given electrolyte type: (A), (B).
  2. Type of electrolyte (1-1, 2-1, 2-2 ...) = charges on the ions: (C), (D).
  3. All four.

Answer: option (3) — (A), (B), (C) and (D)

NoteThe sentence runs off the edge of the re-typeset page after “Here, the”; the bracketed words are the obvious completion.
Q167CUET 2025 · 26 May, Shift 2 · Q8 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here
While charging the lead storage battery......
  1. PbSO4 on anode is reduced to Pb
  2. PbSO4 on cathode is reduced to Pb
  3. PbSO4 on anode is oxidized to Pb
  4. PbSO4 on cathode is oxidized to Pb
Concept to recallDischarge: anode Pb + SO42− → PbSO4 + 2e−; cathode PbO2 → PbSO4. NCERT: on charging “PbSO4(s) on anode and cathode is converted into Pb and PbO2, respectively” (anode/cathode named as in discharge).
  1. Charging reverses the discharge reactions.
  2. At the Pb plate (the anode of discharge) PbSO4 + 2e− → Pb + SO42−: a reduction.
  3. So PbSO4 on the anode is reduced to Pb.

Answer: option (1) — PbSO4 on anode is reduced to Pb

TrapBecoming Pb (from +2 to 0) is always a reduction, so (3) and (4) are out at once.
NoteDuring charging the Pb plate is, strictly, the cathode of the electrolytic cell, so option (2) is also defensible; the question follows NCERT’s wording, which keeps the discharge names.

Q174CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Sets A–D · Set A Q32NTA final key
Passage (15 May 2024, Q32–36): the H2–O2 fuel cell

A battery or cell converts the chemical energy of a redox reaction into electrical energy. In a fuel cell (a galvanic cell) the energy of combustion of fuels such as H2 or ethanol is converted directly into electricity. In the H2–O2 cell, H2 is oxidised at the anode and O2 reduced at the cathode:
Anode: H2 + 2OH− → 2H2O + 2e−
Cathode: O2 + 2H2O + 4e− → 4OH−
67.2 L of H2 at STP reacts in 15 minutes.

The number of moles of hydrogen oxidised is:
  1. 0.33 moles
  2. 33.3 moles
  3. 3.0 moles
  4. 1.33 moles
Concept to recallAt STP one mole of an ideal gas occupies 22.4 L.
  1. n = 67.2/22.4 = 3.0 mol H2.

Answer: option (3) — 3.0 moles

Q188CUET 2023 · 22 May, Shift 3 · Q2NTA final key

  2. Sn4+(aq)|Sn2+(aq)||Cr3+(aq)|Cr(s)
  3. Cr(s)|Cr3+(aq)||Sn4+(aq)|Sn2+(aq)
  4. Cr(s)|Cr3+(aq)||Sn2+(aq)|Sn4+(aq)
Concept to recallLower E° = anode (left, oxidation); cell notation: anode | anode ion || cathode ions | (cathode).

Q189CUET 2023 · 22 May, Shift 3 · Q36NTA final key
The cell reaction occurring at anode in the electrolysis of aqueous NaCl solution is :

  2. Cl−(aq) → ½Cl2(g) + e−, E°cell = 1.36 V
  3. Na+(aq) + e− → Na(s), E°cell = − 2.71 V
  4. 2H2O(l) → O2(g) + 4H+(aq) + 4e−, E°cell = − 1.23 V
Concept to recallThe anode is where oxidation occurs; O2 evolution has a high overpotential, so Cl− is oxidised.

  2. Thermodynamically water oxidation (1.23 V) is easier, but its overpotential makes Cl− → Cl2 win.

TrapChoosing (4) on E° alone ignores overpotential.

Q192CUET 2023 · 23 May, Shift 3 · Q22NTA final key

Q199CUET 2023 · 26 May, Shift 3 (Oswaal typed copy) · Q13key re-derived

  3. 0.34 V

Concept to recallE°cell = E°cathode − E°anode (both as reduction potentials); 1 M solutions, so E = E°.
  1. Cu (higher E°) is the cathode, Sn the anode.
  2. E = 0.34 − (−0.14) = 0.48 V.

Answer: option (1) — 0.48 V

TrapSubtracting without the sign of the Sn potential gives 0.20 V.
Q200CUET 2023 · 31 May, Shift 2 · Q23NTA final key
What will happen during the electrolysis of aqueous solution of CuSO4 by using platinum electrodes?

  4. D. Oxygen will be released at cathode.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. B and D
  2. C and D
  3. A and C
  4. B and C
Concept to recallInert electrodes: cathode reduces the easiest species (Cu2+, E° = +0.34 V); anode oxidises water (SO42− is not oxidised).

Answer: option (3) — A and C

Q201CUET 2023 · 31 May, Shift 2 · Q27NTA final key
Equilibrium constant is 2 × 1037 at 298K for Zn (s) + Cu2+(aq) → Zn2+(aq) + Cu (s). Predict the spontaneity of cell and calculate E°cell. [log 2 = 0.3010]
  1. Spontaneous, 1.103 V
  2. Non spontaneous, 1.103 V
  3. Spontaneous, 2.206 V
  4. Non spontaneous, 2.206 V
Concept to recallE°cell = (0.0591/n) log K; K > 1 ⇔ E° > 0 ⇔ ΔG° < 0 (spontaneous).
  1. log K = 37.301; n = 2.
  2. E° = 0.02955 × 37.301 = 1.102 V ≈ 1.10 V, positive ⇒ spontaneous.

Answer: option (1) — Spontaneous, 1.103 V

Q202CUET 2023 · 31 May, Shift 2 · Q32NTA final key

Q203CUET 2023 · 5 June, Shift 1 · Q1 · Prepp reconstructionworked here
How much calcium will be obtained when 4 Faradays of electricity is passed through molten CaCl2?
  1. 20 g
  2. 40 g
  3. 80 g
  4. 160 g
Concept to recallFaraday’s first law: Ca2+ + 2e− → Ca, so 2 F deposit 1 mol (40 g) of Ca.
  1. 4 F = 4 mol e− ⇒ 2 mol Ca.
  2. Mass = 2 × 40 = 80 g.

Answer: option (3) — 80 g

Trap160 g assumes one electron per Ca (forgets the 2+ charge).

Q204CUET 2023 · 5 June, Shift 1 · Q2 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
0.01 M aqueous solutions of following salts were prepared. Their conductivity values were measured at 25°C. Which of the following will possess highest conductivity at 25°C?
  1. LiCl
  2. RbCl
  3. NaCl
  4. CsCl
Concept to recallIn water, smaller alkali ions are more heavily hydrated and move more slowly; the large Cs+ ion is least hydrated and most mobile.
  1. Hydrated size: Li+ > Na+ > K+ > Rb+ > Cs+, so mobility runs the other way.
  2. Same anion, same concentration ⇒ CsCl conducts best.

Answer: option (4) — CsCl

NoteThis is the textbook answer. Measured limiting ionic conductivities of Rb+ (77.8) and Cs+ (77.2 S cm2 mol−1) are in fact almost equal, but the hydration argument is what the question expects.
Q205CUET 2023 · 5 June, Shift 1 · Q26 · Prepp reconstructionworked here
When electric current is passed through acidified water, 448 mL of hydrogen gas at STP is collected at the cathode in 965 seconds. The current passed in amperes is:

  2. 2.5
  3. 3.0
  4. 4.0
Concept to recall2H+ + 2e− → H2: 2 F per mol H2; Q = It.

  2. Q = 0.04 × 96500 = 3860 C.
  3. I = 3860/965 = 4.0 A.

Answer: option (4) — 4.0

Q206CUET 2023 · 07 Jun, Shift 3 · Prepp reconstruction · Q18key re-derived

Q207CUET 2023 · 07 Jun, Shift 3 · Prepp reconstruction · Q35key re-derived
The cell Zn | Zn2+ (1 M) || Cu2+ (1 M) | Cu (E°cell = 1.10 V) was allowed to be completely discharged at 298 K. The relative concentration of Zn2+/Cu2+ is:
  1. 9.65 × 104
  2. Antilog 24.8
  3. 37.7
  4. 1037.3
Concept to recallFully discharged cell: Ecell = 0, so [Zn2+]/[Cu2+] = Kc, with log Kc = nE°/0.0591.
  1. At equilibrium E = 0 ⇒ E° = (0.0591/2) log ([Zn2+]/[Cu2+]).
  2. log ratio = 2 × 1.10/0.0591 = 37.2 (37.3 with 0.059).
  3. Ratio ≈ 1037.3.

Q208CUET 2023 · 07 Jun, Shift 3 · Prepp reconstruction · Q4 also CUET 2023 · 10 Jun, Shift 1 · Prepp reconstruction · Q5 (same lists, options reordered; answer there is option (4), (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(II))key re-derived
Match List – I with List – II.
List – IList – II
(A) Λm of KCl increases on dilution(I) is a linear graph
(B) Λm of CH3COOH increases on dilution(II) is a non-linear graph
(C) Λm of KCl versus (molarity)1/2(III) due to increased degree of ionisation
(D) Λm of CH3COOH versus (molarity)1/2(IV) due to weakening of interionic attractions
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
  2. (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
  3. (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
  4. (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(I)
Concept to recallStrong electrolyte: Λm = Λ°m − A√c (straight line), rises on dilution as interionic attraction weakens. Weak electrolyte: Λm rises steeply because α increases; plot is a curve.
  1. KCl (strong): rise on dilution is due to weaker interionic attraction → (A)-(IV); its Λm–√c plot is linear → (C)-(I).
  2. CH3COOH (weak): rise is due to greater ionisation → (B)-(III); plot is non-linear → (D)-(II).

Answer: option (2) — (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)

Q209CUET 2023 · 08 Jun, Shift 3 · Prepp reconstruction · Q18key re-derived

Q212CUET 2023 · 10 Jun, Shift 1 · Prepp reconstruction · Q1key re-derived

Q214CUET 2023 · 11 Jun, Shift 3 · Q31 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
Which of the following statements is incorrect with respect to the plot of molar conductivity (Λm) versus square root of concentration (c1/2) for electrolytes in solution?
  1. For strong electrolytes, a straight line with extrapolatable intercept of limiting molar conductivity (Λ°m) is obtained.

Q215CUET 2023 · 11 Jun, Shift 3 · Q41 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived

Q219CUET 2023 · 11 Jun, Shift 3 · Q45 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived

Q229CUET 2023 · 22 Jun, Shift 2 · Q37NTA final key

  4. 8.8%

Q231CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q13NTA final key
Which of the following statements is not correct about cell potential?
  1. Difference in the electrode potential
  2. Measured when current is flowing
  3. Cell potential depends on temperature
  4. Measured by potentiometer
Concept to recallCell potential = Ecathode − Eanode; it varies with T and concentration (Nernst). It is called the emf when no current is drawn.
  1. (1) and (3) are plainly correct.
  2. NCERT: the emf is the cell potential when no current flows; a potentiometer measures it at the null point (zero current).
  3. NTA’s key marks (4), i.e. it treats “cell potential” as the working potential measured while current flows (by a voltmeter), and the potentiometer as measuring the emf, not the cell potential.

Answer: option (4) — Measured by potentiometer

NoteNTA’s final key is (4), “measured by potentiometer”, i.e. it treats cell potential as the terminal voltage measured while current flows, and a potentiometer as measuring the emf. On the NCERT reading (cell potential = emf, measured at zero current), option (2) “measured when current is flowing” would be the incorrect statement; the key has been kept, but expect this question to be ambiguous.

  1. (B), (C), (D) only
  2. (A), (B), (D) only
  3. (B), (C), (D), (E) only
  4. (A), (C), (E) only
Concept to recallE°cell = (0.0591/n) log Kc at 298 K; ΔG° = −nFE°; Kohlrausch: Λ°m(AxBy) = xλ°+ + yλ°−; G* = l/A = κ/G.
  1. (A) wrong: the denominator is n, not nF.
  2. (B) wrong: Na2SO4 gives two Na+, so 2λ°(Na+) is needed.
  3. (C) right: κ = G × (l/A), so cell constant = κ/G.
  4. (D) wrong: the minus sign is missing (ΔG° = −nFE°).
  5. (E) right: the Daniell cell notation.
  6. Not correct: (A), (B), (D).

Answer: option (2) — (A), (B), (D) only

Q233CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q34NTA final key
Given: E°K+/K = −2.93 V, E°Ag+/Ag = 0.80 V, E°Hg2+/Hg = 0.79 V, E°Mg2+/Mg = −2.37 V, E°Cr3+/Cr = −0.74 V.
Choose the correct order:
  1. (A) Ag < Hg < Cr < Mg < K (increasing reducing power)
  2. (B) Ag < Hg < Cr < Mg < K (decreasing oxidising power)
  3. (C) Ag > Hg > Cr > Mg > K (decreasing oxidising power)
  4. (D) Hg > Cr > Ag > K > Mg (increasing reactivity)
  5. (E) K > Mg > Cr > Hg > Ag (decreasing reactivity order)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (A), (C) and (E) only
  2. (B), (C) and (E) only
  3. (C), (D) and (E) only
  4. (A) and (B) only
Concept to recallThe more negative E°(Mn+/M), the stronger the metal as a reducing agent and the more reactive it is; the more positive, the stronger the oxidising power of the couple.
  1. Order of E°: Ag (0.80) > Hg (0.79) > Cr (−0.74) > Mg (−2.37) > K (−2.93).
  2. Reducing power and reactivity rise in the reverse order: Ag < Hg < Cr < Mg < K ⇒ (A) and (E) right.
  3. Oxidising power falls Ag > Hg > Cr > Mg > K ⇒ (C) right, (B) is backwards.
  4. (D) is jumbled. Answer: (A), (C), (E).

Answer: option (1) — (A), (C) and (E) only

Q234CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q6NTA final key
A galvanic cell converts:
  1. Electrical energy to chemical energy
  2. Chemical energy to electrical energy
  3. Light energy to electrical energy
  4. Electrical energy to light energy
Concept to recallGalvanic (voltaic) cell: a spontaneous redox reaction (ΔG < 0) drives electrons through an external circuit. Electrolytic cell: electrical energy drives a non-spontaneous reaction.
  1. In a galvanic cell, e.g. the Daniell cell, the free energy of Zn + Cu2+ → Zn2+ + Cu appears as electrical work.
  2. So chemical energy → electrical energy.

Answer: option (2) — Chemical energy to electrical energy

TrapOption (1) is the electrolytic cell.
Q235CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q9NTA final key
In the formation of a leclanche cell, the space between electrodes is filled with:
  1. (A) ZnCl2
  2. (B) NH4Cl
  3. (C) AlCl3
  4. (D) ZnS
  5. (E) NH4NO3
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (A) and (E) only
  2. (A) and (B) only
  3. (C) and (D) only
  4. (D) and (E) only
Concept to recallDry (Leclanché) cell: Zn container anode, graphite rod cathode surrounded by MnO2 + carbon; the electrolyte is a moist paste of NH4Cl and ZnCl2.
  1. The space between the electrodes holds a moist paste of ammonium chloride and zinc chloride.
  2. So (A) ZnCl2 and (B) NH4Cl.

Answer: option (2) — (A) and (B) only

Q236CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q6NTA final key
Number of electrons exchanged during the following reaction are/is
2Fe3+(aq) + 2I−(aq) → 2Fe2+(aq) + I2(s)
  1. 1
  2. 2
  3. 3
  4. 4
Concept to recalln in ΔG° = −nFE° is the number of electrons transferred in the balanced equation as written.
  1. Each Fe3+ gains 1 e−; two of them gain 2 e−.
  2. 2I− → I2 + 2e−. So n = 2.

Answer: option (2) — 2

Q237CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q7NTA final key
The reactions taking place during electrolysis of aqueous solution of CuCl2 with platinum electrodes are:
  1. (A) Cu2+(aq) + 2e− → Cu(s)
  2. (B) H+(aq) + e− → ½H2(g)
  3. (C) H2O(l) + e− → ½H2(g) + OH−(aq)
  4. (D) Cl−(aq) → ½Cl2(g) + e−
  5. (E) 2OH−(aq) → H2O(l) + ½O2(g) + 2e−
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. A and E only
  2. A and D only
  3. A and B only
  4. A and C only
Concept to recallCathode: the species with the higher reduction potential is reduced (Cu2+, +0.34 V, beats water). Anode (inert Pt): Cl− is oxidised in preference to water because of the overpotential of O2.
  1. Cathode: Cu2+ + 2e− → Cu (A).
  2. Anode: Cl− → ½Cl2 + e− (D).
  3. Answer: A and D.

Answer: option (2) — A and D only

Q238CUET 2022 · 10 Aug, Shift 1 (SET 06) · Q5NTA final key
Among the following statements related to ionic conductance, choose the correct statements.
(A) Ionic conductance depends on the nature of electrolyte
(B) Ionic conductance is due to the movements of electrons
(C) Ionic conductance is also called electronic conductance
(D) Ionic conductance depends on temperature
(E) Ionic conductance also depends on the nature of solvent
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. A, B and C only
  2. B, C and D only
  3. B, C and E only
  4. A, D and E only
Concept to recallElectrolytic (ionic) conductance is carried by moving ions; it depends on the electrolyte, the solvent (its viscosity), concentration and temperature.
  1. B and C describe metallic (electronic) conduction — false for ionic conductance.
  2. A, D, E are the listed factors that govern ionic conductance.

Answer: option (4) — A, D and E only

TrapElectronic conductance is the metallic kind; ionic conductance is by migration of ions.
Q239CUET 2022 · 10 Aug, Shift 1 (SET 06) · Q6NTA final key
Λom for NaCl, HCl and NaOAc are 126.4, 425.9 and 91.0 S cm2 mol−1 respectively. Calculate Λ° for HOAc
  1. 390.5 S cm2 mol−1
  2. 643.3 S cm2 mol−1
  3. 461.3 S cm2 mol−1
  4. 208.5 S cm2 mol−1
Concept to recallKohlrausch: Λ°(HOAc) = Λ°(HCl) + Λ°(NaOAc) − Λ°(NaCl).
  1. Add the two salts/acids that contain H+ and OAc−; subtract the one that brings in the unwanted Na+ and Cl−.
  2. Λ° = 425.9 + 91.0 − 126.4 = 390.5 S cm2 mol−1.

Answer: option (1) — 390.5 S cm2 mol−1

TrapAdding all three (643.3) or the wrong subtraction (208.5, 461.3).
Q240CUET 2022 · 10 Aug, Shift 1 (SET 06) · Q7NTA final key
How much charge is required for the reduction of 1 mol of MnO4− to Mn2+ ?
  1. 1 F
  2. 5 F
  3. 3 F
  4. 6 F
Concept to recallCharge = n F, where n is the change in oxidation number per ion.
  1. Mn goes from +7 (MnO4−) to +2.
  2. n = 5 electrons per ion ⇒ 5 F per mole.

Answer: option (2) — 5 F

Q241CUET 2022 · 10 Aug, Shift 1 (SET 06) · Q8NTA final key
The products formed at cathode and anode by electrolysis of aqueous NaCl solution respectively are
  1. Na, Cl2
  2. Na, O2
  3. H2, Cl2
  4. H2, O2
Concept to recallIn aqueous electrolysis the species easiest to reduce/oxidise reacts; overpotential of O2 makes Cl− discharge at the anode.
  1. Cathode: H2O is reduced (E° −0.83 V) far more easily than Na+ (−2.71 V) ⇒ H2.
  2. Anode: O2 formation needs a large overpotential, so Cl− → Cl2.

Answer: option (3) — H2, Cl2

TrapNa metal is obtained only from molten NaCl.

Chemical Kinetics121 questions

Q242CUET 2026 · 24 May, Shift 1 · Q10NTA final key
The constant ‘k’ in a rate law expression of a reaction is
  1. is dependent on the concentration of reactants.
  2. is dimensionless.
  3. dependent on temperature.
  4. called the Arrhenius constant.
Concept to recallRate constant k = A e−Ea/RT: independent of concentration, depends on T; units (mol L−1)1−n s−1.
  1. k does not change with concentration, and it has units except by accident of order.
  2. The Arrhenius constant is A, not k. k rises with temperature: the correct statement.

Answer: option (3) — dependent on temperature.

Q243CUET 2026 · 24 May, Shift 1 · Q12NTA final key
Hydrogenation of ethene represented by,
C2H4(g) + H2(g) → C2H6(g)
is an example of
  1. Second order reaction.
  2. First order reaction.
  3. Zero-order reaction.
  4. Third Order reaction.
Concept to recallOrder is found by experiment, not from the equation. NCERT: rate = k[C2H4] for hydrogenation of ethene.
  1. The experimental rate law is rate = k[C2H4]; H2 does not appear.
  2. So the order is 1.

Answer: option (2) — First order reaction.

TrapMolecularity of the equation is 2, but order is not read from stoichiometry.
Q244CUET 2026 · 24 May, Shift 1 · Q13NTA final key
Species that are formed in one step of reaction mechanism and used up in another step are called
  1. catalysts
  2. inhibitors
  3. intermediates
  4. promotors
Concept to recallIntermediate: made in one elementary step, consumed in a later one. A catalyst is consumed first and regenerated.
  1. Formed then used up = intermediate (e.g. IO− in H2O2 + I− decomposition).
  2. A catalyst is the opposite: used first, regenerated later.

Answer: option (3) — intermediates

Q245CUET 2026 · 24 May, Shift 1 · Q15NTA final key
Among the following, which are examples of first-order reactions?
(A) 22688Ra → 42He + 22286Rn
(B) 2NH3 →(1130 K, Pt catalyst) N2(g) + 3H2(g)
(C) 2N2O5(g) → 2N2O4(g) + O2(g)
(D) C2H4(g) + H2 → C2H6(g)
  1. (A), (B) and (D) only
  2. (A) and (C) only
  3. (B), (C) and (D) only
  4. (A), (C) and (D) only
Concept to recallFirst order (NCERT examples): radioactive decay, N2O5 decomposition, hydrogenation of ethene. NH3 on hot Pt is zero order (surface saturated).
  1. All radioactive decay is first order: (A).
  2. N2O5 decomposition, rate = k[N2O5]: (C).
  3. Ethene hydrogenation, rate = k[C2H4]: (D).
  4. NH3 on Pt at high pressure: rate = k, zero order, so (B) is out.

Answer: option (4) — (A), (C) and (D) only

Q246CUET 2026 · 24 May, Shift 1 · Q16NTA final key
Arrange the following rate expressions (of hypothetical reactions) in the increasing arrangement of their order of reaction: Assume the concentrations of A and B in all the rate expressions is same.
(A) Rate = k[A]1/2[B]3/2 (B) Rate = k[A]1/2[B]1/2 (C) Rate = k[A]3/2[B]−1 (D) Rate = k[A]2[B]1
  1. (A), (B), (C), (D)
  2. (C), (B), (A), (D)
  3. (B), (A), (D), (C)
  4. (C), (B), (D), (A)
Concept to recallOverall order = sum of the exponents in the rate law (may be fractional or include a negative term).
  1. (A) 1/2 + 3/2 = 2; (B) 1/2 + 1/2 = 1; (C) 3/2 − 1 = 1/2; (D) 2 + 1 = 3.
  2. Increasing: C (1/2) < B (1) < A (2) < D (3).

Answer: option (2) — (C), (B), (A), (D)

Q247CUET 2026 · 6 June, Shift 1 · Q1NTA final key
For the following reaction choose the incorrect expression of rate of reaction.
5Br−(aq) + BrO3−(aq) + 6H+(aq) → 3Br2(aq) + 3H2O(l)
  1. Rate = −15 Δ[Br−]Δt
  2. Rate = −16 Δ[H+]Δt
  3. Rate = −13 Δ[Br2]Δt
  4. Rate = −Δ[BrO3−]Δt
Concept to recallRate = −(1/a) d[reactant]/dt = +(1/b) d[product]/dt: minus sign for reactants (they decrease), plus for products.
  1. Reactants Br−, H+, BrO3− carry a minus sign with 1/5, 1/6, 1/1: those three are right.
  2. Br2 is a product, so Rate = +(1/3)Δ[Br2]/Δt. The minus sign makes that expression incorrect.

Answer: option (3) — Rate = −13 Δ[Br2]Δt

TrapThe coefficient 1/3 is right; the sign is what is wrong.
Q248CUET 2026 · 6 June, Shift 1 · Q20NTA final key
Match List-I with List-II
List-IList-II
(A) Collision Theory(I) k = ([R]0 − [R])/t
(B) Arrhenius Equation(II) k = A e−Ea/RT
(C) Rate constant for zero order(III) k = (1/t) ln([R]0/[R])
(D) Rate constant for first order(IV) Rate = PZABe−Ea/RT
  1. (A)–(IV), (B)–(II), (C)–(III), (D)–(I)
  2. (A)–(IV), (B)–(II), (C)–(I), (D)–(III)
  3. (A)–(II), (B)–(IV), (C)–(I), (D)–(III)
  4. (A)–(II), (B)–(IV), (C)–(III), (D)–(I)
Concept to recallCollision theory: rate = P ZAB e−Ea/RT. Zero order: [R] = [R]0 − kt. First order: k = (1/t) ln([R]0/[R]).
  1. (A)–(IV), (B)–(II).
  2. Zero order is linear in [R]: (C)–(I). First order has the log: (D)–(III).

Answer: option (2) — (A)–(IV), (B)–(II), (C)–(I), (D)–(III)

Q249CUET 2026 · 6 June, Shift 1 · Q22NTA final key
75% of a first order reaction was completed in 32 minutes. How long will it take to undergo 50% completion? Given: log 2 = 0.3010
  1. 8 min
  2. 12 min
  3. 16 min
  4. 24 min
Concept to recallFirst order: t75% = 2 t1/2 (two half-lives take 100% → 50% → 25%).
  1. 75% complete means 25% left = two half-lives.
  2. t1/2 = 32/2 = 16 min.

Answer: option (3) — 16 min

Q250CUET 2026 · 6 June, Shift 1 · Q37NTA final key
Choose the correct statements
(A) For a gaseous reaction, if the concentration of gas is expressed in terms of their partial pressure ‘atm’ and time in ‘minutes’ then unit of rate are atm−1 min.
(B) The sum of power of the concentration of the reactants in the rate law expression is called order of that reaction.
(C) The thermal decomposition of HI on gold surface is an example of second order reaction.
(D) The overall rate of the reaction is controlled by the slowest step in a reaction called the rate determining step.
  1. (A) and (B) only
  2. (B) and (C) only
  3. (C) and (D) only
  4. (B) and (D) only
Concept to recallRate = change in concentration (or pressure) per unit time: atm min−1. Decomposition of HI on gold is zero order (surface saturated).
  1. (A) false as printed: the unit is atm min−1, not atm−1 min.
  2. (B) true: definition of order.
  3. (C) false: HI on gold is zero order.
  4. (D) true: the slowest step is rate determining.

Answer: option (4) — (B) and (D) only

Q251CUET 2026 · 6 June, Shift 1 · Q4NTA final key
The order of a reaction whose rate constant k = 0.693 × 10−6 L mol−1 s−1 is
  1. 0
  2. 1
  3. 2
  4. 3
Concept to recallUnits of k = (mol L−1)1−n s−1: zero order mol L−1 s−1, first s−1, second L mol−1 s−1.
  1. L mol−1 s−1 = (mol L−1)−1 s−1, so 1 − n = −1 and n = 2.

Answer: option (3) — 2

Trap0.693 suggests ln 2 and first order, but the units decide.
Q252CUET 2026 · 11 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q3 also 2026 11 May S1 Q10 (memory-based, collegedunia) (repeated within the same set)key re-derived
The rate of the reaction, 2NO + Cl2 → 2NOCl is given by the rate equation, rate = k[NO]2[Cl2]. The value of the rate constant can be increased by
  1. increasing the concentration of NO.
  2. increasing the temperature.
  3. increasing the concentration of the Cl2.
  4. doing all of these.
Concept to recallk depends on temperature (k = A e−Ea/RT) and on a catalyst, never on concentrations.
  1. Raising [NO] or [Cl2] raises the rate, not k.
  2. Raising T makes e−Ea/RT larger, so k increases.

Answer: option (2) — increasing the temperature.

Trap“Rate” and “rate constant” are different: concentration changes only the first.
Q253CUET 2026 · 15 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q2key re-derived
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R:
Assertion (A): A reaction can have zero activation energy.
Reason (R): The minimum extra amount of energy absorbed by reactant molecules so that their energy becomes equal to threshold value, is called activation energy.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
  2. Both A and R are true and R is NOT the correct explanation of A
  3. A is true but R is false
  4. A is false but R is true
Concept to recallEa = threshold energy − average energy of the reactants. If the reactants already have the threshold energy (e.g. radical recombination), Ea = 0.
  1. R is the textbook definition of activation energy: true.
  2. A is also true: Ea can be zero when the reactants already possess the threshold energy (radical–radical combination has Ea ≈ 0).
  3. R defines Ea but does not explain why it can vanish: (2).

Answer: option (2) — Both A and R are true and R is NOT the correct explanation of A

TrapDo not mark A false just because almost every reaction has an energy barrier.
Q254CUET 2026 · 15 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q3key re-derived
The following data is for a reaction between reactants A and B:
Rate (mol L−1 s−1)[A][B]
2 × 10−30.1 M0.1 M
4 × 10−30.2 M0.1 M
1.6 × 10−20.2 M0.2 M
The order of the reaction with respect to A and B, respectively are:
  1. 1, 0
  2. 0, 1
  3. 1, 2
  4. 2, 1
Concept to recallMethod of initial rates: change one concentration, keep the other fixed, and compare rates: rate ratio = (concentration ratio)order.
  1. Rows 1→2: [A] doubles, [B] fixed; rate 2 → 4 (×2): order in A = 1.
  2. Rows 2→3: [B] doubles, [A] fixed; rate 4 → 16 (×4 = 22): order in B = 2.

Answer: option (3) — 1, 2

TrapRows 1 and 3 change both concentrations at once: never compare them directly.
Q255CUET 2026 · 15 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q4 also 2026 19 May S1 Q1 (memory-based, collegedunia) (as “90% in time t: 99.9% takes?”, answer 3t)key re-derived
t99.9% with respect to t90% for a first order reaction is:
  1. Two
  2. One
  3. Three
  4. Four
Concept to recallFirst order: t = (2.303/k) log([R]0/[R]).
  1. t90% = (2.303/k) log 10 = 2.303/k.
  2. t99.9% = (2.303/k) log 1000 = 3 × 2.303/k.
  3. Ratio = 3.

Answer: option (3) — Three

Trap99.9% is not “a bit more than 90%”: it takes three times as long.
Q256CUET 2026 · 15 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q5key re-derived
99% of a first order reaction was completed in 32 minutes. When will 99.9% of the reaction complete?
  1. 48 minute
  2. 49 minute
  3. 46 minute
  4. 50 minute
Concept to recallFirst order: t ∝ log([R]0/[R]); 99% done means log 100 = 2, 99.9% means log 1000 = 3.
  1. t99% = (2.303/k) × 2 = 32 min.
  2. t99.9% = (2.303/k) × 3 = 32 × 3/2 = 48 min.

Answer: option (1) — 48 minute

Q257CUET 2026 · 15 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q6key re-derived
The slope of Arrhenius Plot (ln k v/s 1/T) of the first-order reaction is −5 × 103 K. The value of Ea of the reaction is. Choose the correct option for your answer. [Given R = 8.314 J K−1 mol−1]
  1. 166 kJ mol−1
  2. −83 kJ mol−1
  3. 41.5 kJ mol−1
  4. 83.0 kJ mol−1
Concept to recallln k = ln A − Ea/(RT): slope of ln k vs 1/T = −Ea/R. (For log10 k the slope is −Ea/2.303R.)
  1. Ea = −slope × R = 5 × 103 × 8.314 J mol−1
  2. = 41 570 J mol−1 ≈ 41.5 kJ mol−1.

Answer: option (3) — 41.5 kJ mol−1

Trap83 kJ comes from wrongly doubling; 95.7 kJ would come from using the log10 slope formula on an ln plot.
Q258CUET 2026 · 18 May, Shift 2 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q1worked here
For the reaction
2A + B → 3C + D
Which of the following does not express the reaction rate?
  1. −d[B]dt
  2. d[D]dt
  3. −12 d[A]dt
  4. 13 d[C]dt
Concept to recallRate of reaction = −(1/a) d[reactant]/dt = +(1/c) d[product]/dt, each divided by its stoichiometric coefficient so that every expression gives the same number.
  1. Rate = −½ d[A]/dt = −d[B]/dt = ⅓ d[C]/dt = d[D]/dt.
  2. All four options are on this list, so every one of them expresses the rate.
  3. No option “does not express” it.

No option is correct as printed — see the note.

TrapB has coefficient 1 and D has coefficient 1, so −d[B]/dt and d[D]/dt need no factor.
NoteNo option is correct as recalled. The site prints (1), −d[B]/dt, but its own rate expression contains exactly that term. The original question probably had a wrongly scaled term such as −d[A]/dt or d[C]/dt.
Q259CUET 2026 · 19 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q2key re-derived
According to collision theory, increasing the starting concentration of a collection of reacting molecules directly results in a change in which of the following system factors?
  1. Activation energy
  2. Collision frequency
  3. Rate constant
  4. Fraction of molecules with energy greater than activation energy
Concept to recallRate = P ZAB e−Ea/RT. Concentration changes the collision frequency Z; temperature changes the energetic fraction e−Ea/RT.
  1. More molecules per unit volume collide more often: Z rises.
  2. Ea, k and the fraction above Ea are set by the reaction and the temperature.

Answer: option (2) — Collision frequency

TrapThe fraction of energetic molecules is a temperature effect.
Q260CUET 2026 · 21 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q9key re-derived
The half-life of a first order reaction is 1386 s. The rate constant k is:
  1. 5 × 10−4 s−1
  2. 2 × 10−4 s−1
  3. 1 × 10−3 s−1
  4. 4 × 10−3 s−1
Concept to recallFirst order: t1/2 = 0.693/k, independent of concentration.
  1. k = 0.693/1386 s = 5.0 × 10−4 s−1.

Answer: option (1) — 5 × 10−4 s−1

Q261CUET 2026 · 22 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q1key re-derived
A first-order reaction has a specific rate constant (k) equal to 2.303 × 10−3 s−1. Calculate the exact time required for the initial concentration of the reactant to be reduced to exactly 1/10th of its original value.
  1. 100 s
  2. 2303 s
  3. 1000 s
  4. 693 s
Concept to recallFirst order: t = (2.303/k) log([R]0/[R]).
  1. [R]0/[R] = 10, so log 10 = 1.
  2. t = 2.303/(2.303 × 10−3) = 1000 s.

Answer: option (3) — 1000 s

Trap693 s would be the half-life with k = 10−3; this question asks for 90% completion.
Q262CUET 2026 · 29 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q4 also 2026 29 May S2 Q5 (memory-based, collegedunia)key re-derived
The SI unit of rate constant for a first order reaction is:
  1. mol L−1 s−1
  2. s−1
  3. L mol−1 s−1
  4. mol−1 L s−1
Concept to recallUnits of k = (mol L−1)1−n s−1 for order n.
  1. n = 1: (mol L−1)0 s−1 = s−1.

Answer: option (2) — s−1

Q263CUET 2026 · 30 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q5key re-derived
For a first-order reaction, the rate constant increases by a factor of 16 when the temperature is increased from 300 K to 340 K. The activation energy of the reaction is closest to:
  1. 28 kJ mol−1
  2. 57 kJ mol−1
  3. 85 kJ mol−1
  4. 114 kJ mol−1
Concept to recalllog(k2/k1) = (Ea/2.303R)(T2 − T1)/(T1T2).
  1. log 16 = 1.204; (T2 − T1)/(T1T2) = 40/102 000 = 3.92 × 10−4 K−1.
  2. Ea = 1.204 × 2.303 × 8.314 / 3.92 × 10−4 = 5.88 × 104 J mol−1.
  3. ≈ 59 kJ mol−1; the closest option is 57.

Answer: option (2) — 57 kJ mol−1

TrapDropping the 2.303 gives about 25 kJ, near (1).
NoteThe exact value is 58.8 kJ mol−1; the site also gets 5.88 × 104 J and picks 57 as closest.

Q267CUET 2025 · 13 May, Shift 1 · Q41NTA final key
Passage (summarised): rate of reaction and catalysts

The rate of a reaction is the speed at which it takes place; it depends on factors such as the concentration of the reactants and the temperature. The rate law is written r = k[A]x[B]y, where x and y are the orders with respect to A and B, and the overall order is x + y. A catalyst raises the rate by providing an alternative pathway of lower activation energy; it speeds the forward and backward reactions equally and does not change the Gibbs energy of the reaction.

The rate of a gaseous reaction is given by r = k[A][B]. If the volume of the reaction vessel is suddenly reduced to (1/4)th of its initial value, the reaction rate relating to the initial rate will become
  1. 2 times
  2. 1/4 times
  3. 16 times
  4. 1/16 times
Concept to recallConcentration = n/V. Shrinking the volume to 1/4 multiplies every concentration by 4.
  1. [A] and [B] each become 4 times.
  2. r′ = k(4[A])(4[B]) = 16 r.

Answer: option (3) — 16 times

Trap1/16 comes from thinking the concentrations fall when the volume falls.

Q271CUET 2025 · 13 May, Shift 1 · Q45NTA final key
Passage (summarised): rate of reaction and catalysts

The rate of a reaction is the speed at which it takes place; it depends on factors such as the concentration of the reactants and the temperature. The rate law is written r = k[A]x[B]y, where x and y are the orders with respect to A and B, and the overall order is x + y. A catalyst raises the rate by providing an alternative pathway of lower activation energy; it speeds the forward and backward reactions equally and does not change the Gibbs energy of the reaction.

The role of a catalyst is to change
  1. Gibbs energy of the reaction.
  2. Enthalpy of a reaction.
  3. Activation energy of a reaction.
  4. Equilibrium constant.
Concept to recallA catalyst lowers Ea through an alternative path; ΔH, ΔG and K are state properties it cannot change.
  1. The catalyst offers a path of lower activation energy.
  2. It speeds forward and reverse reactions equally, so ΔG and K stay the same; ΔH is unchanged too.

Answer: option (3) — Activation energy of a reaction.

Which of the following statements, for the reaction of type A → B, are correct?

  3. (C) false: the rate law is k[A]2, not k[2A]2.

2N2O5(g) → 4NO2(g) + O2(g)

  1. 4.07 × 10−2 mol L−1 h−1, 6.79 × 10−4 mol L−1 min−1, 1.13 × 10−5 mol L−1 s−1
  2. 2.907 × 10−2 mol L−1 h−1, 6.79 × 10−4 mol L−1 min−1, 1.13 × 10−5 mol L−1 s−1
  3. 12.07 × 10−2 mol L−1 h−1, 7.79 × 10−4 mol L−1 min−1, 5.13 × 10−5 mol L−1 s−1
  4. 8.1 × 10−2 mol L−1 h−1, 13.5 × 10−4 mol L−1 min−1, 2.25 × 10−5 mol L−1 s−1

Q298CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Sets A–D · Set A Q46NTA final key

  2. Increase by eight times of its initial value
  3. Increase by four times of its initial value
  4. Remain unchanged
Concept to recallRate = k[A2]2[X]; doubling the volume halves every concentration.

Q299CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Sets A–D · Set A Q49NTA final key

Q300CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Sets A–D · Set A Q50NTA final key
For a complex reaction, the order of reaction is equal to
  1. Sum of stoichiometric coefficients in balanced chemical reaction
  2. The molecularity of overall reaction
  3. Order of fastest step of the reaction
  4. The molecularity of slowest step of reaction
Concept to recallThe overall rate of a complex reaction is controlled by its slowest (rate-determining) step; for an elementary step, order = molecularity.
  1. The slowest step is rate-determining, so its molecularity (an elementary step) gives the order.
  2. Stoichiometric coefficients of the overall equation do not fix the order.

Answer: option (4) — The molecularity of slowest step of reaction

NoteStrictly, the order of a complex reaction is found by experiment; the slow-step rule holds when no intermediate appears in that step. NTA keys option (4).
Q301CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Sets A–D · Set A Q7NTA final key

Q313CUET 2023 · 22 May, Shift 3 · Q34NTA final key
Which of the following is not correct about the order of a reaction ?

  1. E.g. 2N2O5 → 4NO2 + O2 is first order, not second.

Q315CUET 2023 · 23 May, Shift 3 · Q23NTA final key

Q316CUET 2023 · 23 May, Shift 3 · Q27NTA final key
If we plot graph for first order reaction involving reactant R, then it will be a straight line if plotted for :

Q318CUET 2023 · 25 May, Shift 3 · Q34 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
The activation energy for a reaction at a temperature T K was found to be 2.303 RT J/mol. The ratio of the rate constant to Arrhenius factor is

Q319CUET 2023 · 25 May, Shift 3 · Q4 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
According to Arrhenius rate equation, rate constant k is equal to Ae−Ea/RT. Which of the following options represents the graph of ln k vs 1/T?

  4. Graph (4): a rising line cutting the 1/T axis
Concept to recallln k = ln A − (Ea/R)(1/T): straight line, slope −Ea/R (negative), intercept ln A.

Trapln k rises with T, so it falls as 1/T grows; a rising line would need a negative activation energy.
Q320CUET 2023 · 26 May, Shift 3 (Oswaal typed copy) · Q29key re-derived

Q324CUET 2023 · 31 May, Shift 2 · Q19NTA final key

Q326CUET 2023 · 5 June, Shift 1 · Q4 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived

Q327CUET 2023 · 5 June, Shift 1 · Q8 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived

Q340CUET 2023 · 11 Jun, Shift 3 · Q4 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
Which of the following statements is incorrect with respect to the use of a catalyst in the reversible reaction?

  3. The catalyst decreases the activation energy of the overall reaction.
  4. The catalyst itself does not undergo any chemical change.
Concept to recallA catalyst lowers Ea of the forward and reverse steps equally; it does not shift the equilibrium.

  2. Hence “only the forward reaction” is the wrong statement.

Answer: option (1) — The catalyst increases the rate of only the forward reaction.

Q354CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q25NTA final key

Q356CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q7NTA final key
The incorrect equation for Arrhenius equation for activation energy is:
  1. ln k = ln A − EaRT ln e

Concept to recallk = A e−Ea/RT ⇒ ln k = ln A − Ea/RT ⇒ log k = log A − Ea/(2.303 RT); two temperatures: log(k2/k1) = [Ea/2.303R][(T2−T1)/T1T2].
  1. (1): ln e = 1, so it is ln k = ln A − Ea/RT — correct.
  2. (3) and (4) are the standard two-temperature and logarithmic forms — correct.
  3. (2) puts log A in the denominator instead of adding it: log k = −Ea/(2.303 R T log A) is not the Arrhenius equation.

Q357CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q1NTA final key

TrapAdding all four (100 kJ) ignores that the constants in the denominator subtract.

  4. Actinoids show a greater range of oxidation states than lanthanoids
Concept to recallLanthanoids are soft, silvery-white metals; hardness rises along the series (samarium is steel-hard).

  2. Poor 5f shielding makes the actinoid contraction larger: true; actinoids show more oxidation states: true.
  3. Lanthanoids are soft metals that tarnish readily, so “all are hard” is the incorrect statement.

Concept to recall3d10 alone does not decide stability: Cu2+(aq) is the more stable ion because its hydration enthalpy is far more negative, which more than repays the second ionisation enthalpy (NCERT, d- and f-block elements).

NoteThis is an NCERT Exemplar MCQ (Unit 8), whose key is “Cu(II) is more stable”; its second option there reads “Cu(II) is less stable”, so the recalled (2) “Cu(I) is less stable” is probably a slip of memory. Q383CUET 2026 · 22 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q8key re-derived
The steady, progressive decrease in the atomic and ionic radii of transition metals along the lanthanide series (Lanthanide Contraction) is primarily caused by:
  1. A continuous decrease in the absolute nuclear proton count within the central atomic cores.
  2. The exceptionally poor shielding effect of the diffuse 4f-electrons, which allows the increasing nuclear charge to pull the outer electron shell inward.
  3. The strong shielding ability of the 5d-electrons completely blocking the nuclear pull.
  4. A sudden jump in the principal quantum number of the outer valence shells.
Concept to recallEach step adds one proton and one 4f electron; 4f electrons shield one another poorly, so the effective nuclear charge on the outer shell rises and the size falls.
  1. Nuclear charge increases (not decreases) across the series.
  2. Poor 4f shielding lets the growing charge pull the 5s5p6s shell in: (2).

Answer: option (2) — The exceptionally poor shielding effect of the diffuse 4f-electrons, which allows the increasing nuclear charge to pull the outer electron shell inward.

TrapThe cause is poor shielding, not strong shielding.

Q397CUET 2025 · 21 May, Shift 2 · Q46 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here
Passage (summarised): catalytic activity of transition metals

Transition metals and their compounds are good catalysts because they can adopt several oxidation states and can form complexes. Examples: vanadium(V) oxide in the Contact process, finely divided iron, and nickel in catalytic hydrogenation. On a solid catalyst, bonds form between reactant molecules and surface atoms (the first-row metals use their 3d and 4s electrons); this raises the concentration of reactants at the surface and weakens bonds in the reacting molecules, lowering the activation energy. Because transition-metal ions can change oxidation state, they are especially effective catalysts.

  1. TiCl4
  2. PdCl2
  3. MnO2
  4. KMnO4
Concept to recallNCERT industrial catalysts: Wacker process (ethene → ethanal) PdCl2; Ziegler–Natta TiCl4 + Al(CH3)3; Contact process V2O5; Haber process Fe.
  1. CH2=CH2 + ½O2 → CH3CHO, with PdCl2 (CuCl2 re-oxidises Pd).

Answer: option (2) — PdCl2

In the form of dichromate, Cr(VI) is a strong oxidising agent in acidic medium but Mo(VI) in MoO3 and W(VI) in WO3 are not. Choose the correct reason from the options given below:

  2. (B) Mo(VI) and W(VI) are more stable than Cr(VI)
  3. (C) Higher oxidation states of heavier members of group-6 of transition series are more stable
  4. (D) Lower oxidation states of heavier members of group-6 of transition series are more stable
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (A), and (D) only
  2. (A) and (C) only
  3. (B) and (C) only
  4. (B), and (D) only
Concept to recallDown a d-block group (3d → 4d → 5d) the higher oxidation states become more stable; an unstable high state is a strong oxidant because it wants to be reduced.
  1. Cr(VI) readily goes to Cr(III): it is unstable, hence oxidising.
  2. Mo(VI), W(VI) are stable, so they do not oxidise: (B) true.
  3. Reason: higher states are favoured for heavier members: (C) true.

Answer: option (3) — (B) and (C) only

TrapThis is the reverse of the p-block, where the inert-pair effect stabilises the lower states of heavy members.

  3. stability of Cu+ and Cu2+ depends on nature of copper salt
  4. Cu+ and Cu2+ are equally stable
Concept to recallIn water Cu2+(aq) is more stable than Cu+(aq) despite the d10 configuration of Cu+: the much more negative hydration enthalpy of the small, doubly charged ion outweighs the second ionisation enthalpy. So 2Cu+ → Cu2+ + Cu.

  2. Cu+ 3d10, Cu2+ 3d9, yet Cu2+(aq) is more stable: (2) true.

Answer: option (2) — Cu+ is 3d10 and Cu2+ is 3d9 but Cu2+ is more stable.

  3. 4.90 BM
  4. 3.87 BM

Q416CUET 2025 · 27 May, Shift 2 · Q46 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here
Passage (27 May, Q46–50): dichromate and permanganate

Na2Cr2O7 and K2Cr2O7 are strong oxidants in acid: Cr2O72− + 14H+ + 6e− → 2Cr3+ + 7H2O (E° = 1.33 V). Chromate and dichromate interconvert with pH. Chromate is tetrahedral; dichromate is two tetrahedra sharing a corner (Cr–O–Cr angle 126°). KMnO4 is made by fusing MnO2 with an alkali hydroxide and an oxidant such as KNO3, giving dark green K2MnO4, which disproportionates in neutral or acid solution to permanganate. Permanganate is a strong oxidant whose reduction product (manganate, MnO2 or Mn2+) depends on the H+ concentration; its dark purple crystals are isostructural with KClO4; it is only moderately soluble (6.4 g per 100 g water at 293 K) and decomposes at 513 K.

  1. 2
  2. 3/5
  3. 2/5
  4. 1/5

  1. 2MnO4− + 16H+ + 5S2− → 2Mn2+ + 8H2O + 5S.
  2. Per mole of S2−: 2/5 mol KMnO4.

Answer: option (3) — 2/5

TrapInverting the electron ratio gives 5/2; one sulphide supplies 2 electrons, one permanganate takes 5.

Concept to recallHaber process N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3: iron catalyst (made from iron oxide, promoted with K2O and Al2O3).
  1. V2O5 is the contact-process catalyst; Pt is used in the Ostwald process.
  2. Haber uses iron, prepared from iron oxide: (1).

Answer: option (1) — Iron oxide

TrapV2O5 belongs to H2SO4 manufacture.
NoteIn the syllabus: NCERT’s d-block chapter (catalytic properties) names finely divided iron as the Haber-process catalyst. Strictly the active catalyst is iron metal, reduced from the iron oxide charged into the converter; iron oxide is the only iron option offered.
Q422CUET 2025 · date unknown · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q2key re-derived
Which of the following compounds will be repelled when placed in an external magnetic field?
  1. FeCl3
  2. FeSO4
  3. NaCl
  4. CuSO4
Concept to recallDiamagnetic substances (all electrons paired) are weakly repelled; paramagnetic ones (unpaired electrons) are attracted.
  1. Fe3+ d5, Fe2+ d6, Cu2+ d9: all have unpaired electrons.
  2. Na+ and Cl− are closed-shell: NaCl is diamagnetic and is repelled.

Answer: option (3) — NaCl

TrapThe three transition-metal salts are all paramagnetic.
NoteAnswerable from the magnetic properties of transition-metal ions (d-block unit), so treated as in the CUET 2026 syllabus.
Q423CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Sets A–D · Set A Q37NTA final key
Passage (15 May 2024, Q37–41): d- and f-block elements

The passage lists the three transition series (Sc–Zn, Y–Cd, La and Hf–Hg) and notes that, moving left to right in a series, the d orbitals fill progressively and properties change accordingly. It then lists the lanthanoids (Ce–Lu) and actinoids (Th–Lr), whose chemical properties change little across the series; the 5f elements are radioactive and mostly synthesised artificially, so less is known about their chemistry.

Identify the incorrect statement.
  1. Second ionisation enthalpy of Ag is greater than second ionisation enthalpy of Pd.
  2. Zr and Hf shares almost identical nuclear properties.
  3. Melting point of Mn is lower than that of Cr.
  4. Interstitial compounds are non-stoichiometric and neither ionic nor covalent in nature.
Concept to recallLanthanoid contraction makes Zr and Hf almost the same size, so their chemical properties are almost identical; their nuclei (atomic numbers 40 and 72) are entirely different.
  1. (1) true: Ag+ is 4d10, a stable filled shell, so removing a second electron costs more (Ag 2070 vs Pd 1875 kJ mol−1).
  2. (3) true: Mn (1519 K) melts far below Cr (2180 K).
  3. (4) true (NCERT).
  4. (2) is the incorrect statement: the similarity is chemical, not nuclear.

Answer: option (2) — Zr and Hf shares almost identical nuclear properties.

Q424CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Sets A–D · Set A Q38NTA final key
Passage (15 May 2024, Q37–41): d- and f-block elements

The passage lists the three transition series (Sc–Zn, Y–Cd, La and Hf–Hg) and notes that, moving left to right in a series, the d orbitals fill progressively and properties change accordingly. It then lists the lanthanoids (Ce–Lu) and actinoids (Th–Lr), whose chemical properties change little across the series; the 5f elements are radioactive and mostly synthesised artificially, so less is known about their chemistry.

Which of the following is the correct order of second ionisation enthalpy?
  1. V > Cr > Mn
  2. V < Cr < Mn
  3. V < Cr > Mn
  4. V > Cr < Mn
Concept to recallThe second electron of Cr comes from the stable half-filled 3d5 of Cr+, so Cr has an unusually high ΔiH2.
  1. ΔiH2 (kJ mol−1): V 1414, Cr 1592, Mn 1509.
  2. So V < Cr > Mn.

Answer: option (3) — V < Cr > Mn

It then lists the lanthanoids (Ce–Lu) and actinoids (Th–Lr), whose chemical properties change little across the series; the 5f elements are radioactive and mostly synthesised artificially, so less is known about their chemistry.

Which of the following pair of compounds exhibits same colour in aqueous solution?
