  3. VOCl2, FeCl2
  4. VOCl2, MnCl2
Concept to recallColours of aqua ions: VO2+ blue (V4+, d1); Cu2+ blue (d9); Fe2+ pale green (d6); Mn2+ pale pink (d5).
  1. VOCl2 (vanadyl, blue) and CuCl2 (Cu2+, blue) give the same colour.

Answer: option (2) — VOCl2, CuCl2

Q426CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Sets A–D · Set A Q40NTA final key
Passage (15 May 2024, Q37–41): d- and f-block elements

The passage lists the three transition series (Sc–Zn, Y–Cd, La and Hf–Hg) and notes that, moving left to right in a series, the d orbitals fill progressively and properties change accordingly. It then lists the lanthanoids (Ce–Lu) and actinoids (Th–Lr), whose chemical properties change little across the series; the 5f elements are radioactive and mostly synthesised artificially, so less is known about their chemistry.

Which metal has the highest oxidation state in the first row transition series?
  1. Cr
  2. Fe
  3. Mn
  4. V
Concept to recallHighest oxidation state = 4s + 3d electrons up to Mn: Mn +7 (MnO4−); beyond Mn it falls.
  1. V +5, Cr +6, Mn +7, Fe +6 (rare). Mn shows the highest, +7.

Answer: option (3) — Mn

Q427CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Sets A–D · Set A Q41NTA final key
Passage (15 May 2024, Q37–41): d- and f-block elements

The passage lists the three transition series (Sc–Zn, Y–Cd, La and Hf–Hg) and notes that, moving left to right in a series, the d orbitals fill progressively and properties change accordingly. It then lists the lanthanoids (Ce–Lu) and actinoids (Th–Lr), whose chemical properties change little across the series; the 5f elements are radioactive and mostly synthesised artificially, so less is known about their chemistry.

Why do the actinoids exhibit higher number of oxidation states than lanthanoids?
  1. 4f orbitals are more diffused than the 5f orbitals.
  2. Energy difference between 5f and 6d is less with respect to the energy difference between 4f and 5d.
  3. Energy difference between 5f and 6d is more with respect to the energy difference between 4f and 5d.
  4. Actinoids are more reactive in nature than the lanthanoids.
Concept to recall5f, 6d and 7s levels are close in energy, so a variable number of electrons can take part in bonding; 4f is buried and lies well below 5d.
  1. Small 5f–6d gap ⇒ many oxidation states (e.g. U +3 to +6, Np/Pu up to +7).
  2. (1) is reversed: 5f orbitals are the more diffuse.

Answer: option (2) — Energy difference between 5f and 6d is less with respect to the energy difference between 4f and 5d.

Q428CUET 2024 · 29 May (pen & paper, 306 E New) · Book A · Q10NTA final key
Match List I with List II for the oxidation state of central atoms :
List-IList-II
(A) Cr2O72−(I) +3
(B) MnO4−(II) +5
(C) VO3−(III) +7
(D) FeF63−(IV) +6
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (A) – (I), (B) – (II), (C) – (III), (D) – (IV)
  2. (A) – (IV), (B) – (III), (C) – (II), (D) – (I)
  3. (A) – (I), (B) – (II), (C) – (IV), (D) – (III)
  4. (A) – (IV), (B) – (I), (C) – (III), (D) – (II)
Concept to recallSum of oxidation numbers = charge on the ion; O = −2, F = −1.
  1. Cr2O72−: 2x − 14 = −2 → x = +6 (IV).
  2. MnO4−: x − 8 = −1 → +7 (III).
  3. VO3−: x − 6 = −1 → +5 (II).
  4. FeF63−: x − 6 = −3 → +3 (I).

Answer: option (2) — (A) – (IV), (B) – (III), (C) – (II), (D) – (I)

Q429CUET 2024 · 29 May (pen & paper, 306 E New) · Book A · Q26NTA final key
Which of the following ions will be coloured in the aqueous solution ?

  2. (B) Nb3+
  3. (C) Cu+
  4. (D) Y3+
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (C) and (D) only
  2. (A), (B) and (D) only
  3. (A) and (B) only
  4. (A), (B), (C) and (D)
Concept to recallColour comes from d–d transitions, which need a partly filled d subshell (d1–d9); d0 and d10 ions are colourless.
  1. Ti3+: 3d1 → coloured (purple).
  2. Nb3+: 4d2 → coloured.
  3. Cu+: 3d10 → colourless. Y3+: 4d0 → colourless.
  4. Answer: (A) and (B) only.

Answer: option (3) — (A) and (B) only

Q430CUET 2024 · 29 May (pen & paper, 306 E New) · Book A · Q28NTA final key
Match List-I with List-II :
List-IList-II
(A) Mn2+(I) Pyrolusite ore
(B) Spin only Magnetic Moment(II) An alloy of 4f metal, iron and traces of S, C, Al and Ca
(C) MnO2(III) μs = √n(n + 2) BM
(D) Misch metal(IV) Highest oxidation states
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (A) – (IV), (B) – (III), (C) – (II), (D) – (I)
  2. (A) – (II), (B) – (III), (C) – (I), (D) – (IV)
  3. (A) – (IV), (B) – (III), (C) – (I), (D) – (II)
  4. (A) – (I), (B) – (III), (C) – (IV), (D) – (II)
Concept to recallμ = √(n(n+2)) BM for n unpaired electrons. Pyrolusite = MnO2. Misch metal ≈ 95 % lanthanoid + 5 % Fe with traces of S, C, Ca, Al. Mn shows the largest range of oxidation states (+2 to +7) in the 3d series.
  1. (B) spin-only moment → formula (III); (C) MnO2 → pyrolusite (I); (D) Misch metal → the lanthanoid alloy (II).
  2. That leaves (A) Mn2+ → (IV), i.e. manganese, the element with the highest (and most) oxidation states in its row.

Answer: option (3) — (A) – (IV), (B) – (III), (C) – (I), (D) – (II)

Q431CUET 2024 · 29 May (pen & paper, 306 E New) · Book A · Q39NTA final key
Passage (29 May 2024, Q39–43): physical properties of transition metals

Transition metals are very hard and have low volatility; their melting and boiling points are high. Along a row the melting points rise to a maximum near d5 and then fall as the atomic number increases. The high melting points are attributed to the participation of a large number of (n−1)d electrons, in addition to the ns electrons, in interatomic metallic bonding.

Which transition metal is liquid at room temperature ?
  1. Hg
  2. Cu
  3. Ag
  4. Au
Concept to recallHg (5d106s2) has no unpaired d electrons for metallic bonding and a tightly held 6s pair, so its metallic bond is very weak (m.p. 234 K).
  1. Mercury is the only metal liquid at room temperature.

Answer: option (1) — Hg

Q432CUET 2024 · 29 May (pen & paper, 306 E New) · Book A · Q40NTA final key
Passage (29 May 2024, Q39–43): physical properties of transition metals

Transition metals are very hard and have low volatility; their melting and boiling points are high. Along a row the melting points rise to a maximum near d5 and then fall as the atomic number increases. The high melting points are attributed to the participation of a large number of (n−1)d electrons, in addition to the ns electrons, in interatomic metallic bonding.

Which is the hardest metal ?
  1. Zn
  2. Cu
  3. Hg
  4. Cd
Concept to recallMetallic bond strength (hence hardness, m.p.) grows with the number of unpaired (n−1)d electrons; d10 metals with a full 3d/4d set (Zn, Cd, Hg) are soft.
  1. Zn, Cd, Hg have full d10 and only ns2 electrons for bonding: soft (Hg is a liquid).
  2. Cu (3d104s1) also uses some d-electron bonding: hardest of the four (Mohs ≈ 3).

Answer: option (2) — Cu

NoteOf these four only. The hardest transition metal overall is chromium.
Q433CUET 2024 · 29 May (pen & paper, 306 E New) · Book A · Q41NTA final key
Passage (29 May 2024, Q39–43): physical properties of transition metals

Transition metals are very hard and have low volatility; their melting and boiling points are high. Along a row the melting points rise to a maximum near d5 and then fall as the atomic number increases. The high melting points are attributed to the participation of a large number of (n−1)d electrons, in addition to the ns electrons, in interatomic metallic bonding.

In any row, melting points of these metals rise to a maximum at d5. Which transition metal is an exception ?
  1. Ti
  2. V
  3. Cr
  4. Mn
Concept to recallMn (3d54s2) and Tc have anomalously low melting points: the stable half-filled d5 set holds its electrons and contributes little to metallic bonding.

  2. Mn is the exception.

Answer: option (4) — Mn

TrapCr is also d5 (3d54s1) but its m.p. is high; the dip is at Mn.

Q435CUET 2024 · 29 May (pen & paper, 306 E New) · Book A · Q43NTA final key
Passage (29 May 2024, Q39–43): physical properties of transition metals

Transition metals are very hard and have low volatility; their melting and boiling points are high. Along a row the melting points rise to a maximum near d5 and then fall as the atomic number increases. The high melting points are attributed to the participation of a large number of (n−1)d electrons, in addition to the ns electrons, in interatomic metallic bonding.

How many electrons are needed in reduction of Cr2O72− to Cr3+ ?

  2. Six

Q436CUET 2024 · 19 Jul (re-test, CBT) · Q30NTA final key
Match List-I with List-II.

Q437CUET 2024 · 19 Jul (re-test, CBT) · Q31NTA final key
Increasing order of ionic radii of the followings :

  2. (B) Lu3+
  3. (C) Y3+
  4. (D) La3+
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (A) < (B) < (C) < (D)
  2. (A) < (C) < (B) < (D)
  3. (B) < (C) < (A) < (D)
  4. (C) < (B) < (D) < (A)
Concept to recallLanthanoid contraction: Ln3+ radius falls steadily from La3+ (103 pm) to Lu3+ (86 pm). Y3+ (90 pm) sits between Ho3+ and Er3+.

  2. Increasing: Lu3+ < Y3+ < Eu3+ < La3+, i.e. (B) < (C) < (A) < (D).

Q441CUET 2023 · 21 May, Shift 3 · Q5 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived

B. V

  3. D > C > B > A > E
  4. C > D > B > E > A

Q442CUET 2023 · 21 May, Shift 3 · Q6 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
Least basic compound among the following would be
  1. La(OH)3
  2. Lu(OH)3
  3. Ce(OH)3
  4. Gd(OH)3
Concept to recallLanthanoid contraction: Ln3+ shrinks from La to Lu, so M–OH bonds become more covalent and the hydroxides less basic.
  1. Basic strength: La(OH)3 > Ce(OH)3 > … > Gd(OH)3 > … > Lu(OH)3.
  2. Lu3+ is the smallest ion ⇒ Lu(OH)3 is least basic.

Answer: option (2) — Lu(OH)3

Q444CUET 2023 · 22 May, Shift 3 · Q28NTA final key

  2. (3) and (4) are standard consequences of the contraction; (1) reflects that La has no 4f electron.

Answer: option (2) — La(OH)3 is less basic than Lu(OH)3

Q449CUET 2023 · 23 May, Shift 3 · Q49NTA final key
Passage: One of the notable features of the transition element is the great variety of oxidation states it may show in its compounds. The elements which give the greatest number of oxidation states occur in or near the middle of the series. Manganese, for example exhibits all the oxidation states from +2 to +7. The lesser number of oxidation states at the extreme ends is either due to losing or sharing of few electrons (Sc, Ti) or too many d electrons of higher valence. Early in the first series scandium (II) is virtually unknown and titanium (IV) which is more stable than Ti (III) or Ti (II). On the other end, the only oxidation state of zinc is +2.
Cr2+ is reducing but Mn3+ is oxidising in nature although both have d4 configuration. It is due to the reason that Cr configuration changes from
  1. d4 to d3
  2. d4 to d5
  3. d2 to d3
  4. d9 to d10
Concept to recallCr2+ → Cr3+ reaches the stable half-filled t2g3; Mn3+ → Mn2+ reaches stable d5.
  1. Cr2+ (d4) loses an electron → Cr3+ (d3): it acts as a reducing agent.
  2. Mn3+ (d4) gains one → Mn2+ (d5): it acts as an oxidising agent.

Answer: option (1) — d4 to d3

NoteNTA’s final key is (1) for the English medium; its Hindi-medium column marks this question dropped.

Q454CUET 2023 · 25 May, Shift 3 · Q44 · Prepp reconstructionworked here
Passage (summarised): the d-block (groups 3–12) fills d-orbitals in four long periods; transition metals have partly filled d-orbitals and show variable oxidation states, coloured ions, catalytic activity and paramagnetism. B. Mn (Z = 25)

  4. Co > Mn > Fe > Cr
Concept to recallThe higher E°(M3+/M2+), the harder it is to oxidise M2+, i.e. the more stable the +2 state.

Highest oxidation state of manganese in fluoride is +4 (MnF4) but highest oxidation state in oxides is +7 (Mn2O7) because

  3. Fluorine stabilises lower oxidation state

Q502CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q22NTA final key
Actinoid contraction is of greater extent than lanthanide contraction because:
  1. poor shielding effect of 4f electrons
  2. poor shielding effect of 5d electrons
  3. more poor shielding effect of 5f electrons than 4f electrons
  4. more poor shielding effect of 4f electrons than 5f electrons
Concept to recallAcross a series each added f electron shields the extra nuclear charge imperfectly; 5f orbitals are more diffuse than 4f, so they shield even less.
  1. Contraction is caused by imperfect shielding by the f electrons being added.
  2. 5f electrons shield more poorly than 4f, so the effective nuclear charge rises faster across the actinoids: a larger contraction.

Answer: option (3) — more poor shielding effect of 5f electrons than 4f electrons

Q503CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q33NTA final key
Cr2+ is stronger reducing agent than Fe2+ because:

  3. oxidises easily to form Cr4+
  4. Fe2+ is quite stable and does not oxidise
Concept to recallCr2+ (d4) → Cr3+ (d3, half-filled t2g3, very stable in water); E°(Cr3+/Cr2+) = −0.41 V.
  1. Cr2+ → Cr3+ gives d3, a half-filled t2g level, especially stable in aqueous solution (high hydration enthalpy).
  2. So Cr2+ gives up its electron readily: a strong reductant. NCERT gives this reason.

Answer: option (2) — d3 configuration of Cr3+ is more stable than d5 configuration of Fe3+ in aqueous solution

NoteNCERT phrases it as Cr2+ going from d4 to d3 (half-filled t2g) while Fe2+ goes from d6 to d5; option (2) is the keyed answer.

Concept to recallSpectrochemical series: F− < C2O42− < H2O < NH3 < en < CN−. Larger Δo ⇒ higher energy absorbed ⇒ shorter λ (Δ = hc/λ).
  1. Δo: CN− > NH3 > ox2− > F− for the same Co(III).
  2. λ absorbed is the reverse: A < B < D < C.

Answer: option (1) — (A), (B), (D), (C)

TrapOrdering by Δo instead of by wavelength gives the reversed sequence (C, D, B, A), which is offered.
Q515CUET 2026 · 6 June, Shift 1 · Q21NTA final key
IUPAC name of [Co(NH3)4(H2O)Cl]Cl2
  1. Tetraammineaquachloridocobalt(II) chloride
  2. Tetraammineaquachloridocobalt(III) chloride
  3. Tetraammineaquachloridocobalt(I) chloride
  4. Tetraammineaquachloridocobalt(0) chloride
Concept to recallOxidation state: complex-ion charge = metal + sum of ligand charges.
  1. The complex ion is [Co(NH3)4(H2O)Cl]2+ (two Cl− outside).
  2. x + 0 + 0 − 1 = +2 ⇒ x = +3: cobalt(III).

Q516CUET 2026 · 6 June, Shift 1 · Q28NTA final key
Select the correct assumptions in Crystal Field Theory (CFT) from the following:
(A) Ligands are treated as point charge or point dipole.
(B) The five d orbitals in an isolated gaseous metal atom are non-degenerate
(C) Degeneracy of the d orbitals is restored with the approach of ligand towards metal
(D) Metal-ligand bond is ionic arising purely from electrostatic interactions
  1. (B) and (C) only
  2. (A) and (D) only
  3. (B), (C) and (D) only
  4. (A), (B) and (D) only
Concept to recallCFT: purely electrostatic M–L bond, ligands as point charges/dipoles; the five d orbitals of a free ion are degenerate and the ligand field splits them.
  1. (A) and (D) are the CFT assumptions.
  2. (B) and (C) reverse the truth: free-ion d orbitals are degenerate and ligands remove the degeneracy.

Answer: option (2) — (A) and (D) only

Q517CUET 2026 · 6 June, Shift 1 · Q33NTA final key
What would be the geometrical shape of [NiCl4]2− and [PtCl4]2− compounds?
  1. Both [NiCl4]2− and [PtCl4]2− are square planar.
  2. Both [NiCl4]2− and [PtCl4]2− are tetrahedral.
  3. [NiCl4]2− is square planar while [PtCl4]2− is tetrahedral.
  4. [NiCl4]2− is tetrahedral while [PtCl4]2− is square planar
Concept to recallNi2+ (3d8) with weak-field Cl−: no pairing, sp3, tetrahedral, paramagnetic. Pt2+ (5d8): large splitting for 5d, always square planar (dsp2).
  1. [NiCl4]2−: two unpaired electrons, sp3: tetrahedral.
  2. [PtCl4]2−: d8 of a 5d metal pairs up, dsp2: square planar.

Answer: option (4) — [NiCl4]2− is tetrahedral while [PtCl4]2− is square planar

Q518CUET 2026 · 6 June, Shift 1 · Q5NTA final key
Choose the Incorrect option regarding valence bond theory of coordination compound.
  1. It does not give a quantitative interpretation of the thermodynamic stabilities of coordination compounds.
  2. It does not explain the colour exhibited by coordination compounds.
  3. It does not give quantitative interpretation of magnetic data.
  4. It does not distinguish between outer orbital and inner orbital complexes.
Concept to recallNCERT limitations of VBT: no quantitative magnetic data, no colour, no quantitative stability, wrong predictions for some 4-coordinate geometries, no distinction between weak and strong ligands.
  1. The first three are standard limitations of VBT.
  2. VBT itself introduced inner-orbital (d2sp3) and outer-orbital (sp3d2) complexes, so the last statement is false.

Answer: option (4) — It does not distinguish between outer orbital and inner orbital complexes.

Q519CUET 2026 · 6 June, Shift 1 · Q9NTA final key
The complex [Co(NH3)6]3+ is
  1. sp3d2 hybridised, and paramagnetic in nature.
  2. sp3d2 hybridised, and diamagnetic in nature.
  3. d2sp3 hybridised, and paramagnetic in nature.
  4. d2sp3 hybridised, and diamagnetic in nature.
Concept to recallCo3+ (3d6) with NH3: the six electrons pair in three 3d orbitals (t2g6), leaving two 3d free: inner-orbital d2sp3, low spin.
  1. 3d6 paired into 3 orbitals: no unpaired electron ⇒ diamagnetic.
  2. Two empty 3d + 4s + three 4p: d2sp3, octahedral.

Answer: option (4) — d2sp3 hybridised, and diamagnetic in nature.

Q520CUET 2026 · 18 May, Shift 2 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q3key re-derived
For which value of x and y, the following square planar compound shows geometrical isomers [Pt(Cl)x(Br)y]2−
  1. 1, 3
  2. 3, 1
  3. 2, 2
  4. 1, 1
Concept to recallSquare planar MA4 and MA3B show no geometrical isomers; MA2B2 shows cis and trans.
  1. Pt(II) is square planar with four ligands, so x + y = 4: (1, 1) is impossible.
  2. (1, 3) and (3, 1) are MAB3 / MA3B: every arrangement is the same.
  3. x = y = 2: the two Cl can be adjacent (cis) or opposite (trans).

Answer: option (3) — 2, 2

Q521CUET 2026 · 19 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q7key re-derived
Which of the following coordination complex ions exhibits structural asymmetry leading to optical isomerism?

  4. [Cr(NH3)5Cl]2+
Concept to recall[M(AA)2X2]: the cis form has no mirror plane (chiral); the trans form has one.

  2. cis: the two chelate rings make a propeller, non-superimposable on its mirror image: optically active.

Q522CUET 2026 · 19 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q8key re-derived

Q523CUET 2026 · 22 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q5key re-derived

  4. Pentaamminedichloridocobalt(III) chloride

  2. Name: pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride.

Q524CUET 2026 · 22 May, Shift 2 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q4key re-derived

  2. [Co(NH3)5Cl]2+ has NH3 and Cl−: heteroleptic.

Q525CUET 2026 · 22 May, Shift 2 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q9key re-derived

  3. dsp2 hybridization and Diamagnetic
  4. sp3d2 hybridization and Diamagnetic

Q526CUET 2026 · 29 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q5key re-derived

  2. [FeF6]3−: Fe3+ d5 high spin, 5.
  3. [Co(NH3)6]3+: d6 low spin, 0. [Ni(CO)4]: Ni(0) d10, 0.

Q527CUET 2026 · 29 May, Shift 2 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q6 also 2026 30 May S2 Q8 (memory-based, collegedunia) (same four complexes, options in another order)key re-derived

  4. [Mn(H2O)6]2+

  2. [Ni(CN)4]2− 0: diamagnetic.

Q528CUET 2026 · 29 May, Shift 2 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q9key re-derived
Which of the following complexes shows the highest crystal field stabilization energy (CFSE) in octahedral geometry?
  1. d3
  2. d5 high spin
  3. d8
  4. d10
Concept to recallOctahedral CFSE = (−0.4x + 0.6y)Δo for t2gxegy.
  1. d3: t2g3 → −1.2Δo.
  2. d5 high spin: t2g3eg2 → 0.
  3. d8: t2g6eg2 → −2.4 + 1.2 = −1.2Δo.
  4. d10: 0.

Answer: option (1) — d3

TrapHigh-spin d5 and d10 both have zero CFSE: the eg electrons cancel the t2g gain.
NoteAs recalled, (1) and (3) tie at −1.2Δo; the site picks (1), arguing that d8 also pays pairing energy for its three t2g pairs. Strictly the CFSE values are equal; read this as “which has CFSE −1.2Δo with no pairing”.
Q529CUET 2026 · 30 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q6key re-derived
A coordination compound [CoF6]3− is converted into [Co(CN)6]3−. Which of the following correctly represents the hybridization and number of unpaired electrons in the final complex?

  3. sp3d2, 2 unpaired electrons
  4. d2sp3, 2 unpaired electrons

  2. Two vacant 3d orbitals give d2sp3; 0 unpaired.

Answer: option (2) — d2sp3, 0 unpaired electrons

Trap(1) describes the starting fluoride complex.
Q530CUET 2026 · 30 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q7worked here
An octahedral coordination compound of chromium(III) reacts with one mole of EDTA to form a stable chelate. The original complex has the formula [Cr(en)2Cl2]+, where en represents ethane-1,2-diamine. The total number of geometrical and optical isomers possible for the complex is:
  1. 2
  2. 3
  3. 4
  4. 5
Concept to recall[M(AA)2X2]: two geometrical isomers (cis, trans); only cis is chiral, giving a d/l pair.
  1. Geometrical: cis and trans.
  2. trans has a mirror plane: one isomer. cis is chiral: d and l.
  3. Total distinct stereoisomers = 1 + 2 = 3.

Answer: option (2) — 3

TrapAdding geometrical and optical counts double-counts the cis isomer.
NoteThe site prints (3) 4, counting “2 geometrical + 2 optical”. That counts the cis form twice: the two optical isomers are the cis form. The distinct isomers are trans, d-cis and l-cis: 3. The EDTA sentence is not needed.
Q531CUET 2026 · 31 May, Shift 2 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q6key re-derived
A coordination compound has the formula [Co(NH3)4Cl2]Cl. The magnetic moment of the complex is found to be approximately 4.9 BM. The hybridization and geometry of the complex ion are respectively:

  3. d2sp3, octahedral
  4. sp3d2, octahedral

  2. No vacant 3d orbitals: hybridisation uses 4s 4p 4d → sp3d2, octahedral.

Answer: option (4) — sp3d2, octahedral

NoteReal [Co(NH3)4Cl2]+ is low spin and diamagnetic; the question tells you to take the measured 4.9 BM as given, and the answer follows from that.
Q532CUET 2026 · 31 May, Shift 2 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q7key re-derived

  2. Charge: +3 − 4 = −1, consistent.
  3. [M(EDTA)]− exists as a pair of enantiomers.

Q541CUET 2025 · 21 May, Shift 2 · Q25 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here
CuSO4 is colorless but CuSO4.5H2O is blue in color. Which of the following statements is incorrect about the color of CuSO4.5H2O?
  1. In CuSO4.5H2O water act as ligand
  2. crystal field splitting takes place in CuSO4.5H2O
  3. presence of SO42− ion in coordination sphere imparts the color of CuSO4.5H2O
  4. d-d transition takes place in CuSO4.5H2O
Concept to recallColour of a complex: ligands split the d orbitals; d–d transitions absorb visible light. Without ligands (anhydrous) there is no splitting and no colour.
  1. In the pentahydrate four H2O molecules are ligands round Cu2+.
  2. They split the 3d9 set; a d–d transition absorbs red-orange light, so the salt looks blue.
  3. The colour is due to the water ligands, not to sulphate: statement 3 is the incorrect one.

NoteStrictly, in the crystal two sulphate oxygens do occupy the distant axial positions round Cu2+; but the colour arises from d–d transitions in the field of the ligands (chiefly the four waters), not from the sulphate ion as such, which is why statement 3 is the one keyed as incorrect.

Q580CUET 2023 · 22 May, Shift 3 · Q41NTA final key
Passage: Transition metals form a large number of complexes or coordination compounds in which the metal atoms are bound to a number of anions or neutral molecules. The valence bond theory explain the formation, magnetic behaviour and geometrical shapes while the crystal field theory explains the effect of different crystal fields on the degeneracy of d-orbitals energies of the central metal atom/ion. This provides for the quantitative estimation of orbital separation energies, magnetic moments and spectral and stability parameters.

(A) [Ni(CN)4]2−
(B) [Ni(CO)4]
(C) [NiCl4]2−
(D) [Ni(NH3)6]2+

  2. (B) and (D) only
  3. (B) and (C) only
  4. (A) and (D) only
Concept to recall[Ni(CN)4]2− dsp2 square planar, diamagnetic; [Ni(CO)4] sp3 tetrahedral, diamagnetic; [NiCl4]2− sp3 tetrahedral, 2 unpaired; [Ni(NH3)6]2+ octahedral, 2 unpaired.
  1. Both tetrahedral: Ni(CO)4 (Ni0, 3d10, diamagnetic) and [NiCl4]2− (Ni2+ 3d8, weak field, paramagnetic).
  2. B and C.

Answer: option (3) — (B) and (C) only

Q581CUET 2023 · 22 May, Shift 3 · Q42NTA final key
Passage: Transition metals form a large number of complexes or coordination compounds in which the metal atoms are bound to a number of anions or neutral molecules.   3. [MnCl4]2− is sp3 (5 unpaired), so dsp2 is wrong.

Answer: option (4) — [MnCl4]2− - dsp2

Q582CUET 2023 · 22 May, Shift 3 · Q43NTA final key
Passage: Transition metals form a large number of complexes or coordination compounds in which the metal atoms are bound to a number of anions or neutral molecules. Answer: option (4) — [CoF6]3−

Q583CUET 2023 · 22 May, Shift 3 · Q44NTA final key
Passage: Transition metals form a large number of complexes or coordination compounds in which the metal atoms are bound to a number of anions or neutral molecules. This provides for the quantitative estimation of orbital separation energies, magnetic moments and spectral and stability parameters.
The compound [Pt(NH3)2Cl2] exhibits :

Q584CUET 2023 · 23 May, Shift 3 · Q18NTA final key

  4. D, E and C only

  2. Ionisation: [Co(NH3)4(NO2)Cl]NO2.

Q586CUET 2023 · 23 May, Shift 3 · Q50NTA final key
Passage: One of the notable features of the transition element is the great variety of oxidation states it may show in its compounds. The lesser number of oxidation states at the extreme ends is either due to losing or sharing of few electrons (Sc, Ti) or too many d electrons of higher valence. Early in the first series scandium (II) is virtually unknown and titanium (IV) which is more stable than Ti (III) or Ti (II). On the other end, the only oxidation state of zinc is +2.

Q607CUET 2023 · 10 Jun, Shift 1 · Prepp reconstruction · Q38key re-derived

  2. −2.4Δo
  3. −0.4Δo
  4. −1.6Δo
Concept to recallOctahedral: each t2g electron −0.4Δo, each eg electron +0.6Δo (pairing energy aside).
  1. Low-spin d6 = t2g6eg0.
  2. CFSE = 6 × (−0.4Δo) = −2.4Δo (+ 2P for pairing, ignored here).

Q608CUET 2023 · 11 Jun, Shift 3 · Q14 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
In octahedral coordination entities:

  2. t2g set has lower energy than eg set.
  3. eg set has lower energy than t2 set.
  4. eg set has lower energy than t2g set.
Concept to recallOctahedral field: eg (dx²−y², dz²) point at the ligands and rise; t2g lie between them and fall.
  1. In an octahedron the three t2g orbitals are lowered by 0.4Δo and the two eg raised by 0.6Δo.
  2. “t2” and “e” (no g) are the tetrahedral labels, where the order is reversed.

Answer: option (2) — t2g set has lower energy than eg set.

Q613CUET 2023 · 13 Jun, Shift 3 · Q3 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
Which will form the most stable complex?
  1. NCS−
  2. CN−
  3. H2O
  4. C2O42−
Concept to recallChelate effect: a polydentate ligand binding through two or more donor atoms gives a ring and a more stable complex.
  1. NCS−, CN− and H2O are unidentate.
  2. Oxalate is bidentate; the five-membered chelate ring makes its complexes the most stable.

Answer: option (4) — C2O42−

NoteThe intended idea is the chelate effect: a bidentate ligand forms a more stable complex than comparable unidentate ligands. Strictly, stability depends on the metal, which is not named (cyanide complexes such as [Fe(CN)6]4− are more stable than the oxalato ones), so read the question as a test of the chelate effect.

Q625CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q46NTA final key
Passage (23 Jun 2023, Q46–50): bonding in coordination compounds

Werner’s theory could not answer why only certain elements form coordination compounds, why the bonds are directional, or why the compounds have characteristic magnetic and optical properties. Approaches put forward: Valence Bond Theory (VBT), Crystal Field Theory (CFT), Ligand Field Theory and Molecular Orbital Theory. In VBT the metal atom or ion, under the influence of the ligands, uses its (n−1)d, ns, np or ns, np, nd orbitals for hybridisation to give equivalent orbitals of definite geometry (octahedral, tetrahedral, square planar, …), which overlap with ligand orbitals that donate electron pairs.

The formula which correctly represents Potassium tetra hydroxo zincate (II) is:
  1. K[Zn(OH)4]
  2. K3[Zn(OH)4]3
  3. K4[Zn(OH)4]
  4. K2[Zn)OH)4]
Concept to recallCharge of the complex ion = oxidation state of metal + sum of ligand charges; enough K+ to balance it.
  1. Zn(II) + 4 OH− ⇒ charge = +2 − 4 = −2: [Zn(OH)4]2−.
  2. Two K+ balance it: K2[Zn(OH)4].

Answer: option (4) — K2[Zn)OH)4]

NoteOption (4) is printed “K2[Zn)OH)4]”, a typographical slip for K2[Zn(OH)4]; NTA keys it.

In VBT the metal atom or ion, under the influence of the ligands, uses its (n−1)d, ns, np or ns, np, nd orbitals for hybridisation to give equivalent orbitals of definite geometry (octahedral, tetrahedral, square planar, …), which overlap with ligand orbitals that donate electron pairs.

  4. [CoCl3(NH3)3]·3NH3

Q627CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q48NTA final key
Passage (23 Jun 2023, Q46–50): bonding in coordination compounds

Werner’s theory could not answer why only certain elements form coordination compounds, why the bonds are directional, or why the compounds have characteristic magnetic and optical properties. Approaches put forward: Valence Bond Theory (VBT), Crystal Field Theory (CFT), Ligand Field Theory and Molecular Orbital Theory. In VBT the metal atom or ion, under the influence of the ligands, uses its (n−1)d, ns, np or ns, np, nd orbitals for hybridisation to give equivalent orbitals of definite geometry (octahedral, tetrahedral, square planar, …), which overlap with ligand orbitals that donate electron pairs.

  1. Square Planar
  2. Tetrahedral
  3. Inner octahedral
  4. Outer octahedral
Concept to recallNi(0) is 3d84s2; CO is a strong-field ligand that pairs the 4s electrons into 3d, giving 3d10 and empty 4s + 4p ⇒ sp3.

  2. After rearrangement 3d10 is full; the empty 4s and three 4p orbitals hybridise: sp3.

Q628CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q49NTA final key
Passage (23 Jun 2023, Q46–50): bonding in coordination compounds

Werner’s theory could not answer why only certain elements form coordination compounds, why the bonds are directional, or why the compounds have characteristic magnetic and optical properties. Approaches put forward: Valence Bond Theory (VBT), Crystal Field Theory (CFT), Ligand Field Theory and Molecular Orbital Theory. In VBT the metal atom or ion, under the influence of the ligands, uses its (n−1)d, ns, np or ns, np, nd orbitals for hybridisation to give equivalent orbitals of definite geometry (octahedral, tetrahedral, square planar, …), which overlap with ligand orbitals that donate electron pairs.

  1. sp3
  2. dsp2
  3. sp3d2
  4. d2sp3
Concept to recallWeak-field ligands (F−) do not pair d electrons: outer-orbital (n s, n p, n d) complex. Strong field (CN−, NH3 with Co3+) gives inner d2sp3.
  1. Co3+ is 3d6.
  2. F− is weak field: the 3d electrons stay unpaired (4 unpaired), so no 3d orbital is free.
  3. Hybridisation uses 4s, 4p and 4d: sp3d2, outer-orbital, high-spin, paramagnetic.

Answer: option (3) — sp3d2

Trap[Co(NH3)6]3+ is d2sp3; changing the ligand to F− changes the answer.

Q631CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q19NTA final key
[Co(NH3)4Cl(NO2)]Cl will show:
  1. (A) Solvate isomerism
  2. (B) Linkage isomerism
  3. (C) Coordination isomerism
  4. (D) Ionisation isomerism

  1. A and B only
  2. B and C only
  3. B and D only
  4. C and D only
Concept to recallLinkage: an ambidentate ligand (NO2− via N or O). Ionisation: a counter-ion swaps with a ligand. Coordination: both cation and anion are complexes. Solvate: water inside vs outside.

  2. The outer Cl− can swap with the inner Cl or NO2, e.g. [Co(NH3)4Cl2]NO2 ⇒ ionisation.
  3. Only one complex ion and no water ⇒ no coordination or solvate isomerism. Answer: B and D.

Q632CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q32NTA final key

  1. t2g5 eg1
  2. t2g6 eg0
  3. t2g4 eg2
  4. t2g2 eg4
Concept to recallΔo < P (weak field): electrons occupy eg before pairing (high spin). Δo > P (strong field): pairing in t2g first (low spin).
  1. First five electrons: t2g3 eg2, one in each orbital.
  2. Sixth electron pairs in t2g: t2g4 eg2, 4 unpaired.

Answer: option (3) — t2g4 eg2

Trapt2g6 eg0 is the low-spin (Δo > P) case.

Q634CUET 2022 · 10 Aug, Shift 1 (SET 06) · Q46NTA final key
Passage: According to the valence bond theory, the metal atom or ion under the influence of ligands can use its (n-1)d, ns, np, nd orbitals for hybridisation to yield a set of equivalent orbitals of definite geometry. These hybridised orbitals are allowed to overlap with ligand orbitals that can donate electron pairs for bonding. It is usually possible to predict the geometry of a complex from the knowledge of its magnetic behaviour on the basis of the valence bond theory. Consider the formation of [Co(NH3)5Cl]Cl2 and answer the following question:
The IUPAC name of the above coordination entity is
  1. Chloridopentaamminecobaltate (II) chloride
  2. Chloridopentaamminecobaltate (II) dichloride
  3. Pentaamminechloridocobaltate (III) chloride
  4. Pentaamminechloridocobalt (III) dichloride
Concept to recallName the cation first; ligands alphabetically (ammine before chlorido); a cationic complex keeps the metal’s plain name; oxidation state in Roman numerals.
  1. x + 5(0) + (−1) = +2 ⇒ Co is +3.
  2. Ligands: ammine (a) before chlorido (c) ⇒ pentaamminechlorido.
  3. Complex is a cation ⇒ “cobalt”, not “cobaltate”.

Answer: option (4) — Pentaamminechloridocobalt (III) dichloride

Trap“-ate” is used only for anionic complexes.
NoteThe IUPAC name is pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride (the number of counter-ions is not stated); option (4) is the only one with the right ligand order, the cation name “cobalt” and +3.

Q638CUET 2022 · 10 Aug, Shift 1 (SET 06) · Q50NTA final key
Passage: According to the valence bond theory, the metal atom or ion under the influence of ligands can use its (n-1)d, ns, np, nd orbitals for hybridisation to yield a set of equivalent orbitals of definite geometry. These hybridised orbitals are allowed to overlap with ligand orbitals that can donate electron pairs for bonding. It is usually possible to predict the geometry of a complex from the knowledge of its magnetic behaviour on the basis of the valence bond theory. Consider the formation of [Co(NH3)5Cl]Cl2 and answer the following question:
The primary valence of Co in above coordination entity is
  1. 1
  2. 2
  3. 3
  4. 4
Concept to recallWerner: primary valence = oxidation state (ionisable); secondary valence = coordination number (non-ionisable).
  1. Oxidation state of Co: x + 0 − 1 = +2 ⇒ x = +3.
  2. Two Cl− lie outside the bracket and ionise (precipitate 2 AgCl); the third primary-valence Cl is inside and also counts toward the secondary valence.
  3. NTA keyed 2 (the number of ionisable Cl−).

Answer: option (2) — 2

TrapPrimary valence in NCERT = oxidation number (3 here); the count of ionisable Cl− is 2.
NoteNCERT defines the primary valence as the oxidation state, which for Co here is +3 (option 3). NTA’s final key is (2), i.e. it counts the two ionisable Cl− outside the bracket (the primary valence “satisfied by” ionisable chloride in this compound). The key was re-read twice (6926450 → B). NTA’s answer is kept; by the textbook definition the answer is 3.

Q650CUET 2026 · 18 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q5key re-derived
Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding the transition state of a bimolecular nucleophilic substitution (SN2) reaction?
  1. The central carbon atom transitions to an sp3 hybridization state with a tetrahedral geometry.
  2. The central carbon atom adopts an unstable pentacoordinate arrangement with approximate sp2 hybridization.
  3. The reaction forms a stable, isolation-ready carbocation intermediate.
  4. Both the nucleophile and the leaving group carry full, non-interacting formal charges.
Concept to recallSN2 is one step: the nucleophile attacks from the back as the leaving group departs; in the transition state carbon is bonded partially to both (five groups, trigonal bipyramidal).
  1. The three other groups lie flat (sp2-like) with a p orbital holding Nu···C···X.
  2. There is no intermediate (that is SN1), and the charges are partial (δ−), not full.

Answer: option (2) — The central carbon atom adopts an unstable pentacoordinate arrangement with approximate sp2 hybridization.

TrapA carbocation intermediate belongs to SN1.
Q651CUET 2026 · 18 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q9worked here
Among the given pairs of isomeric organic compounds, which pair is correctly arranged in order of INCREASING boiling point?

  2. t-Butyl chloride < n-Butyl chloride
  3. p-Dichlorobenzene < o-Dichlorobenzene
  4. Isopentane < Neopentane
Concept to recallAmong isomers, branching makes a molecule more compact (smaller surface area), so van der Waals forces and the boiling point fall. Melting points follow symmetry instead: p-dichlorobenzene melts highest.
  1. (1) false: n-butyl alcohol 391 K, t-butyl alcohol 355 K.
  2. (2) true: t-butyl chloride 324 K < n-butyl chloride 351 K (branching).
  3. (4) false: neopentane 283 K < isopentane 301 K.
  4. The intended answer is (2).

Answer: option (2) — t-Butyl chloride < n-Butyl chloride

Trapp-Dichlorobenzene has the highest melting point of the three isomers (symmetry, better packing), not the highest boiling point.
NoteAs recalled, (3) is also true: NCERT’s own table gives p-dichlorobenzene b.p. 448 K and o-dichlorobenzene 453 K. The site keys (2), the branching pair; (3) is the trap of confusing the melting-point order (para highest) with the boiling-point order.

Q654CUET 2026 · 26 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q10key re-derived
The correct order of the rate of the reaction for the following reaction with respect to nucleophiles is:

  2. ClO4− > CH3COO− > OH− > PhO−
  3. CH3COO− > PhO− > OH− > ClO4−
  4. OH− > PhO− > CH3COO− > ClO4−

Q660CUET 2025 · 13 May, Shift 1 · Q21NTA final key

(A) Ambident nucleophiles(I) Symmetrical object

Concept to recallAmbident nucleophiles attack through two different atoms (CN− via C or N; NO2− via O or N). A Nicol prism produces plane-polarised light. An achiral (symmetrical) object is superimposable on its mirror image. β-Elimination follows Saytzeff’s rule.
  1. (A) ambident → cyanides and nitrites (III).
  2. (B) plane-polarised light → Nicol prism (IV).
  3. (C) superimposable mirror image → symmetrical object (I).
  4. (D) β-elimination → Saytzeff rule (II).

Answer: option (1) — (A) – (III), (B) – (IV), (C) – (I), (D) – (II)

Q661CUET 2025 · 13 May, Shift 1 · Q22NTA final key

Concept to recallSN2: one step, back-side attack, Walden inversion. SN1: carbocation, racemisation.

  2. The three other groups flip over like an umbrella: inversion of configuration.

Answer: option (3) — inversion of configuration

  3. (D) branch on C3, further away.
  4. (A) unbranched — fastest.
  5. Increasing: (B) < (C) < (D) < (A).

Answer: option (3) — (B), (C), (D), (A)

NoteThis ordering is worked as an in-text example in NCERT’s Haloalkanes chapter.
Q690CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Sets A–D · Set A Q22NTA final key
Although chlorine is an electron withdrawing group, yet it is ortho- and para-directing in electrophilic aromatic substitution reaction because
  1. (A) Chlorine withdraws electrons through inductive effect.
  2. (B) Chlorine destabilises the intermediate carbocation formed during electrophilic substitution.
  3. (C) Chlorine accepts electrons through resonance.
  4. (D) Chlorine releases electrons through resonance.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (A), (B) and (D) only
  2. (A), (B) and (C) only
  3. (A), (C) and (D) only
  4. (B), (C) and (D) only
Concept to recallCl: −I effect deactivates the ring (destabilises the arenium ion); +R effect (lone pair donation) raises electron density at o/p and stabilises the o/p arenium ions more than the meta one.
  1. −I: A true, and it destabilises the carbocation intermediate: B true (that is why the ring is deactivated).
  2. +R: Cl releases electrons through resonance: D true; C is the opposite and false.
  3. Answer: (A), (B) and (D).

Answer: option (1) — (A), (B) and (D) only

Q691CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Sets A–D · Set A Q26NTA final key
Match List-I with List-II:
List-IList-II
(A) Swarts Reaction(I) C6H5NH2 + NaNO2 + HX + Cu2X2 → C6H5X + N2
(B) Finkelstein reaction(II) 2RX + 2Na → R – R + 2NaX
(C) Sandmeyer’s reaction(III) RX + AgF → R – F + AgX
(D) Wurtz reaction(IV) RX + NaI → R – I + NaX
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (A) - (I), (B) - (II), (C) - (III), (D) - (IV)
  2. (A) - (I), (B) - (III), (C) - (II), (D) - (IV)
  3. (A) - (I), (B) - (II), (C) - (IV), (D) - (III)
  4. (A) - (III), (B) - (IV), (C) - (I), (D) - (II)
Concept to recallSwarts: R–X + AgF/Hg2F2 → R–F. Finkelstein: R–X + NaI (acetone) → R–I. Sandmeyer: ArN2+ + Cu2X2 → ArX. Wurtz: 2RX + 2Na → R–R.
  1. A–III, B–IV, C–I, D–II.

Answer: option (4) — (A) - (III), (B) - (IV), (C) - (I), (D) - (II)

Q692CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Sets A–D · Set A Q31NTA final key
For SN2 reaction, the increasing order of the reactivity of the following alkyl halides is:
  1. (A) CH3CH2CH2CH2Br
  2. (B) CH3CH2CH(Br)CH3
  3. (C) (CH3)3CBr
  4. (D) (CH3)2CHCH2Br
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (A) < (B) < (C) < (D)
  2. (A) < (C) < (B) < (D)
  3. (B) < (A) < (D) < (C)
  4. (C) < (B) < (D) < (A)
Concept to recallSN2 is a backside attack: rate falls with steric hindrance at and next to the reacting carbon: 1° > 1° with β-branching > 2° > 3°.
  1. C (3°) is slowest, then B (2°).
  2. D is primary but branched at C-2, so slower than the unbranched primary A.
  3. C < B < D < A.

Answer: option (4) — (C) < (B) < (D) < (A)

Q693CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Sets A–D · Set A Q43NTA final key
Identify the correct order of organic compounds in the following chemical reaction:
__?__ + Mg –(Dry Ether)→ __?__ –(H2O)→ __?__ –(Cl2, Δ)→ __?__
  1. (A) CH3MgBr
  2. (B) CH3Br
  3. (C) CH3Cl
  4. (D) CH4
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (B), (A), (D), (C)
  2. (A), (C), (B), (D)
  3. (B), (A), (C), (D)
  4. (C), (B), (D), (A)
Concept to recallRX + Mg (dry ether) → RMgX; RMgX + H2O → RH; RH + Cl2 (heat/light) → RCl (free radical substitution).
  1. CH3Br + Mg → CH3MgBr → (H2O) CH4 → (Cl2, Δ) CH3Cl.
  2. Order B, A, D, C.

Answer: option (1) — (B), (A), (D), (C)

Q694CUET 2024 · 29 May (pen & paper, 306 E New) · Book A · Q1NTA final key
What product is obtained when chloroform reacts with oxygen in presence of light ?
  1. Phosgene gas
  2. Phosphine gas
  3. Chlorine gas
  4. Hydrogen gas
Concept to recallChloroform is slowly oxidised by air in light to the poisonous gas phosgene (carbonyl chloride, COCl2); it is stored in closed dark bottles filled to the brim.
  1. 2CHCl3 + O2 →(light) 2COCl2 + 2HCl.
  2. COCl2 is phosgene.

Answer: option (1) — Phosgene gas

TrapPhosphine is PH3 — it contains no carbon or chlorine. The names only sound alike.
Q695CUET 2024 · 29 May (pen & paper, 306 E New) · Book A · Q20 also CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) Book A Q31, word for wordNTA final key
For SN2 reaction, the increasing order of the reactivity of the following alkyl halides is :
  1. (A) CH3CH2CH2CH2Br
  2. (B) CH3CH2CH(Br)CH3
  3. (C) (CH3)3CBr
  4. (D) (CH3)2CHCH2Br
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (A) < (B) < (C) < (D)
  2. (A) < (C) < (B) < (D)
  3. (B) < (A) < (D) < (C)
  4. (C) < (B) < (D) < (A)
Concept to recallSN2 is a one-step backside attack: the less crowded the carbon (and its neighbour), the faster. 1° > 2° > 3°; branching at the β-carbon also slows it.
  1. (C) 3°: slowest. (B) 2°: next.
  2. (D) and (A) are both 1°, but (D) is branched at C-2 (β), which crowds the backside.
  3. Increasing order: (C) < (B) < (D) < (A).

Answer: option (4) — (C) < (B) < (D) < (A)

TrapThe order is reversed for SN1, where 3° reacts fastest.
Q696CUET 2024 · 29 May (pen & paper, 306 E New) · Book A · Q38NTA final key
Passage (29 May 2024, Q34–38): reactivity of aldehydes and ketones

Aldehydes are generally more reactive than ketones in nucleophilic addition, for two reasons. Steric: a ketone carries two large groups on the carbonyl carbon, which hinder the approach of the nucleophile more than the one group (and an H) of an aldehyde. Electronic: two electron-releasing alkyl groups reduce the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon more than one does.

(NCERT text set as printed; Q35 on amines does not draw on it.)

The order of reactivity of the given haloalkanes towards nucleophile is
  1. RI > RBr > RCl
  2. RCl > RBr > RI
  3. RBr > RCl > RI
  4. RBr > RI > RCl
Concept to recallFor the same R, the weakest C–X bond (and the best leaving group) reacts fastest: R–I > R–Br > R–Cl > R–F.
  1. C–X bond enthalpy falls from Cl to I, and I− is the best leaving group.
  2. So RI > RBr > RCl.

Answer: option (1) — RI > RBr > RCl

NotePrinted under the aldehyde/ketone passage; it does not use it.
Q697CUET 2024 · 19 Jul (re-test, CBT) · Q35NTA final key
Reactivity order of following towards nucleophilic substitution reactions will be :
  1. (A) 4-Nitro-1-chlorobenzene
  2. (B) 2,4-Dinitro-1-chlorobenzene
  3. (C) Chlorobenzene
  4. (D) 2,4,6-Trinitro-1-chlorobenzene
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (A) < (B) < (C) < (D)
  2. (A) < (C) < (B) < (D)
  3. (B) < (A) < (D) < (C)
  4. (C) < (A) < (B) < (D)
Concept to recall−NO2 at ortho/para to Cl withdraws electrons by resonance and stabilises the carbanion intermediate; each extra o/p nitro group lowers the temperature needed for substitution.
  1. Chlorobenzene needs 623 K and 300 atm; 4-nitro: 443 K; 2,4-dinitro: 368 K; 2,4,6-trinitro: warm water (322 K).
  2. Increasing reactivity: (C) < (A) < (B) < (D).

Answer: option (4) — (C) < (A) < (B) < (D)

Q698CUET 2024 · 19 Jul (re-test, CBT) · Q40NTA final key
Reactivity order of the following alkyl halides towards dehydrohalogenation is :
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (A) > (B) > (C) > (D)
  2. (A) > (C) > (B) > (D)
  3. (D) > (B) > (C) > (A)
  4. (D) > (C) > (B) > (A)
Concept to recallFor the same alkyl group, elimination (like substitution) is fastest when the C–X bond is weakest: R–I > R–Br > R–Cl > R–F.
  1. All four are 2-halobutanes; only the halogen changes.
  2. C–X bond enthalpy: C–F > C–Cl > C–Br > C–I.
  3. Reactivity: (A) I > (B) Br > (C) Cl > (D) F.

Answer: option (1) — (A) > (B) > (C) > (D)

Q699CUET 2024 · 19 Jul (re-test, CBT) · Q41NTA final key
Passage (19 Jul 2024 re-test, Q41–45): nucleophilic substitution in haloalkanes

A nucleophile attacks the electron-deficient part of a substrate. In a nucleophilic substitution a nucleophile replaces the group already present; haloalkanes are typical substrates, because the carbon bonded to the halogen carries a partial positive charge. The halogen leaves as a halide ion (the leaving group).

When NaOH reacts with R-X, what is the major product ?
  1. Alcohol
  2. Ether
  3. Ester
  4. Acid
Concept to recallOH− (aqueous KOH/NaOH) replaces X: R–X + OH− → R–OH + X−.
  1. Hydroxide is the nucleophile; the product is an alcohol.

Answer: option (1) — Alcohol

TrapWith alcoholic KOH, elimination to an alkene dominates instead.
Q700CUET 2024 · 19 Jul (re-test, CBT) · Q42NTA final key
Passage (19 Jul 2024 re-test, Q41–45): nucleophilic substitution in haloalkanes

A nucleophile attacks the electron-deficient part of a substrate. In a nucleophilic substitution a nucleophile replaces the group already present; haloalkanes are typical substrates, because the carbon bonded to the halogen carries a partial positive charge. The halogen leaves as a halide ion (the leaving group).

When KCN reacts with R-X, what is the major product ?
  1. Alcohol
  2. Ether
  3. Isonitrile
  4. Nitrile
Concept to recallKCN is ionic; CN− is ambident but attacks through the more stable C–C bond-forming carbon: R–C≡N (nitrile).
  1. R–X + KCN → R–CN + KX.
  2. The major product is the alkyl cyanide (nitrile).

Answer: option (4) — Nitrile

TrapAgCN (covalent) gives the isonitrile instead — next question.
Q701CUET 2024 · 19 Jul (re-test, CBT) · Q43NTA final key
Passage (19 Jul 2024 re-test, Q41–45): nucleophilic substitution in haloalkanes

A nucleophile attacks the electron-deficient part of a substrate. In a nucleophilic substitution a nucleophile replaces the group already present; haloalkanes are typical substrates, because the carbon bonded to the halogen carries a partial positive charge. The halogen leaves as a halide ion (the leaving group).

When AgCN reacts with R-X, what is the major product ?
  1. Alcohol
  2. Ether
  3. Isonitrile
  4. Nitrile
Concept to recallAgCN is mainly covalent: only the lone pair on N is free to attack, giving R–N≡C (isocyanide).
  1. R–X + AgCN → R–NC + AgX.
  2. Major product: isonitrile.

Answer: option (3) — Isonitrile

Q702CUET 2024 · 19 Jul (re-test, CBT) · Q44NTA final key
Passage (19 Jul 2024 re-test, Q41–45): nucleophilic substitution in haloalkanes

A nucleophile attacks the electron-deficient part of a substrate. In a nucleophilic substitution a nucleophile replaces the group already present; haloalkanes are typical substrates, because the carbon bonded to the halogen carries a partial positive charge. The halogen leaves as a halide ion (the leaving group).

When KNO2 reacts with R-X, what is the major product ?
  1. Alcohol
  2. Nitroalkane
  3. Isonitrile
  4. Alkyl nitrite
Concept to recallNitrite is ambident (−O–N=O). Ionic KNO2 attacks through O: alkyl nitrite R–O–N=O. Covalent AgNO2 attacks through N: nitroalkane R–NO2.
  1. R–X + KNO2 → R–O–N=O + KX.
  2. Major product: alkyl nitrite.

Answer: option (4) — Alkyl nitrite

TrapNitroalkane is the AgNO2 product.
Q703CUET 2023 · 21 May, Shift 3 · Q18 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
Which of the following is an optically active compound? (The options are skeletal formulae.)
  1. Pentan-3-ol, CH3CH2CH(OH)CH2CH3
  2. Pentan-2-ol, CH3CH(OH)CH2CH2CH3
  3. 4-Methylheptane, (CH3CH2CH2)2CHCH3
  4. A closed skeleton drawn with a cross-shaped centre (illegible)
Concept to recallOptical activity needs a chiral carbon (four different groups) and no plane of symmetry.
  1. Pentan-3-ol: C-3 carries two ethyls ⇒ not chiral.
  2. Pentan-2-ol: C-2 carries H, OH, CH3, C3H7 ⇒ chiral ⇒ optically active.
  3. The H/CH3 carbon in (3) carries two identical propyl arms ⇒ not chiral.

Answer: option (2) — Pentan-2-ol, CH3CH(OH)CH2CH2CH3

NoteThe options are drawings; they are named here. Option (4) is printed as a garbled closed figure and cannot be read.
Q704CUET 2023 · 21 May, Shift 3 · Q22 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
The most reactive halide towards SN1 reaction is
  1. (C6H5)2CH–Cl
  2. C6H5–CH2Cl
  3. C6H11–CH2Cl (cyclohexylmethyl chloride)
  4. CH2=CH–CH2–Cl
Concept to recallSN1 rate follows carbocation stability; each phenyl on the cationic carbon spreads the charge by resonance.
  1. Ph2CH+ is stabilised by two rings > PhCH2+ (one ring) > allyl > a primary alkyl cation.
  2. So diphenylmethyl chloride ionises fastest.

Answer: option (1) — (C6H5)2CH–Cl

Q705CUET 2023 · 21 May, Shift 3 · Q3 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
Consider the following alcohol:
aCH3–bCH(aCH3)–cC(dCH3)(eCH2–fCH3)–dCH3
Identify tertiary carbon:
  1. aC
  2. eC
  3. bC
  4. cC
Concept to recallA carbon’s degree = number of other carbons bonded to it: 1° (one), 2° (two), 3° (three), 4° (four).
  1. Ca: bonded to one C ⇒ 1°. Ce: to Cc and Cf ⇒ 2°.
  2. Cb: to two CH3 (a) and Cc ⇒ three carbons ⇒ 3°.
  3. Cc: to Cb, two Cd and Ce ⇒ four carbons ⇒ 4° (quaternary).

Answer: option (3) — bC

TrapCc has the most branches but is quaternary, not tertiary.
NoteThe paper calls the structure an “alcohol” but prints no OH group (the skeleton is 2,3,3-trimethylpentane); the question only asks for the 3° carbon, so it is answerable as printed.
Q706CUET 2023 · 21 May, Shift 3 · Q30 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
Consider the following reaction: chlorobenzene —[Na, dry ether]→ biphenyl. Name of the reaction is:
  1. Balz–Schiemann reaction
  2. Wurtz reaction
  3. Wurtz–Fittig reaction
  4. Fittig reaction
Concept to recallWurtz: R–X + R–X; Wurtz–Fittig: Ar–X + R–X; Fittig: Ar–X + Ar–X (all with Na in dry ether).
  1. Both partners are aryl halides ⇒ Fittig reaction.

Answer: option (4) — Fittig reaction

Q707CUET 2023 · 21 May, Shift 3 · Q37 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
2-Methylpropene can be prepared by the reaction of
  1. (CH3)3C–Br + CH3ONa
  2. (CH3)3C–ONa + CH3Br
  3. (CH3)3C–ONa + CH3–CH2–Br
  4. (CH3)3C–ONa + CH3–CH(Br)–CH3
Concept to recallA tertiary halide with a strong base (alkoxide) undergoes elimination, not Williamson substitution.
  1. (CH3)3CBr + CH3O− → (CH3)2C=CH2 + CH3OH + Br−.
  2. (2) and (3) give ethers (SN2 on a 1° halide); (4) eliminates to propene, not 2-methylpropene.

Answer: option (1) — (CH3)3C–Br + CH3ONa

Q708CUET 2023 · 22 May, Shift 3 · Q16NTA final key
The appropriate reagent for the following conversion is :
  1. SO2Cl2
  2. N-Chlorosuccinamide
  3. Cl2/FeCl3
  4. SOCl2
Concept to recallRing halogenation of arenes is electrophilic substitution with X2 + Lewis acid (FeCl3); CH3 is o/p-directing.
  1. Cl2 + FeCl3 → Cl+ (FeCl4−), which attacks the ring.
  2. Toluene gives o- and p-chlorotoluene; the para isomer is the one drawn.
  3. SO2Cl2 and N-chlorosuccinimide chlorinate the side chain (free radical); SOCl2 converts R–OH to R–Cl.

Answer: option (3) — Cl2/FeCl3

TrapLight/heat conditions put Cl on the CH3 group (benzyl chloride), not the ring.
Q709CUET 2023 · 22 May, Shift 3 · Q26NTA final key
An alkyl halide with molecular formula C5H11Br on dehydrohalogenation give two isomeric alkenes X and Y with formula C5H10. On reductive ozonolysis X and Y gave four compounds CH3CHO, CH3–CO–CH3, (CH3)2CHCHO, HCHO. The alkyl halide is :
  1. 3-Bromopentane
  2. 2-Bromo-3-methylbutane
  3. 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane
  4. 1-Bromo-2-2-dimethyl propane
Concept to recallOzonolysis splits C=C into two carbonyls; rebuild each alkene by joining the carbonyl carbons.
  1. CH3CHO + (CH3)2CO ⇒ X = (CH3)2C=CHCH3 (2-methylbut-2-ene).
  2. (CH3)2CHCHO + HCHO ⇒ Y = (CH3)2CH–CH=CH2 (3-methylbut-1-ene).
  3. Both come from (CH3)2CH–CHBr–CH3: 2-bromo-3-methylbutane.

Answer: option (2) — 2-Bromo-3-methylbutane

Trap2-bromo-2-methylbutane gives 2-methylbut-2-ene and 2-methylbut-1-ene, whose ozonolysis gives butanone, not (CH3)2CHCHO.
Q710CUET 2023 · 22 May, Shift 3 · Q5NTA final key
The correct IUPAC name of CH3 – CH(C2H5) – CH2 – Br is:
(C2H5 drawn on the middle carbon)
  1. 1-Bromo-2-methylbutane
  2. 1-Bromo-2-ethylpropane
  3. 1-Bromo-2-ethyl-2-methyl ethane
  4. 2-Methyl-1-bromobutane
Concept to recallLongest chain through the substituent; lowest locants; prefixes in alphabetical order.
  1. BrCH2–CH(CH3)–CH2CH3: the longest chain is 4 C (through the ethyl group).
  2. Br on C1, CH3 on C2; alphabetical: bromo before methyl ⇒ 1-bromo-2-methylbutane.

Answer: option (1) — 1-Bromo-2-methylbutane

Trap“2-ethylpropane” misses the longest chain; (4) breaks the alphabetical order.
Q711CUET 2023 · 23 May, Shift 3 · Q19NTA final key
What will be the hybridisation of highlighted carbon in the given haloarene
  1. sp2
  2. sp3
  3. sp
  4. sp3d
Concept to recallIn haloarenes the halogen is bonded to an sp2 ring carbon (C–X shorter and stronger than in haloalkanes).
  1. Every benzene-ring carbon is sp2, including the one carrying X.

Answer: option (1) — sp2

Q712CUET 2023 · 23 May, Shift 3 · Q3NTA final key
Identify A and B respectively in the following equation.
Concept to recallElimination regiochemistry: alcoholic KOH gives the more substituted (Saytzeff) alkene; a bulky, hindered base removes the more accessible H and gives the less substituted (Hofmann) alkene.
  1. Substrate: 1-chloro-1-methylcyclopentane (3° halide).
  2. KOH/C2H5OH: ring H removed ⇒ B = 1-methylcyclopentene (trisubstituted, Saytzeff).
  3. (C2H5)3N (bulky): CH3 hydrogen removed ⇒ A = methylenecyclopentane (Hofmann).
  4. Option (1).

Answer: option (1) —

TrapBoth reagents are bases; the difference is steric bulk, which flips the product.
Q713CUET 2023 · 23 May, Shift 3 · Q37NTA final key
H3C–CH2–CH2–CH2–CH=CH2 ⟶HBr A
A will be
  1. H3C–CH2–CH2–CH2–CH2–CH2Br
  2. H3C–CH2–CH2–CH2–CHBr–CH3
Concept to recallMarkovnikov: H adds to the carbon with more H; Br goes to the carbon that gives the more stable carbocation.
  1. H+ adds to the terminal CH2 ⇒ 2° carbocation at C2.
  2. Br− attacks C2 ⇒ 2-bromohexane.

Answer: option (2) — H3C–CH2–CH2–CH2–CHBr–CH3

Trap(1) is the anti-Markovnikov product (needs peroxide).
Q714CUET 2023 · 25 May, Shift 3 · Q17 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
The synthesis of alkyl fluoride is best accomplished by the following reaction
CH3Br + AgF → CH3F + AgBr
The reaction is termed as:
  1. Swarts reaction
  2. Finkelstein reaction
  3. Wurtz reaction
  4. Fittig reaction
Concept to recallSwarts: R–Cl/Br + metallic fluoride (AgF, Hg2F2, CoF2, SbF3) → R–F. Finkelstein: R–X + NaI/acetone → R–I.
  1. Halogen exchange to a fluoride using AgF ⇒ Swarts reaction.

Answer: option (1) — Swarts reaction

Q715CUET 2023 · 25 May, Shift 3 · Q20 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
H3C–CH(CH3)–CH(OH)–CH3 + HBr → A. A (predominantly) is
  1. CH3–CH(Br)–CH(CH3)–CH3
  2. CH3–CH(CH3)–CH(Br)–CH3
  3. CH3–CH(CH3)–CH2–CH2–Br
  4. CH3–C(Br)(CH3)–CH2–CH3
Concept to recallSecondary alcohols react with HX by SN1; the carbocation rearranges (1,2-hydride shift) to a more stable tertiary one.
  1. Protonation and loss of water give a 2° cation at C-2 (counting from the CH(OH) end).
  2. A hydride shifts from the neighbouring CH(CH3)2 carbon → 3° cation (CH3)2C+–CH2CH3.
  3. Br− attacks → 2-bromo-2-methylbutane.

Answer: option (4) — CH3–C(Br)(CH3)–CH2–CH3

TrapOptions (1) and (2) are the same molecule, 2-bromo-3-methylbutane, written from opposite ends: the product without rearrangement.
Q716CUET 2023 · 25 May, Shift 3 · Q25 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
Aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution reactions under ordinary conditions because
A. approach of nucleophile is retarded
B. carbon carrying halogen atom is sp3 hybridised
C. the substrate molecule is destabilised due to resonance
D. of partial double bond character between carbon and halogen
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. A and D only
  2. B and C only
  3. A and C only
  4. B and D only
Concept to recallAryl halides resist SN: resonance gives C–X partial double-bond character; C is sp2; the π-electron cloud repels the nucleophile; phenyl cation is unstable.
  1. A true (electron-rich ring repels the nucleophile); D true.
  2. B false: the carbon is sp2. C false: resonance stabilises the molecule.

Answer: option (1) — A and D only

Q717CUET 2023 · 26 May, Shift 3 (Oswaal typed copy) · Q19key re-derived
Which of the following statements are correct about alkyl halides:
(A) Alkylhalides are polar so they are soluble in water (B) RX on reaction with alc. KOH give alkenes (C) RX on reaction with AgNO2 give RONO (D) SN1 proceeds with inversion in configuration (E) R–X have higher boiling point than parent alkanes
  1. (B), (E) only
  2. (A), (C) only
  3. (D), (E) only
  4. (B), (C) only
Concept to recallHaloalkanes cannot form H-bonds with water (insoluble); alc. KOH eliminates; AgNO2 (covalent) gives nitroalkanes R–NO2, KNO2 gives alkyl nitrites R–ONO; SN1 racemises.
  1. (A) false; (B) true (dehydrohalogenation).
  2. (C) false: AgNO2 gives R–NO2. (D) false: SN1 gives racemisation.
  3. (E) true: greater mass and polarity than the alkane.

Answer: option (1) — (B), (E) only

Q718CUET 2023 · 26 May, Shift 3 (Oswaal typed copy) · Q37key re-derived
The correct order of reactivity of following halides towards SN1 reaction is:
(I) C6H5Cl (II) C6H5CH2Cl (III) C6H5CH2Br (IV) C6H5CH2I
  1. (IV) > (III) > (II) > (I)
  2. (I) > (II) > (III) > (IV)
  3. (IV) > (II) > (III) > (I)
  4. (I) > (III) > (II) > (IV)
Concept to recallSN1 rate depends on carbocation stability and leaving-group ability (I− > Br− > Cl−). Aryl halides do not ionise.
  1. II, III, IV all give the resonance-stabilised benzyl cation; the better leaving group reacts faster: IV > III > II.
  2. Chlorobenzene (partial C=Cl double bond, unstable phenyl cation) is least reactive.

Answer: option (1) — (IV) > (III) > (II) > (I)

Q719CUET 2023 · 31 May, Shift 2 · Q11NTA final key
Among the following statements on the nitration of aromatic compounds, the false one is:
  1. The nitration of benzene is almost the same as that of hexadeutereo benzene
  2. The rate of nitration of toulene is greater than that of benzene
  3. The rate of nitration of benzene is greater than that of hexadeutereo benzene
  4. Nitration is an electrophilic substitution reaction.
Concept to recallIn nitration the slow step is attack of NO2+ on the ring; C–H (or C–D) breaks in a fast step, so there is no kinetic isotope effect.
  1. C6H6 and C6D6 nitrate at the same rate ⇒ (1) true, (3) false.
  2. Toluene (activated by CH3) nitrates faster; nitration is SEAr.

Answer: option (3) — The rate of nitration of benzene is greater than that of hexadeutereo benzene

NoteNitration of benzene itself is Class XI chemistry; it is filed here with the aromatic substitution of haloarenes.
Q720CUET 2023 · 31 May, Shift 2 · Q3NTA final key
Which of the following reagents can bring about the given conversion?
3-Nitrobromobenzene to 3-Nitrobenzoic acid.
  1. (a) Mg-dry ether (b) CO2 (c) H+-H2O
  2. (a) KCN (b) H3O+
  3. (a) KMnO4/OH− (b) H+-H2O
  4. (a) CrO3/H2SO4 followed by H+-H2O
Concept to recallArBr → ArMgBr → (CO2) → ArCOOMgBr → (H3O+) ArCOOH: the C–Br carbon becomes the COOH carbon.
  1. Aryl bromides do not undergo SN with CN−; KMnO4 and CrO3 need a side chain to oxidise.
  2. Only the Grignard/CO2 route adds a carbon at the Br position ⇒ option (1).

Answer: option (1) — (a) Mg-dry ether (b) CO2 (c) H+-H2O

NoteIn practice a nitro group reacts with Grignard reagents, so this route is idealised; it is the textbook answer and NTA’s key.
Q721CUET 2023 · 31 May, Shift 2 · Q30NTA final key
Among the following reaction(s) which gives (give) tert-butylbenzene as the major product
  1. A. benzene + (CH3)3CBr, C2H5ONa
  2. B. benzene + butyl chloride (drawn as a C4 chain with Cl), AlCl3
  3. C. benzene + (CH3)2C=CH2, H2SO4
  4. D. benzene + (CH3)2CHCH2OH, BF3·OEt2
  5. E. benzene + butyl chloride, H2SO4
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. B, C and D
  2. A, C and D
  3. A, D and E
  4. B, D and E
Concept to recallFriedel–Crafts alkylation goes through carbocations, which rearrange to the most stable (tertiary) cation.
  1. C: isobutylene + H+ → (CH3)3C+ → t-butylbenzene. True.
  2. D: isobutyl alcohol/BF3 → 1° cation → hydride shift → t-butyl cation. True.
  3. A: ethoxide with a 3° bromide causes elimination; no Lewis acid, no alkylation. False.
  4. C and D true and A false leaves only option (1).

Answer: option (1) — B, C and D

NoteReagents are drawn as skeletal formulas in the paper. For B to give t-butylbenzene the chloride must be isobutyl chloride (1° → 3° shift); n-butyl chloride would give mainly sec-butylbenzene. The option choice does not depend on B.
Q722CUET 2023 · 31 May, Shift 2 · Q45NTA final key
Passage: The benzene ring in phenol gives the characteristic electrophilic substitution reactions (halogenation, nitration, sulphonation, alkylation). The phenolic group activates the ortho and para positions by conjugation, so these reactions are fast; phenols do not respond to nucleophilic substitution.
Chlorobenzene + CH3COCl → (anhyd. AlCl3) → A (2-chloroacetophenone, ortho) + B (4-chloroacetophenone, para). Minor product in above reaction is:
  1. A
  2. B
  3. A and B in same quantity
  4. Depends on quantity of X
Concept to recallHalogen is an o/p director; the bulky acyl electrophile and the Cl atom make ortho attack sterically hindered.
  1. para-Isomer B is major; ortho A is minor.

Answer: option (1) — A

NoteThe reactant is drawn as a chlorobenzene ring carrying a second label X para to Cl; it is read as chlorobenzene.
Q723CUET 2023 · 5 June, Shift 1 · Q11 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
Match List I with List II
List IList II
(A) SN1 reaction(I) Vic-dibromide
(B) Bromination of alkenes(II) Gem-dibromide

  3. (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(III)
  4. (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(IV)
Concept to recallSN1 goes through a planar carbocation ⇒ racemisation. Alkylidene (gem) halides carry both X on one carbon.
  1. A-III; B: Br2 adds across C=C ⇒ vicinal dibromide, I; C-II; D: more substituted alkene ⇒ Saytzeff, IV.

Q724CUET 2023 · 5 June, Shift 1 · Q13 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
Methyl bromide reacts with silver nitrite to form:
  1. Nitromethane
  2. Methyl nitrite
  3. Ethanenitrite
  4. Grignard reagent

Q725CUET 2023 · 5 June, Shift 1 · Q40 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
An alkyl halide with molecular formula C6H13Br on dehydrohalogenation gave two isomeric alkenes A and B with molecular formula C6H12. On reductive ozonolysis, A and B gave four compounds CH3COCH3, CH3CHO, CH3CH2CHO and (CH3)2CHCHO. The alkyl halide is:
  1. 2-Bromohexane
  2. 2,2-Dimethyl-1-bromobutane
  3. 2-Bromo-2,3-dimethylbutane
  4. 3-Bromo-2-methylpentane
Concept to recallOzonolysis cuts C=C into two C=O; join the fragments back to rebuild each alkene, then find the halide that can give both.
  1. Acetone + propanal ⇒ A = (CH3)2C=CHCH2CH3.
  2. 2-Methylpropanal + ethanal ⇒ B = (CH3)2CHCH=CHCH3.
  3. Both have C=C next to C-3 of 2-methylpentane ⇒ Br on C-3: 3-bromo-2-methylpentane.

Answer: option (4) — 3-Bromo-2-methylpentane

Q726CUET 2023 · 5 June, Shift 1 · Q42 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
Passage (as printed): a ketone [A] which undergoes haloform reaction gives compound [B] on reduction. Compound [B] on heating with sulphuric acid gives compound [C] which forms a monoozonide [D]. The compound [D] on hydrolysis in the presence of zinc dust gives compound [E]. Compound [E] on oxidation gives C2H4O2 [F].
The compound [B] formed can be prepared from reaction of aq. KOH with:

  2. CH3–CH(Cl)–CH3
  3. CH3–CH(Cl)–CH2–CH3
  4. CH3–C(CH3)(Cl)–CH3

  1. B = butan-2-ol ⇒ needs 2-chlorobutane, CH3CH(Cl)CH2CH3.

Answer: option (3) — CH3–CH(Cl)–CH2–CH3

Q727CUET 2023 · 07 Jun, Shift 3 · Prepp reconstruction · Q16worked here
Out of the following which will not undergo SN1 reaction pathway:
  1. 1-Chloro-1,1,1-triphenylmethane
  2. 2-Iodo-2-methylpropane
  3. 1-Bromo-3,3-dimethylbutane
  4. 3-Bromoprop-1-ene
Concept to recallSN1 needs a stable carbocation: 3°, benzylic or allylic. Simple 1° alkyl halides do not ionise.
  1. Ph3C–Cl → trityl cation (very stable); (CH3)3C–I → 3° cation; CH2=CH–CH2Br → allyl cation.
  2. BrCH2CH2C(CH3)3 is a primary halide: its 1° cation is too unstable, so no SN1.

Answer: option (3) — 1-Bromo-3,3-dimethylbutane

NotePrepp’s unofficial key prints option (1). 1-Chloro-1,1,1-triphenylmethane (trityl chloride) ionises to the very stable triphenylmethyl cation and is a classic SN1 substrate, so that key is wrong.
Q728CUET 2023 · 07 Jun, Shift 3 · Prepp reconstruction · Q39key re-derived
Which of the following alkyl halides will undergo SN2 reaction most readily?
  1. 1-Bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane
  2. 1-Bromo-2-methylbutane
  3. 1-Bromobutane
  4. 1-Bromo-3-methylbutane
Concept to recallSN2 is a backside attack: any branching near the reacting carbon slows it.
  1. All four are primary. Branching: at C-2 in neopentyl bromide (very hindered) and 1-bromo-2-methylbutane; at C-3 in 1-bromo-3-methylbutane.
  2. Unbranched 1-bromobutane is least hindered → fastest.

Answer: option (3) — 1-Bromobutane

Q729CUET 2023 · 07 Jun, Shift 3 · Prepp reconstruction · Q6worked here
Ph–CH(Cl)–CH3 (+) ⟶ alc. KCN, Δ → ?
Product formed is:
  1. Ph–CH(CN)–CH3 (±)
  2. Ph–CH(CN)–CH3 (−)
  3. Ph–CH=CH2
  4. Ph–CH(CN)CH3 (+)
Concept to recallBenzylic (and 2°/3°) halides ionise easily: SN1 via a planar, resonance-stabilised carbocation → racemisation.
  1. 1-Chloro-1-phenylethane is secondary and benzylic: its carbocation is stabilised by the ring, so substitution goes SN1.
  2. The carbocation is planar; CN− attacks both faces equally.
  3. Product: 2-phenylpropanenitrile as a racemic (±) mixture.

Answer: option (1) — Ph–CH(CN)–CH3 (±)

TrapThe sign of rotation of a product is not predictable from the reactant’s sign, so (−) cannot be chosen as “inversion”.
NotePrepp’s unofficial key prints option (4). That option keeps the (+) sign, i.e. a single enantiomer; a secondary benzylic halide reacts by SN1 through a planar carbocation and gives the racemate.
Q730CUET 2023 · 08 Jun, Shift 3 · Prepp reconstruction · Q17key re-derived

  2. Finkelstein reaction
  3. Swarts reaction

Answer: option (3) — Swarts reaction

Q731CUET 2023 · 08 Jun, Shift 3 · Prepp reconstruction · Q30key re-derived
Arrange the following compounds in the increasing order of the rate of reaction towards nucleophilic substitution.
  1. (A) chlorobenzene
  2. (B) 2-chlorotoluene
  3. (C) 3-chlorotoluene
  4. (D) 4-chlorotoluene
  5. (E) 1-chloro-2,4-dimethylbenzene
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. E < D < C < B < A
  2. E < C < D < A < B
  3. B < C < D < A < E
  4. C < B < A < D < E
Concept to recallNucleophilic aromatic substitution is helped by electron-withdrawing groups and hindered by electron-donating ones such as CH3.
  1. Most electron-rich ring (two CH3), E, is slowest; chlorobenzene, with no CH3, is fastest.
  2. Only E < … < A fits: option (1).

Answer: option (1) — E < D < C < B < A

NoteTwo donor groups at o and p (E) must be least reactive and plain chlorobenzene (A) most; option (1) is the only one with both ends right. The ranking of the three monomethyl isomers depends on how +I and hyperconjugation are weighed and is not something to learn.
Q732CUET 2023 · 08 Jun, Shift 3 · Prepp reconstruction · Q34key re-derived

  2. Pent-2-ene
  3. Pent-3-ene

Q733CUET 2023 · 10 Jun, Shift 1 · Prepp reconstruction · Q17key re-derived
The reaction of toluene with Cl2 in the presence of FeCl3 gives X and reaction in presence of light gives Y. Thus, X and Y are
  1. X = Benzyl chloride, Y = m-Chlorotoluene
  2. X = Benzal chloride, Y = o-Chlorotoluene

  4. X = o and p-chlorotoluene, Y = trichloromethylbenzene
Concept to recallLewis acid (FeCl3), dark: ring substitution, o/p to CH3. Light/heat: free-radical side-chain substitution, which with excess Cl2 goes to C6H5CCl3.

  2. Y: side-chain chlorination → benzyl, benzal, then benzotrichloride (trichloromethylbenzene).

Q734CUET 2023 · 10 Jun, Shift 1 · Prepp reconstruction · Q26key re-derived

Q735CUET 2023 · 10 Jun, Shift 1 · Prepp reconstruction · Q4key re-derived
Identify the product ‘X’ in the following reaction: (CH3)3C–Br + Na+ −O–CH3 → X + CH3OH

  2. CH2=C(CH3)–OCH3

Q736CUET 2023 · 10 Jun, Shift 1 · Prepp reconstruction · Q40key re-derived
Which one of the following is most reactive towards substitution nucleophilic unimolecular (SN1) reaction?

  3. C6H5C(CH3)(C6H5)Br

  2. Ph2CH+ (2°) > PhCH+CH3 > PhCH2+ follow.

Q737CUET 2023 · 11 Jun, Shift 3 · Q40 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
From the following, choose the ones which are not secondary haloalkanes:

(E) 2-Bromo-3-methylbutane

  2. (A) and (C) only
  3. (C) and (D) only
  4. (D) and (E) only
Concept to recall1°/2°/3° halide: the carbon carrying X is bonded to 1/2/3 other carbons.

Q738CUET 2023 · 11 Jun, Shift 3 · Q5 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
The relative reactivity order of following halides towards SN1 reaction is:

  3. (I) > (IV) > (II) > (III)
  4. (III) > (II) > (I) > (IV)

Q739CUET 2023 · 11 Jun, Shift 3 · Q8 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
What will be the product for the following reactions?
CH3–X →KCN A    CH3–X →AgNO2 B

  3. A: CH3CN, B: CH3–O–N=O
  4. A: CH3NC, B: CH3–NO2

Q740CUET 2023 · 13 Jun, Shift 3 · Q24 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
Match List-I with List-II:
List-IList-II
(A) CH3CH2Br + alc. KOH →(I) CH3CH2NO2

Q741CUET 2023 · 13 Jun, Shift 3 · Q30 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
Which of the following alkyl halide will undergo SN1 reaction most readily?

  2. (CH3)3C–Cl

Q742CUET 2023 · 15 Jun, Shift 1 · Q10 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
In which of the following molecules is the carbon atom marked with asterisk (*) a stereocentre or chiral centre?

Q743CUET 2023 · 15 Jun, Shift 1 · Q16 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived

Q744CUET 2023 · 15 Jun, Shift 1 · Q5 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived

Q745CUET 2023 · 20 Jun, Shift 3 · Q26NTA final key

Q747CUET 2023 · 20 Jun, Shift 3 · Q30NTA final key

Q748CUET 2023 · 22 Jun, Shift 2 · Q17NTA final key

Q749CUET 2023 · 22 Jun, Shift 2 · Q20NTA final key

Q750CUET 2023 · 22 Jun, Shift 2 · Q21NTA final key

  3. CH3I > CH3Br > CH3Cl > CH3F
  4. CH3F > CH3Cl > CH3I > CH3Br
Concept to recallμ = charge × bond length: C–F is most polar but shortest, so CH3Cl has the largest μ. NCERT (Table 6.3): CH3Cl 1.860 > CH3F 1.847 > CH3Br 1.830 > CH3I 1.636 D.
  1. True order: CH3Cl > CH3F > CH3Br > CH3I — not printed.
  2. NTA’s final key is option (3): in the Assamese-medium paper option (3) is exactly this true order, so the English option (3) is a misprint of it.

Answer: option (3) — CH3I > CH3Br > CH3Cl > CH3F

NoteNTA’s final key is (3) (option Id 485584144423), which in the English paper reads CH3I > CH3Br > CH3Cl > CH3F, the reverse of the real trend. In the Assamese-medium version of the same question, option (3) is printed CH3Cl > CH3F > CH3Br > CH3I, which is the correct order (NCERT: 1.860, 1.847, 1.830, 1.636 D), so the English option (3) is evidently a misprint of the intended answer. We record NTA’s key.
Q751CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q14NTA final key
C2H5OH –X→ C2H5Cl –Y→ C2H5CN
X and Y used in the above reaction are:
  1. HgCl2 and AgCN
  2. SOCl2 and KCN
  3. Cl2 and KCN
  4. ZnCl2/HCl and AgCN
Concept to recallROH + SOCl2 → RCl + SO2↑ + HCl↑. KCN is ionic and attacks through C to give nitriles; AgCN is covalent and attacks through N to give isocyanides.
  1. X: thionyl chloride converts ethanol to chloroethane (by-products are gases).
  2. Y: KCN gives ethanenitrile-type product C2H5CN (propanenitrile).
  3. AgCN would give the isocyanide C2H5NC, so (1) and (4) fail.

Answer: option (2) — SOCl2 and KCN

TrapZnCl2/HCl (Lucas reagent) does make the chloride, but AgCN then gives the isocyanide.
Q752CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q3NTA final key
Which of the given alkylhalide would undergo racemisation when hydrolysis is done with aq. KOH?
  1. Ethyl Chloride
  2. n-propyl Chloride
  3. isopropyl Chloride
  4. n-butyl Chloride
Concept to recallRacemisation needs (i) a chiral carbon bearing the halogen and (ii) an SN1 path through a planar carbocation that the nucleophile attacks from either face.
  1. Ethyl, n-propyl and n-butyl chloride are primary (SN2, no carbocation); isopropyl chloride is secondary but its carbon carries two identical CH3 groups, so it is not chiral.
  2. Strictly, none of the four as printed has a stereocentre, so none can show racemisation.
  3. The intended compound is evidently sec-butyl chloride (2-chlorobutane, CH3CH(Cl)CH2CH3): chiral, secondary, and it racemises on SN1 hydrolysis. NTA keys the butyl chloride option.

Answer: option (4) — n-butyl Chloride

TrapChoosing isopropyl chloride because it is secondary: it forms a carbocation, but with no chiral centre there is nothing to racemise.
NoteAs printed (“n-butyl”) no option is chiral. NTA’s final key gives option (4); it is read here as a misprint for sec-butyl chloride, the textbook example of racemisation.
Q753CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q35NTA final key
Predict the product for the reaction: C6H5COOAg + Br2 → ?

  2. C6H5Br (bromobenzene)
  3. m-BrC6H4COOH
  4. p-BrC6H4COOH

  1. Silver benzoate + bromine is the Hunsdiecker reaction.
  2. Decarboxylative bromination: the COO group leaves as CO2 and Br takes its place.
  3. Product: bromobenzene.

Answer: option (2) — C6H5Br (bromobenzene)

NoteThe paper draws the structures; they are written here as formulas.
Q754CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q38NTA final key
Arrange the following nucleophiles in the decreasing order of their attacking strength:
  1. (A) C6H5COO− (benzoate)
  2. (B) CH3CH2CH2COO−
  3. (C) CH3CH2CH2CH2S−
  4. (D) CH3CH2CH2CH2O−
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (B) > (D) > (A) > (C)
  2. (C) > (D) > (B) > (A)
  3. (C) > (B) > (D) > (A)
  4. (B) > (A) > (C) > (D)
Concept to recallIn protic solvents nucleophilicity rises down a group (RS− > RO−: larger, more polarisable, less solvated). Charge delocalised by resonance (carboxylates) lowers it; more delocalisation (benzoate) lowers it further.
  1. Thiolate > alkoxide (polarisability).
  2. Alkoxide (localised charge) > carboxylate (charge spread over two O).
  3. Butanoate > benzoate (the ring withdraws and delocalises further).
  4. Order: C > D > B > A.

Answer: option (2) — (C) > (D) > (B) > (A)

NoteOption A is drawn as a structure in the paper.
Q755CUET 2022 · 10 Aug, Shift 1 (SET 06) · Q26NTA final key
Among the following statements, choose the correct statements.
(A) SN2 reaction proceeds with stereo chemical inversion.
(B) The process of conversion of Racemic mixture into enantiomer is known as Racemisation
(C) A mixture containing 2 enantiomers in equal proportions is known as Racemic mixture.
(D) The stereoisomers related to each other as superimposable mirror image are called enantiomers.
(E) The objects which are non- superimposable on their mirror image are said to be chiral and this property is known as chirality.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. A, B and C only
  2. A, C and E only
  3. B, C and E only
  4. C, D and E only
Concept to recallSN2 = back-side attack ⇒ Walden inversion. Racemisation = enantiomer → racemic mixture. Enantiomers = non-superimposable mirror images.
  1. A true; C true; E true.
  2. B reversed: racemisation converts an enantiomer into a racemic mixture.
  3. D false: enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images.

Answer: option (2) — A, C and E only

TrapB and D each swap one word; read them against the definitions.
Q756CUET 2022 · 10 Aug, Shift 1 (SET 06) · Q27NTA final key

Q757CUET 2026 · 24 May, Shift 1 · Q46NTA final key
Passage (summarised): Alcohols, phenols and ethers (24 May 2026, Q46–50)

Alcohols and phenols form when an H of an aliphatic or aromatic hydrocarbon is replaced by –OH; they are used in industry and daily life (spirit for polishing wood is mainly ethanol; sugar, cotton and paper are built from –OH compounds). Common names: alkyl group + “alcohol” (CH3OH, methyl alcohol); the simplest hydroxy derivative of benzene is phenol, and its disubstituted derivatives are named ortho (1,2), meta (1,3) and para (1,4). In ethers the four electron pairs on O are roughly tetrahedral, and the C–O–C angle is slightly more than tetrahedral because of the bulky R groups.

What is the common name for the following structure given below?
  1. Resorcinol
  2. Catechol
  3. Hydroquinone
  4. m-cresol
Concept to recallBenzenediols: 1,2 catechol; 1,3 resorcinol; 1,4 hydroquinone (quinol). Cresols are methylphenols.
  1. Two OH groups para (1,4) to each other: benzene-1,4-diol = hydroquinone.

Answer: option (3) — Hydroquinone

Q759CUET 2026 · 24 May, Shift 1 · Q48NTA final key
Passage (summarised): Alcohols, phenols and ethers (24 May 2026, Q46–50)
