What would be the structure of final product X in the following chemical reaction?
Aniline →(Nitrous acid, 273 K) A →(N,N-dimethylaniline, cold) X
  1. C6H5N(CH3)–CH2–N=N–C6H5
  2. (CH3)2N–C6H4–NH–NH–C6H5 (para)
  3. C6H5–N=N–C6H4–N(CH3)2 (para)
  4. 2-CH3C6H4–N=N–C6H4–2-CH3
Concept to recallAzo coupling: ArN2+ (weak electrophile) attacks the para position of a strongly activated ring (phenol, aromatic amine) in the cold, giving Ar–N=N–Ar′.
  1. A = benzenediazonium chloride.
  2. It couples para to N(CH3)2: X = p-(dimethylamino)azobenzene, an orange-yellow dye (butter yellow).

Answer: option (3) — C6H5–N=N–C6H4–N(CH3)2 (para)

NoteThe options are drawn as structures in the paper; they are written here as condensed formulas in the same order.
Q1062CUET 2026 · 11 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q4key re-derived
Identify the product C in the series.
  1. C6H5OH
  2. C6H5CH2OH
  3. C6H5CHO
  4. C6H5NH2
Concept to recallNitro → amine (Fe/HCl); ArNH2 → ArN2+Cl− (NaNO2/HCl, 0–5 °C); diazonium salt + warm water → phenol + N2.
  1. A = aniline (reduction of the nitro group).
  2. B = benzenediazonium chloride (diazotisation at 273 K).
  3. Warming B with water replaces –N2+ by –OH: C = phenol.

Answer: option (1) — C6H5OH

Q1063CUET 2026 · 11 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q5key re-derived
Which of the following is the strongest base?
  1. Aniline
  2. N-methyl aniline
  3. O-methyl aniline
  4. Benzylamine
Concept to recallIn arylamines the N lone pair is delocalised into the ring; in benzylamine a CH2 separates N from the ring, so it behaves as an alkylamine.
  1. Aniline, N-methylaniline and o-toluidine all have N attached to the ring: lone pair in resonance, weak bases (pKb ≈ 9–10).
  2. Benzylamine, C6H5CH2NH2, has a localised lone pair (pKb ≈ 4.7): strongest base.

Answer: option (4) — Benzylamine

TrapA methyl group helps a little, but nothing beats taking the lone pair out of resonance.
Q1064CUET 2026 · 19 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q5key re-derived
What is the correct increasing order of basic strength for the following amines when measured inside an aqueous medium?
(I) CH3NH2, (II) (CH3)2NH, (III) (CH3)3N, (IV) NH3
  1. IV < III < I < II
  2. IV < I < II < III
  3. III < I < II < IV
  4. I < II < III < IV
Concept to recallIn water, methylamines: 2° > 1° > 3° > NH3 (+I effect balanced by solvation of the ammonium ion and steric hindrance).
  1. pKb: (CH3)2NH 3.27, CH3NH2 3.38, (CH3)3N 4.22, NH3 4.75.
  2. Increasing basicity: NH3 < 3° < 1° < 2°, i.e. IV < III < I < II.

Answer: option (1) — IV < III < I < II

Trap(2) is the gas-phase order (inductive effect only).
Q1065CUET 2026 · 21 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q2key re-derived
Among the following amines, the strongest base in aqueous solution is:

  2. (CH3)3N
  3. (CH3)2NH
  4. CH3NH2
Concept to recallAqueous basicity of methylamines: 2° > 1° > 3° > NH3.
  1. Dimethylamine combines a good +I effect with good solvation of its cation: pKb 3.27, the lowest.

Q1066CUET 2026 · 21 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q6key re-derived

  2. Dimethylamine (2°) gives an alkali-insoluble product; the 3° amines do not react.

Q1067CUET 2026 · 21 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q7key re-derived

Q1068CUET 2026 · 22 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q4key re-derived

Q1069CUET 2026 · 22 May, Shift 2 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q3key re-derived
An organic primary amide is treated with bromine (Br2) and an aqueous solution of sodium hydroxide (NaOH) to yield a primary amine. Which of the following statements correctly describes this transformation (Hofmann Bromamide Degradation)?
  1. The resulting primary amine contains one more carbon atom than the starting amide.
  2. The resulting primary amine contains the exact same number of carbon atoms as the starting amide.
  3. The resulting primary amine contains one less carbon atom than the starting amide due to the loss of the carbonyl group as a carbonate ion.
  4. The reaction converts a secondary amide into a tertiary amine via a molecular rearrangement.
Concept to recallRCONH2 + Br2 + 4NaOH → RNH2 + Na2CO3 + 2NaBr + 2H2O.
  1. R migrates from C to N; the carbonyl carbon leaves as CO32−.
  2. The amine has one carbon fewer than the amide: a step down the series.

Answer: option (3) — The resulting primary amine contains one less carbon atom than the starting amide due to the loss of the carbonyl group as a carbonate ion.

TrapReduction of an amide (LiAlH4) keeps every carbon; Hofmann loses one.
Q1070CUET 2026 · 26 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q2key re-derived

Answer: option (3) — C and E only

Q1071CUET 2026 · 26 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q4key re-derived

Q1079CUET 2025 · 13 May, Shift 1 · Q32NTA final key

Q1086CUET 2025 · 23 May, Shift 2 · Q41 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here
Passage (summarised): amines

Amines are derivatives of ammonia in which hydrogen atoms are replaced by alkyl or aryl groups; they are prepared from nitro compounds, halides, amides, imides and so on. Hydrogen bonding governs their physical properties. In alkylamines the basic strength in protic polar solvents is set by a combination of electron release, steric effects and hydrogen bonding (solvation of the ammonium cation); alkylamines are stronger bases than ammonia, which is more basic than water. Primary and secondary amines associate through hydrogen bonds (more so primary); tertiary amines cannot, having no N–H, and boiling points follow this. In aromatic amines electron-releasing groups raise and electron-withdrawing groups lower basicity. Aryl diazonium salts, made from arylamines, have the diazonium group replaced by many nucleophiles, and couple with phenols or arylamines to give dyes.

Complete the reaction by giving the final product:
Chloroethane + ethanolic (NaCN) + LiAlH4 → ?
  1. CH3CH2NH2
  2. CH3CH2CH2NH2
  3. CH3CH2CN
  4. CH3CH2CH2CN
Concept to recallR–X + CN− → R–CN (one C more); LiAlH4 reduces R–CN to R–CH2NH2 (ascent of series).
  1. CH3CH2Cl + NaCN → CH3CH2CN (propanenitrile).
  2. LiAlH4: CH3CH2CN → CH3CH2CH2NH2 (propan-1-amine).

Answer: option (2) — CH3CH2CH2NH2

TrapEthylamine (option 1) forgets the extra carbon added by cyanide.

Concept to recallThe weakly electrophilic ArN2+ attacks only electron-rich rings.
  1. Phenol and aniline couple readily (strongly activated rings).
  2. Nitrobenzene’s ring is deactivated by –NO2: no coupling.

Answer: option (4) — Nitrobenzene

NoteAnisole is only moderately activated and couples sluggishly, but among these four nitrobenzene is the clear answer. The same idea, with different distractors, is 13 May 2025 Shift 1 Q35.
Q1091CUET 2025 · 24 May, Shift 2 · Q25 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here
Aniline can be distinguished from ethanamine by
  1. Hinsberg’s Reagent
  2. Isocyanide Test
  3. Nitrous acid test
  4. Tollen’s Test
Concept to recallWith HNO2 (NaNO2 + HCl) a 1° aliphatic amine gives an unstable diazonium salt that loses N2 at once (brisk effervescence, alcohol); a 1° aromatic amine at 273–278 K gives a stable diazonium salt (no gas), which couples with β-naphthol to an orange dye.
  1. Both are primary amines: Hinsberg and carbylamine tests respond identically.
  2. Nitrous acid: ethanamine → N2 gas; aniline → benzenediazonium chloride, no gas.
  3. Tollens’ reagent reacts with neither.

Answer: option (3) — Nitrous acid test

TrapThe carbylamine test separates 1° from 2°/3°, not aliphatic from aromatic.
Q1092CUET 2025 · 24 May, Shift 2 · Q26 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here
In the following reaction, the product A is
p-Nitrotoluene → 1. Br2; 2. Sn/HCl; 3. NaNO2/HCl, 273–278 K; 4. H3PO2; 5. KMnO4/H+ → A
  1. p-Bromobenzoic acid
  2. m-Bromobenzoic acid
  3. o-Bromobenzoic acid
  4. 2,4-Dibromobenzoic acid
Concept to recallAn NH2 group can be introduced, used to steer a substituent, and then removed: diazotise and reduce with H3PO2 (ArN2+ → ArH).
  1. Br2/Fe: CH3 (o/p director) and NO2 (meta director) both send Br to the carbon ortho to CH3.
  2. Sn/HCl: NO2 → NH2; diazotise, then H3PO2 replaces N2+ by H → 2-bromotoluene.
  3. KMnO4/H+: CH3 → COOH → o-bromobenzoic acid.

Answer: option (3) — o-Bromobenzoic acid

Q1093CUET 2025 · 24 May, Shift 2 · Q29 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here
Identify the correct statements from the given below:

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

  2. (A), (B) and (C) only
  3. (A), (B), (C) and (D)
  4. (B), (C) and (D) only.
Concept to recallN is less electronegative than O, so it donates its lone pair more readily (amines are more basic). Gabriel synthesis fails for aryl amines (aryl halides do not undergo SN with phthalimide anion).
  1. (A) True.
  2. (B) False: only 1° aliphatic amines.
  3. (C) True: 1° amines have two N–H for H-bonding, 3° none.
  4. (D) True: any 1° amine, aliphatic or aromatic, gives the foul isocyanide.

Q1094CUET 2025 · 24 May, Shift 2 · Q32 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here
Arrange the following amines in increasing order of their basic strength in the gaseous phase
  1. (A) C6H5NH2
  2. (B) C6H5CH2NH2
  3. (C) (CH3)3N
  4. (D) CH3NH2
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (A), (B), (C), (D)
  2. (A), (B), (D), (C)
  3. (B), (A), (D), (C)
  4. (B), (A), (C), (D)
Concept to recallGas phase (no solvation): more alkyl groups = more +I = more basic, so 3° > 2° > 1° > NH3; arylamines are weakest because the lone pair is delocalised into the ring.
  1. Weakest: aniline (A), lone pair in resonance with the ring.
  2. Strongest: trimethylamine (C), three +I groups and no solvation effect in the gas phase.
  3. Benzylamine (B) and methylamine (D) are both 1° alkylamines between them; the order intended is (A) < (B) < (D) < (C).

Answer: option (2) — (A), (B), (D), (C)

NoteOnly option (2) has aniline weakest and trimethylamine strongest, so it is the intended answer. Measured gas-phase proton affinities actually put benzylamine slightly above methylamine (the larger benzyl group is more polarisable); that order, (A) < (D) < (B) < (C), is not offered. Option (1), with trimethylamine below methylamine, is the aqueous order and is the distractor for a student who ignores “gaseous phase”.
Q1095CUET 2025 · 24 May, Shift 2 · Q5 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here
The IUPAC name of allylamine is:

  2. Prop-2-en-1-amine
  3. Prop-1-en-3-amine
  4. Prop-1-en-1-amine
Concept to recallAllyl = CH2=CH–CH2–. Number from the end that gives the principal group (–NH2) the lowest locant.
  1. Allylamine is CH2=CH–CH2–NH2.
  2. Number from the NH2 carbon: NH2 on C1, C=C between C2 and C3.
  3. Name: prop-2-en-1-amine.

Answer: option (2) — Prop-2-en-1-amine

Trap“Prop-1-en-3-amine” numbers from the wrong end: the amine, not the double bond, takes the lowest locant.
Q1096CUET 2025 · 26 May, Shift 2 · Q12 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here
Which of the following amine forms a stable diazonium salt?

  2. Secondary aliphatic amines
  3. Primary aromatic amines
  4. Secondary aromatic amines
Concept to recallArenediazonium salts are stabilised by dispersal of the positive charge over the benzene ring; they are prepared at 273–278 K and used at once.
  1. 1° aromatic amine + NaNO2/HCl at 273–278 K → ArN2+Cl−, stable in cold solution.
  2. Aliphatic diazonium salts lose N2 instantly; 2° amines give N-nitrosamines.

Q1097CUET 2025 · 26 May, Shift 2 · Q16 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here

  4. Secondary and tertiary amines

Q1098CUET 2025 · 26 May, Shift 2 · Q35 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here
Arrange the following amines in increasing order of basicity in aqueous solution

  2. (B) CH3NH2

  2. Increasing basicity: (D), (C), (B), (A).

Q1099CUET 2025 · 26 May, Shift 2 · Q37 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here

  2. Cold water
  3. Warm water

Concept to recallNCERT: benzenediazonium chloride is a colourless crystalline solid, readily soluble in water, stable in cold water but reacting with water when warmed, and it decomposes easily in the dry state.
  1. Dry state: decomposes (even explosively).
  2. Warm water: reacts to give phenol + N2.
  3. Cold water: stable. So both dry state and warm water.

Q1100CUET 2025 · 26 May, Shift 2 · Q9 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here
The Hoffmann bromamide degradation reaction is used for conversion of

  2. Amide to amine
  3. Cyanide to amine

Q1101CUET 2025 · 27 May, Shift 2 · Q13 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here

Q1102CUET 2025 · 27 May, Shift 2 · Q30 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here

  2. (D), (C), (B), (A)
  3. (D), (A), (C), (B)
  4. (C), (A), (D), (B)

Q1103CUET 2025 · 27 May, Shift 2 · Q31 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here

  2. (B), (A), (C), (D)
  3. (D), (B), (A), (C)
  4. (A), (B), (D), (C)
Concept to recallNCERT reasoning: solubility comes from H-bonding with water, which falls as the hydrocarbon part grows; O is more electronegative than N, so an alcohol H-bonds more strongly than the amine of similar mass; aryl amines are only sparingly soluble.

  2. Most: methanamine (smallest).
  3. Between the C4 compounds, NCERT’s O-vs-N argument puts n-butanol above butan-1-amine.

Q1104CUET 2025 · 27 May, Shift 2 · Q7 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here

Q1106CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Sets A–D · Set A Q13NTA final key

  1. p-Nitroaniline

  4. 2,4-Dinitroaniline

Q1107CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Sets A–D · Set A Q14NTA final key
What will be increasing order of basic strength of the following compounds?
C2H5NH2, (C2H5)2NH, (C2H5)3N, C6H5NH2

Q1108CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Sets A–D · Set A Q21NTA final key

  2. (A), (B) and (C) only
  3. (A), (C) and (D) only
  4. (B), (C) and (D) only

  1. C6H5NH2 + AlCl3 → C6H5NH2+–AlCl3− (salt): A.
  2. N carries a positive charge (C), which deactivates the ring for further substitution (D).
  3. Answer: (A), (C), (D).

Q1109CUET 2024 · 29 May (pen & paper, 306 E New) · Book A · Q12NTA final key

  2. Aryl amine
  3. Phenol
  4. Diphenyl ether
Concept to recallSandmeyer (CuCl/HCl, CuBr/HBr) and Gattermann (Cu powder + HX) both replace −N2+ by −Cl or −Br.
  1. ArN2+X− + Cu/HX → ArX + N2.
  2. The product is a haloarene.

Answer: option (1) — Haloarene

Q1110CUET 2024 · 29 May (pen & paper, 306 E New) · Book A · Q13NTA final key
What is the major product of Carbylamine reaction ?
  1. Cyanide
  2. Isocyanide
  3. Nitrile
  4. Alkane

  1. RNH2 + CHCl3 + 3KOH → R–N≡C + 3KCl + 3H2O.
  2. R–NC is an isocyanide (carbylamine).

Answer: option (2) — Isocyanide

Q1111CUET 2024 · 29 May (pen & paper, 306 E New) · Book A · Q27NTA final key
The correct statement/statements from the options given below is/are :
  1. (A) Diazonium salts of aromatic amines are less stable than diazonium salts of aliphatic amines.
  2. (B) Ethylamine is insoluble in water.
  3. (C) Gabriel phthalimide synthesis can be used to prepare primary amines.
  4. (D) Beacuse of +R-effect of –NH2 group, aniline will undergo Friedel-Crafts acylation reaction.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (A) and (B) only
  2. (A), (C) and (D) only
  3. (A) and (C) only
  4. (B), (C) and (D) only
Concept to recallArenediazonium salts are resonance-stabilised (stable below 278 K); alkanediazonium salts decompose at once. Aniline, a Lewis base, forms a salt with AlCl3 and does not undergo Friedel–Crafts reactions.
  1. (A) false: aromatic diazonium salts are more stable than aliphatic ones.
  2. (B) false: ethylamine H-bonds with water and is miscible.
  3. (C) true: Gabriel synthesis gives pure 1° aliphatic amines.
  4. (D) false: the −NH2 binds AlCl3, putting + on N and deactivating the ring.
  5. Only (C) is true, and no option is “(C) only”.

No option is correct as printed — see the note.

Q1112CUET 2024 · 29 May (pen & paper, 306 E New) · Book A · Q29NTA final key
Match List-I with List-II :
List-I (Compound)List-II (Property)
(A) COCl2(I) To distinguish between primary, secondary and tertiary amines
(B) (II) Poisonous gas
(C) (III) Synthesis of primary amines
(D) (IV) Zwitter ion
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (A) – (II), (B) – (I), (C) – (IV), (D) – (III)
  2. (A) – (II), (B) – (I), (C) – (III), (D) – (IV)
  3. (A) – (I), (B) – (II), (C) – (IV), (D) – (III)
  4. (A) – (I), (B) – (II), (C) – (III), (D) – (IV)
Concept to recallHinsberg-type reagents are arenesulphonyl chlorides (benzene- or p-toluene-sulphonyl chloride); sulphanilic acid exists as a zwitter ion; phthalimide is the Gabriel reagent.
  1. (A) COCl2 phosgene: poisonous gas (II).
  2. (B) p-toluenesulphonyl chloride: sulphonamide test for 1°/2°/3° amines (I).
  3. (C) H3N+–C6H4–SO3−, sulphanilic acid: zwitter ion (IV).
  4. (D) phthalimide: Gabriel synthesis of 1° amines (III).

Q1113CUET 2024 · 29 May (pen & paper, 306 E New) · Book A · Q35NTA final key
Passage (29 May 2024, Q34–38): reactivity of aldehydes and ketones

Aldehydes are generally more reactive than ketones in nucleophilic addition, for two reasons. Steric: a ketone carries two large groups on the carbonyl carbon, which hinder the approach of the nucleophile more than the one group (and an H) of an aldehyde. Electronic: two electron-releasing alkyl groups reduce the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon more than one does.

(NCERT text set as printed; Q35 on amines does not draw on it.)

The correct decreasing order of basic strength of following amines in aqueous solution is :
CH3NH2, (CH3)2NH, (CH3)3N, NH3
  1. CH3NH2 > (CH3)2NH > NH3 > (CH3)3N
  2. CH3NH2 > (CH3)2NH > (CH3)3N > NH3
  3. NH3 > (CH3)3N > (CH3)2NH > CH3NH2
  4. (CH3)2NH > CH3NH2 > (CH3)3N > NH3
Concept to recallIn water, methylamines: 2° > 1° > 3° > NH3 (inductive effect, solvation and steric hindrance together).
  1. pKb: (CH3)2NH 3.27, CH3NH2 3.38, (CH3)3N 4.22, NH3 4.75.
  2. Lower pKb = stronger base: 2° > 1° > 3° > NH3.

Answer: option (4) — (CH3)2NH > CH3NH2 > (CH3)3N > NH3

TrapIn the gas phase (no solvation) the order is 3° > 2° > 1° > NH3.
NotePrinted under the aldehyde/ketone passage, but the question is on amines and does not use it.
Q1114CUET 2024 · 19 Jul (re-test, CBT) · Q45NTA final key
Passage (19 Jul 2024 re-test, Q41–45): nucleophilic substitution in haloalkanes

A nucleophile attacks the electron-deficient part of a substrate. In a nucleophilic substitution a nucleophile replaces the group already present; haloalkanes are typical substrates, because the carbon bonded to the halogen carries a partial positive charge. The halogen leaves as a halide ion (the leaving group).

When NH3 reacts with R-X, what is the major product ?
  1. Nitroalkane
  2. Isonitrile
  3. Alkyl nitrite
  4. Primary amine
Concept to recallAmmonolysis (Hofmann): R–X + NH3 → R–NH2 (+ HX); with excess NH3 the primary amine is the major product.
  1. NH3 is the nucleophile: R–X + NH3 → RNH3+X− →(base) RNH2.
  2. Major product (excess NH3): primary amine.

Answer: option (4) — Primary amine

TrapWith excess RX the reaction runs on to 2°, 3° amines and the quaternary salt.
Q1115CUET 2024 · 19 Jul (re-test, CBT) · Q46NTA final key
Passage (19 Jul 2024 re-test, Q46–50): basic strength of aliphatic amines in water

The more stable the substituted ammonium cation, the stronger the amine as a base. Stabilisation by hydration (H-bonding with water) alone would give the order primary > secondary > tertiary, opposite to the order predicted by the inductive effect. With a small group such as −CH3 there is no steric hindrance to H-bonding; with a bigger group such as −C2H5 there is, so changing the alkyl group changes the order. The basic strength of alkylamines in water is thus decided by an interplay of inductive effect, solvation effect and steric hindrance.

Which among the following amines is most basic in aqueous medium ?
  1. (C2H5)2NH
  2. (C2H5)3N
  3. C2H5NH2
  4. NH3
Concept to recallIn water: ethylamines (C2H5)2NH > (C2H5)3N > C2H5NH2 > NH3; methylamines (CH3)2NH > CH3NH2 > (CH3)3N > NH3.
  1. pKb: (C2H5)2NH 3.00, (C2H5)3N 3.25, C2H5NH2 3.29, NH3 4.75.
  2. Lowest pKb: diethylamine, the most basic.

Answer: option (1) — (C2H5)2NH

Q1116CUET 2024 · 19 Jul (re-test, CBT) · Q47NTA final key
Passage (19 Jul 2024 re-test, Q46–50): basic strength of aliphatic amines in water

The more stable the substituted ammonium cation, the stronger the amine as a base. Stabilisation by hydration (H-bonding with water) alone would give the order primary > secondary > tertiary, opposite to the order predicted by the inductive effect. With a small group such as −CH3 there is no steric hindrance to H-bonding; with a bigger group such as −C2H5 there is, so changing the alkyl group changes the order. The basic strength of alkylamines in water is thus decided by an interplay of inductive effect, solvation effect and steric hindrance.

Which base among the following is least basic in aqueous medium ?
  1. (CH3)2NH
  2. CH3NH2
  3. (CH3)3N
  4. NH3
Concept to recallEvery alkylamine is more basic than NH3 (+I effect of alkyl groups).
  1. Order in water: (CH3)2NH > CH3NH2 > (CH3)3N > NH3.
  2. NH3 (pKb 4.75) is the least basic.

Answer: option (4) — NH3

Trap(CH3)3N is the weakest amine here, but still stronger than NH3.
Q1117CUET 2024 · 19 Jul (re-test, CBT) · Q48NTA final key
Passage (19 Jul 2024 re-test, Q46–50): basic strength of aliphatic amines in water

The more stable the substituted ammonium cation, the stronger the amine as a base. Stabilisation by hydration (H-bonding with water) alone would give the order primary > secondary > tertiary, opposite to the order predicted by the inductive effect. With a small group such as −CH3 there is no steric hindrance to H-bonding; with a bigger group such as −C2H5 there is, so changing the alkyl group changes the order. The basic strength of alkylamines in water is thus decided by an interplay of inductive effect, solvation effect and steric hindrance.

The most basic amine in gaseous medium is :
  1. (CH3)2NH
  2. CH3NH2
  3. (CH3)3N
  4. NH3
Concept to recallIn the gas phase there is no solvation, so only the +I effect counts: 3° > 2° > 1° > NH3.
  1. Three CH3 groups push the most electron density onto N.
  2. Trimethylamine is the most basic in the gas phase.

Answer: option (3) — (CH3)3N

TrapIn water the answer would be (CH3)2NH.
Q1118CUET 2024 · 19 Jul (re-test, CBT) · Q49NTA final key
Passage (19 Jul 2024 re-test, Q46–50): basic strength of aliphatic amines in water

The more stable the substituted ammonium cation, the stronger the amine as a base. Stabilisation by hydration (H-bonding with water) alone would give the order primary > secondary > tertiary, opposite to the order predicted by the inductive effect. With a small group such as −CH3 there is no steric hindrance to H-bonding; with a bigger group such as −C2H5 there is, so changing the alkyl group changes the order. The basic strength of alkylamines in water is thus decided by an interplay of inductive effect, solvation effect and steric hindrance.

Which factor is not responsible for basic strength of amines ?
  1. Conjugation factor
  2. Inductive effect
  3. Solvation effect
  4. Steric hinderance
Concept to recallFor alkylamines in water, basicity is the interplay of inductive effect, solvation and steric hindrance (the passage names exactly these three).
  1. The passage lists inductive, solvation and steric effects.
  2. “Conjugation factor” is not among them.

Answer: option (1) — Conjugation factor

NoteStrictly, conjugation (resonance of the N lone pair with the ring) is what makes arylamines weak bases; for the aliphatic amines of the passage it plays no part, which is what NTA intends.
Q1119CUET 2024 · 19 Jul (re-test, CBT) · Q5NTA final key

With a small group such as −CH3 there is no steric hindrance to H-bonding; with a bigger group such as −C2H5 there is, so changing the alkyl group changes the order. Hinsberg's reagent is :

Q1121CUET 2023 · 21 May, Shift 3 · Q12 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
Choose the correct sequential order for the conversion of 3-methylbutan-1-ol to 2-methylpropanal
A. CH3–CH(CH3)–CH2CONH2
B. CH3–CH(CH3)–CH2–CHO
C. CH3–CH(CH3)–CH2–NH2
D. CH3–CH(CH3)–CH2COOH
E. CH3–CH(CH3)–CH2–OH
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. C, D, E, A, B
  2. B, D, A, C, E
  3. D, A, B, E, C
  4. A, C, D, B, E
Concept to recallStepping down one carbon: acid → amide → Hoffmann bromamide degradation (amine with one C fewer) → HNO2 gives the alcohol → mild oxidation gives the aldehyde.
  1. 3-Methylbutan-1-ol → (mild oxidation) B, 3-methylbutanal → (oxidation) D, 3-methylbutanoic acid.
  2. D → (NH3, heat) A, the amide → (Br2/NaOH) C, 2-methylpropan-1-amine (one C lost).
  3. C → (HNO2) E, 2-methylpropan-1-ol; a final PCC oxidation gives 2-methylpropanal.
  4. Order of intermediates: B, D, A, C, E.

Answer: option (2) — B, D, A, C, E

TrapThe carbon count drops only at the Hoffmann step, so the amide must come immediately before the amine.
Q1122CUET 2023 · 21 May, Shift 3 · Q26 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
Which statement is/are true for Gabriel phthalimide synthesis?
A. It is used for the preparation of primary and secondary amines
B. It is only used for the preparation of primary amines
C. Aromatic primary amines can not be prepared by this method
D. Only tertiary amines can be prepared
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. A, B only
  2. A, C only
  3. B, C only
  4. D only
Concept to recallGabriel synthesis: potassium phthalimide + alkyl halide (SN2), then hydrolysis → pure 1° aliphatic amine.
  1. Only one N–C bond is made ⇒ primary amines only (B true, A and D false).
  2. Aryl halides do not undergo SN2 with phthalimide anion ⇒ no aromatic amines (C true).

Answer: option (3) — B, C only

Q1123CUET 2023 · 21 May, Shift 3 · Q39 · Prepp reconstructionworked here
Which of the following statements are correct?
A. p-Nitroaniline is a stronger base than aniline
B. Aniline is weaker base than o-nitroaniline
C. Aniline is a weaker base than ethylamine
D. p-Methoxyaniline is stronger base than aniline
E. Aniline is weaker base than ammonia
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. E, C and D only
  2. C, A and B only
  3. A, B and C only
  4. B, D and A only
Concept to recallBasicity of an amine = availability of the N lone pair: electron-releasing groups raise it, electron-withdrawing groups and ring resonance lower it.
  1. –NO2 withdraws electrons ⇒ nitroanilines are weaker than aniline: A and B false.
  2. Ethylamine (+I) > NH3 > aniline (lone pair in resonance): C and E true.
  3. –OCH3 at para donates by resonance ⇒ D true.

Answer: option (1) — E, C and D only

NotePrepp’s key gives option (3), A, B and C only. A and B are false (an electron-withdrawing –NO2 makes nitroanilines weaker bases than aniline), so the answer is option (1).
Q1124CUET 2023 · 21 May, Shift 3 · Q9 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
The major product of the following reaction will be

  1. m-Nitroaniline (NH2 and NO2 1,3)
  2. o-Nitroaniline (NH2 and NO2 1,2)
  3. p-Nitroaniline (NH2 and NO2 1,4)
  4. 2,6-Dinitroaniline
Concept to recallAcetylation protects –NH2 (no anilinium ion, no oxidation) and keeps it o/p directing; the bulky –NHCOCH3 makes para the major product.
  1. Aniline + acetic anhydride → acetanilide.
  2. Nitration of acetanilide → mainly p-nitroacetanilide.
  3. Acid hydrolysis removes the acetyl group → p-nitroaniline.

Answer: option (3) — p-Nitroaniline (NH2 and NO2 1,4)

TrapDirect nitration of aniline gives ~47% meta (via anilinium ion); protection is exactly what prevents that.
Q1125CUET 2023 · 22 May, Shift 3 · Q10NTA final key
In amines, the nitrogen atom is A and B hybridised, making geometry of amines as C. Then A, B and C respectively are :
  1. trivalent, sp2, trigonal
  2. tetravalent, sp3, tetrahedral
  3. trivalent, sp3, pyramidal
  4. tetravalent, sp2, pyramidal
Concept to recallAmine N: three σ bonds + one lone pair in sp3 orbitals ⇒ pyramidal (C–N–C ≈ 108°).

  2. Four electron pairs ⇒ sp3.
  3. One is a lone pair ⇒ pyramidal shape.

Q1126CUET 2023 · 22 May, Shift 3 · Q29NTA final key

  3. Triethylamine

Q1127CUET 2023 · 22 May, Shift 3 · Q33NTA final key

  3. (CH3)2NH, (CH3)3N, CH3NH2, NH3
  4. (CH3)3N, CH3NH2, (CH3)2NH, NH3

Q1128CUET 2023 · 23 May, Shift 3 · Q12NTA final key
Nitrogen containing compounds are basic in nature & their basic strength depends on ease of availability of lone pair of electrons on nitrogen atoms. For the following nitrogen containing compounds what will be correct order of basicity?Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. A > B > D > C > E
  2. B > A > D > E > C
  3. B > D > A > C > E
  4. A > D > B > E > C
Concept to recallLone pair availability: sp3 N (aliphatic) > sp2 N (pyridine) > N conjugated with a ring (aniline) > N whose lone pair is part of the aromatic sextet (pyrrole).
  1. Piperidine (pKb ≈ 2.9) > cyclohexylamine (≈ 3.3): both sp3; the 2° ring amine is a little stronger.
  2. Pyridine (≈ 8.8): sp2 lone pair, more s-character, held tighter.
  3. Aniline (≈ 9.4): lone pair delocalised into the ring.
  4. Pyrrole: lone pair is part of the aromatic sextet ⇒ practically non-basic.
  5. A > D > B > E > C.

Answer: option (4) — A > D > B > E > C

Q1133CUET 2023 · 25 May, Shift 3 · Q29 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived

Q1135CUET 2023 · 26 May, Shift 3 (Oswaal typed copy) · Q15worked here

Q1141CUET 2023 · 5 June, Shift 1 · Q34 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived

Q1145CUET 2023 · 07 Jun, Shift 3 · Prepp reconstruction · Q9worked here

  1. (A) C6H5–N≡C

Q1175CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q20NTA final key

Q1176CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q22NTA final key

  3. C: CH3NH2 + HNO2 → CH3OH + N2 + H2O: methyl alcohol.

Answer: option (2) — Methyl alcohol

TrapEthyl alcohol forgets that the Hoffmann step loses a carbon.
Q1178CUET 2022 · 10 Aug, Shift 1 (SET 06) · Q41NTA final key
Passage: The reaction of amines with mineral acids to form ammonium salt shows that these are basic in nature. Amines have an unshared pair of electron on nitrogen atom due to which they behave as lewis base. Basicity of amines is related to their structure. Basic character of an amine depends upon the ease of formation of cation by accepting a proton from the acid. The more stable the cation is relative to the amine, more basic is the amine.
Structure of ammonium salt when ethylamine reacts with one mole of HCl?:
  1. C2H5 – NH3+ Cl−
  2. (C2H5)2 – NH2+ Cl−
  3. (C2H5)3– NH+Cl−
  4. (C2H5)4– N+Cl−
Concept to recallRNH2 + HCl → RNH3+Cl− (alkylammonium chloride).
  1. Ethylamine C2H5NH2 accepts one H+: C2H5NH3+Cl−.

Answer: option (1) — C2H5 – NH3+ Cl−

Q1179CUET 2022 · 10 Aug, Shift 1 (SET 06) · Q42NTA final key
Passage: The reaction of amines with mineral acids to form ammonium salt shows that these are basic in nature. Amines have an unshared pair of electron on nitrogen atom due to which they behave as lewis base. Basicity of amines is related to their structure. Basic character of an amine depends upon the ease of formation of cation by accepting a proton from the acid. The more stable the cation is relative to the amine, more basic is the amine.
Among the following amines, which one is most basic (in aqueous solution)?
  1. NH3
  2. C2H5NH2
  3. (C2H5)2NH
  4. (C2H5)3N
Concept to recallIn water: inductive effect + solvation of the cation + steric hindrance. Ethyl series: 2° > 3° > 1° > NH3.
  1. (C2H5)2NH (pKb 3.00) > (C2H5)3N (3.25) > C2H5NH2 (3.29) > NH3 (4.75).

Answer: option (3) — (C2H5)2NH

TrapTertiary is most basic only in the gas phase; in water its cation is poorly solvated.
Q1180CUET 2022 · 10 Aug, Shift 1 (SET 06) · Q43NTA final key
Passage: The reaction of amines with mineral acids to form ammonium salt shows that these are basic in nature. Amines have an unshared pair of electron on nitrogen atom due to which they behave as lewis base. Basicity of amines is related to their structure. Basic character of an amine depends upon the ease of formation of cation by accepting a proton from the acid. The more stable the cation is relative to the amine, more basic is the amine.
The correct order of basicity of amines in gas phase
  1. 1° < 3° < 2°
  2. 3° < 1° < 2°
  3. 2° < 3° < 1°
  4. 1° < 2° < 3°
Concept to recallGas phase: no solvation, so only the +I effect of alkyl groups counts.
  1. More alkyl groups ⇒ more electron density on N and a more stable cation.
  2. 1° < 2° < 3°.

Answer: option (4) — 1° < 2° < 3°

Q1181CUET 2022 · 10 Aug, Shift 1 (SET 06) · Q44NTA final key

Amines have an unshared pair of electron on nitrogen atom due to which they behave as lewis base. Basicity of amines is related to their structure. Basic character of an amine depends upon the ease of formation of cation by accepting a proton from the acid. The more stable the cation is relative to the amine, more basic is the amine.

  3. (C2H5)2NH
  4. C6H5NH2
Concept to recallHighest pKb = weakest base. In arylamines the N lone pair is delocalised into the ring.

Answer: option (4) — C6H5NH2

Q1183CUET 2026 · 24 May, Shift 1 · Q35NTA final key

Q1203CUET 2026 · 30 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (collegedunia) · Q10 also 2026 31 May S2 Q10 (memory-based, collegedunia) (assertion without the mutarotation clause; same answer)key re-derived

Reason (R): In sucrose, both anomeric carbon atoms are involved in glycosidic bond formation.
  1. Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
  2. Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.

Q1209CUET 2025 · 21 May, Shift 2 · Q41 (dubuddy re-typeset)worked here
Passage (summarised): biomolecules

Biomolecules are the organic compounds that are essential constituents of living cells; the large ones are called macromolecules: carbohydrates, enzymes, nucleic acids, amino acids and proteins. Carbohydrates are grouped as sugars and non-sugars (sucrose, glucose, fructose, starch, cellulose). Enzymes take part in the chemical reactions of nucleic acids. The two nucleic acids found in living systems are DNA and RNA. Amino acids carry two functional groups, carboxyl and amino. Proteins are crucial to almost every process in living systems; some of them are hormones, chemical messengers that coordinate biochemical activities.

  1. Two molecules of glucose

  3. Two molecules of fructose
  4. No Reaction

  1. Sucrose is glucose and fructose joined through C1 of glucose and C2 of fructose.
  2. Acid hydrolysis gives one molecule of each: a 1:1 mixture.

Answer: option (2) — 1:1 mixture of Glucose and Fructose

TrapTwo glucoses come from maltose (or cellobiose), not sucrose.

Carbohydrates, formerly written Cx(H2O)y as “hydrates of carbon” (glucose C6H12O6 fits), are classified by their behaviour on hydrolysis: monosaccharides cannot be hydrolysed further (about 20 occur in nature), and polysaccharides give many monosaccharide units. Proteins are polymers of α-amino acids (with –NH2 and –COOH) joined by peptide bonds. When a native protein is subjected to a physical change its globules unfold, its helix uncoils and it loses its biological activity: it is denatured.

  1. Dextrorotatory Glucose and Laevorotatory Fructose

Answer: option (1) — Dextrorotatory Glucose and Laevorotatory Fructose

  1. A–I, B–II; the tertiary structure gives the overall fibrous or globular shape: C–IV; several chains together: D–III.

Answer: option (3) — (A) - (I), (B) - (II), (C) - (IV), (D) - (III)

Q1237CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Sets A–D · Set A Q5NTA final key
The correct structure of dipeptide, Gly-Ala (glycyl alanine) is

Q1241CUET 2024 · 29 May (pen & paper, 306 E New) · Book A · Q9NTA final key

Q1261CUET 2023 · 31 May, Shift 2 · Q2NTA final key

Watson and Crick proposed a double-strand helix for DNA: two nucleic acid chains wound about each other and held together by hydrogen bonds between pairs of bases.   2. So the order is phosphate – sugar – base.

Answer: option (1) — Phosphate - Sugar - base

Q1305CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q49NTA final key
Passage (2 Jul 2023, Q46–50): the DNA double helix

Watson and Crick proposed a double-strand helix for DNA: two nucleic acid chains wound about each other and held together by hydrogen bonds between pairs of bases. The strands are complementary because the hydrogen bonds form between specific base pairs: adenine with thymine, cytosine with guanine.

Nucleic acids have the coded message for the proteins to be sythesised in the cell. Protein synthesis takes place through a process known as:
  1. Transcription
  2. Translation
  3. Protonation
  4. Protination
Concept to recallDNA → mRNA is transcription; mRNA → protein (on ribosomes) is translation.
  1. The actual synthesis of the protein chain from the mRNA message is translation.

Answer: option (2) — Translation

TrapTranscription makes RNA, not protein.
Q1306CUET 2022 · 10 Aug, Shift 1 (SET 06) · Q33NTA final key

  1. Acid Behaviour

  3. Amphoteric Behaviour
  4. Neutral Behaviour
Concept to recallZwitterion H3N+–CHR–COO− carries an acidic group (–NH3+) and a basic group (–COO−).
  1. It can donate a proton (from NH3+) and accept one (on COO−) ⇒ amphoteric.

Answer: option (3) — Amphoteric Behaviour

  2. Maltose = α-D-glucose + α-D-glucose (C1–C4 link).

Answer: option (3) — Maltose

Q1308CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Sets A–D · Set A Q6NTA final key

Concept to recallIn fcc atoms touch along the face diagonal: 4r = √2 a ⇒ r = a/(2√2).

Q1309CUET 2024 · 29 May (pen & paper, 306 E New) · Book A · Q44NTA final key
Which among the following compounds show metal excess defect due to anionic vacancy ?

  2. NaCl
  3. FeO

Concept to recallMetal excess by anion vacancy: an anion site holds an electron (F-centre) — NaCl heated in Na vapour turns yellow. Metal excess by extra interstitial cations: ZnO. FeO is metal deficient.

  2. So NaCl shows metal excess through anionic vacancies.

Answer: option (2) — NaCl

TrapZnO is also metal-excess, but by interstitial Zn2+ ions, not anion vacancies.

Q1318CUET 2023 · 23 May, Shift 3 · Q38NTA final key

  1. p3

Q1396CUET 2023 · 10 Jun, Shift 1 · Prepp reconstruction · Q41key re-derived
Passage (summarised): adsorption

Adsorption arises because surface particles of the adsorbent are not in the same environment as particles in the bulk. Its extent increases with surface area per unit mass of adsorbent at a given temperature and pressure. Physisorption is due to van der Waals forces; in chemisorption real chemical bonds form. Easily liquefied gases are adsorbed more readily than gases that are hard to liquefy. Freundlich gave an empirical relation between the amount of gas adsorbed per unit mass of adsorbent and the pressure at a fixed temperature.

  4. log (x/m) vs log p

  1. Taking logs gives a straight line of log(x/m) against log p, slope 1/n, intercept log k.

Answer: option (4) — log (x/m) vs log p

Q1408CUET 2023 · 15 Jun, Shift 1 · Q31 · Prepp reconstructionkey re-derived
Coagulating power of an ion for a colloidal solution depends on:
  1. Its magnitude of charge only
  2. Its size only
  3. Its tendency to hydrate
  4. Its size and magnitude of charge both
Concept to recallHardy–Schulze: the greater the valence of the oppositely charged ion, the greater its coagulating power (Al3+ > Ba2+ > Na+ for a negative sol).
  1. Charge dominates: a trivalent ion coagulates hundreds of times more strongly than a monovalent one.
  2. For ions of equal charge, the smaller hydrated ion approaches the particle more closely and is more effective, so both matter.

Answer: option (4) — Its size and magnitude of charge both

NoteNot in the CUET 2026 syllabus. The Hardy–Schulze rule ties coagulating power to the charge (valence) of the ion; among ions of the same charge, size (hydration) also matters, which is why “size and magnitude of charge” is the complete answer Prepp gives.

Q1420CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q41NTA final key
Passage (2 Jul 2023, Q41–45): colloids

A colloid is a heterogeneous system in which one substance is dispersed as very fine particles in another, the dispersion medium. Colloids are classified by the physical states of the dispersed phase and medium, the interaction between them, and the type of particles. They are prepared by chemical methods, electrical disintegration (Bredig’s arc) and peptization. Freshly prepared sols contain excess electrolytes and other soluble impurities; reducing these to a minimum is purification, done by dialysis, electrodialysis, ultrafiltration, etc. Colligative properties, the Tyndall effect, colour, Brownian movement, charge on the particles, electrophoresis and coagulation are properties of colloidal solutions.

The formation of micelles takes place only above a particular temperature known as:
  1. Critical temperature
  2. Kraft temperature
  3. Critical micelle concentration
  4. Micelle temperature
Concept to recallAssociated colloids (soaps, detergents) form micelles only above the Kraft temperature (Tk) and above the critical micelle concentration (CMC).
  1. The temperature threshold is the Kraft temperature; the concentration threshold is the CMC.

Answer: option (2) — Kraft temperature

Q1465CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Sets A–D · Set A Q47NTA final key

  3. Total σ = 16.

Q1466CUET 2024 · 29 May (pen & paper, 306 E New) · Book A · Q5NTA final key
Why does Fluorine exhibit only –1 oxidation state ?
  1. It is a halogen.
  2. It is a non-metal.
  3. It is small in size.
  4. It has no d orbitals.
Concept to recallF is the most electronegative element and has no d orbitals in its valence shell, so it cannot expand its octet to show positive oxidation states.
  1. Other halogens (Cl, Br, I) show +1, +3, +5, +7 by promoting electrons into vacant d orbitals.

Q1499CUET 2023 · 5 June, Shift 1 · Q50 · Prepp reconstructionworked here
Which factors are responsible for making fluorine the strongest oxidising agent?
(A) Highest electronegativity
(B) High electron gain enthalpy
(C) High bond dissociation enthalpy
(D) Small size of fluorine
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (A), (B) and (D) only
  2. (B), (C) and (D) only
  3. (A), (C) and (D) only
  4. (B) and (C) only
Concept to recallF2 is the strongest oxidant because of its low F–F bond dissociation enthalpy and the very high hydration enthalpy of the small F− ion.
  1. (C) is false: the F–F bond is weak (low dissociation enthalpy, 158 kJ mol−1), which is one reason F2 reacts so readily.
  2. Every option except (1) contains (C), so (1) is the answer; (A), (B) and (D) are the factors usually listed with it.

Answer: option (1) — (A), (B) and (D) only

NoteNot in the CUET 2026 syllabus. Prepp’s key gives option (2), which includes “high bond dissociation enthalpy”. The F–F bond is unusually weak, so (C) is false and option (1) is the only one without it. (Strictly, chlorine has the more negative electron gain enthalpy; (B) is loosely worded.)
Q1500CUET 2023 · 07 Jun, Shift 3 · Prepp reconstruction · Q47key re-derived
Passage (summarised): anomalous behaviour of nitrogen

Nitrogen differs from the rest of Group 15 because of its small size, high electronegativity, high ionisation enthalpy and the absence of d orbitals. It forms pπ–pπ multiple bonds with itself and with other small, electronegative atoms such as C and O. The heavier members do not form pπ–pπ bonds, because their larger, diffuse orbitals cannot overlap effectively.

Maximum covalency of Nitrogen is:
  1. 2
  2. 3
  3. 4
  4. 5
Concept to recallNitrogen has only four valence orbitals (2s, 2p) and no d orbitals, so its covalency cannot exceed 4 (as in NH4+).
  1. Without d orbitals N can use at most 4 orbitals: maximum covalency 4.

Answer: option (3) — 4

NoteNot in the CUET 2026 syllabus.

Passage (summarised): Groups 15 to 18

Group 15 (nitrogen family): nitrogen forms NH3, HNO3, N2O, NO2 and others; phosphorus exists as white and red forms, white phosphorus glows in the dark, and PH3 is used in smoke screens. Group 16: dry air is 21 % O2 by volume; combined sulphur occurs as sulphates such as gypsum, Epsom salt and baryte; sulphur has rhombic and monoclinic allotropes, and S2, paramagnetic like O2, is the form stable at high temperature. Group 17: F2 is highly reactive, Cl2 is a greenish-yellow gas, and both SO2 and Cl2 bleach. Group 18: some noble gases form compounds; complete hydrolysis of XeF6 gives HF and XeO3.

At elevated temperature (~1000 K) the dominant form of sulphur is:
  1. Rhombic sulphur
  2. Monoclinic sulphur
  3. S8 molecules
  4. S2
Concept to recallAt ~1000 K sulphur vapour is mainly S2, which is paramagnetic like O2.
  1. The passage itself says S2 is the form stable at high temperature.

Answer: option (4) — S2

Q1531CUET 2023 · 20 Jun, Shift 3 · Q18NTA final key

  1. Aspartame is unstable on heating, so it is limited to cold foods and soft drinks.
  2. Sucralose and saccharin are heat-stable.

Answer: option (3) — Aspartame
